(p-94) Surah al-Nahl (The Bee) is Meccan, except from "And if you punish..." to its end. It has one hundred and twenty-eight verses.

﴿The command of Allah has come.﴾ That is, the Hour, or what encompasses it and other than it from the punishment promised to the disbelievers. He expressed it as "the command of Allah" to magnify and to inspire awe, and to signal that its realization in itself, and its coming, depend on His effective decree and His overpowering judgment. Its "coming" is an expression for its drawing near and approaching, in the manner of presenting what is expected as already occurring, or an expression for the coming of its near beginnings, following the mode of attributing the state of causes to their effects. Whichever is meant, it indicates the complete nearness of its occurrence and its immediacy, and it completes the fitting placement of the consequence in His words, mighty and majestic: ﴿So do not hasten it﴾. The prohibition against hastening a thing, although it is valid to make it a consequence of its near occurrence or of the occurrence of its near causes, is not on the same footing as making it a consequence of its occurrence, since with its actual occurrence hastening becomes entirely impossible, not merely by what has been mentioned of its nearness and the occurrence of its beginnings. The address is specifically to the disbelievers, as the reading in the form of the third-person prohibition indicates, and their hastening. Although it was in the manner of mockery, it was taken literally, and they were forbidden from it with a kind of scorn, not together with the believers. This holds whether by "the command of Allah" is meant what has been mentioned, or the punishment promised specifically to the disbelievers. As for the first: it is inconceivable that the believers would hasten the Hour, or what encompasses it and other than it of punishment, such that the prohibition would include them. As for the second: their hastening of it is in the literal sense, while the hastening of the disbelievers is in the manner of mockery, as you have understood. So a single form does not comprehend both, and resorting to intending a figurative meaning that includes both together, without there being some hidden purpose observed, is a contrivance that does not befit the glorious revelation. As for what is narrated, that when ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ was revealed, the disbelievers said among themselves: "This man claims that the Resurrection has drawn near, so let us refrain from some of what we do until we see what will happen." When it was delayed, they said: "We see nothing." Then ﴿The nearness has come upon mankind of their reckoning﴾ was revealed, so they became apprehensive and awaited its nearness. When the days lengthened, they said: "O Muhammad, we see nothing of what you threaten us with." Then ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) leapt up, and the people raised their heads. When ﴿So do not hasten it﴾ was revealed, they were reassured. There is in this no indication of the generality of the address, as has been said, not because it is thought that the initial "fa" (so) rejects it, for it is far from rejecting it as you have verified, but because the basis of their reassurance was their recognition that by the "coming" is meant the claimed coming, not the actual coming that necessitates [the event]; since hastening is impossible, and the prohibition against it entails that its occurrence is impossible, because the prohibition against a thing requires that it be possible in some respect. The basis of that recognition is only the prohibition against hastening, which entails its possibility, which requires that what is hastened has not yet occurred. This does not differ according to the difference of the one who hastens, whoever he may be. Rather, there is in it clear indication of the absence of generality (p-95), because what is meant by the command of Allah is only the Hour, and you have known the impossibility of its hastening proceeding from the believers. Yes, it is permissible to restrict the address to them on the supposition that the command of Allah is an expression for the punishment promised specifically to the disbelievers, but what the inimitable revelation requires is that it is specific to the disbelievers, as you will see. Since their hastening of that was among the results of their polytheism, which entails attributing to Allah, mighty and majestic, what is unfitting for Him, such as incapacity and need of another, and believing that someone might restrain Him from fulfilling His promise and executing His threat, and since they had said within this, "If the punishment comes, then the idols will deliver us from it by their intercession," this was refuted, and it was said by way of resumption: ﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ That is: He is exalted and sanctified in His essence, and far above their polytheism that leads to the emergence of such falsehoods from them, or above having a partner who would repel what He intends for them in any manner. The form of the present tense indicates the renewal and continuance of their polytheism. The shift to the third person indicates that mentioning their abominations calls for turning away from them, casting them out of the rank of direct address, and relating their atrocities to others. On the supposition that the address is restricted to the believers, this nuance would be lost, just as the connection between what is prohibited and the One who is exalted above it would be lost. It was also read in the form of the second-person address.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 2:

﴿He sends down the angels﴾ is an explanation of the necessity of monotheism (tawhid), as was alluded to in a general way by showing the sanctity of the Majesty and His exaltation above anything that could approach the notion of His being associated with anything in anything. It also announces that this is a religion upon which the majority of the prophets, peace be upon them, agreed, and they were commanded to call people to it. It further points to the secret of the suddenness (of the Hour) and to the legislation. The manner of the delivery of revelation and of drawing attention to it is by way of the Messenger's ﷺ knowledge of the coming of what He had promised them, and of its nearness, in order to remove their improbable notion that this knowledge was specific to him, peace be upon him, and to demonstrate the falsity of their view regarding hastening (the punishment) and denial. The use of the present tense form is to indicate that this is a continuous custom of His, glory be to Him. As for "the angels," the intended meaning is either Jibril, peace be upon him. Al-Wahidi said: a single individual may be referred to by the plural when he is a chief, or it means him and those with him from the guardians of revelation, by the command of God, exalted is He.

It was also read as (yunzilu) from (al-inzal), and as (tunazzalu) with one of the two tas dropped, and in the passive form from (al-tanzil). ﴿with the Spirit﴾ means: with the revelation, of which the Qur'an is a part, by way of metaphor, for it gives life to hearts that are dead through ignorance, or it takes the place in religion that the spirit takes in the body. The preposition (bi) is connected either to the verb or to what is a circumstantial element (hal) of its object, i.e., they are invested with the Spirit. ﴿from His command﴾ is an explanation of the Spirit, which here refers to revelation, for it is a command to good; or it is a circumstantial element of it, i.e., while it is originating and emanating from Him; or it is an attribute of it according to the view of those who permit the omission of the relative pronoun together with part of its clause, i.e., with the Spirit that exists from His command, arising from Him. Or it is connected to (yunazzilu), and (min) is causal, like (bi), similar to (ma) in His saying, exalted is He, "because of their errors" (mimma khati'atihim), i.e., He sends them down by His command.

﴿upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾, that He send them down with it upon them, because of their being distinguished by attributes that qualify them for that. ﴿that warn﴾ is a substitute for the Spirit, i.e., He sends them down invested with (an) warn, i.e., with this statement. Those addressed by it are the prophets upon whom the angels descended, and the one who commands is God, glory be to Him, while the angels are carriers of the command, as the preposition (bi) in the substituted noun indicates. The (an) here is either a lightened form of (anna), whose subject pronoun, the pronoun of the matter (dhamir al-sha'n), is omitted, i.e., He sends them down invested with the fact that I say to you: warn! Or it is explanatory (mufassira), on the basis that the sending down of the angels with revelation includes the sense of saying, as if it were said: He says through the angels to whomever of His servants He wills: warn! So it has no place in the grammatical structure. Or it is verbal (masdariyya), because its relative clause may be imperative in form, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [commanded]: establish your face﴾, as was mentioned at the beginning of Surah Hud. Its place is then also in the genitive by way of substitution. Warning (al-indhar) is informing, except that it is specifically about informing of something to be feared, from (nadhara bi al-shay') when one knows a thing and beware of it, and (andhara bihi al-amr indharan) meaning he informed him, warned him, and frightened him in conveying it, as stated in the Qamus, i.e., inform the people ﴿that there is no god except Me﴾. The pronoun here refers to the matter, and the reason for placing it in that position is the claim of its being so well known that it dispenses with stating it explicitly. The benefit of opening the sentence with it is to signal from the outset the grandeur of its content, together with the additional firm establishment of it in the mind. For the pronoun, at first, conveys nothing except an unspecified matter of importance, so the mind remains expectant of what follows, and when it arrives it becomes firmly established there to a greater degree. It is as if it were said: warn that this momentous matter is the following. The announcement of its content regarding what is to be feared is not for its own sake, but from the standpoint of the warned ones' being characterized by what is contrary to it, namely associating partners with God, and that suffices for making its announcement a warning. His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿So fear Me﴾ is an address to those who hasten (the punishment), in the manner of the shift of person (iltifat), and the (fa') is explanatory (fasiha), i.e., when the matter is as mentioned, namely the continuation of His custom, exalted is He, of sending down the angels upon the prophets, peace be upon them, and commanding them to warn people that He has no partner in divinity, then fear Me by failing to uphold its content, and by engaging in what contradicts it, namely association, and its branches, among which is hastening (the punishment) and mockery.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 3:

After the establishment of the proof from revelation (al-dalil al-sam'i) for Tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), he began to set out the rational proofs (al-adilla al-'aqliyya), so it is said: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾

﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾ meaning: He brought them into being in the state in which they are, in their excellent form and their fitting arrangement. ﴿Exalted﴾ and sanctified is He in His essence, especially in His acts, among which is the origination of these two created things. ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾ above their well-known association (of partners with Him), or above the partnership of what they ascribe to Him of falsehood, which neither originates nor restores.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 4:

After having drawn attention to His comprehensive creative act, which encompasses the details of His creatures, he began to enumerate what is in them of His creations, so he began with His act concerning the souls, and said:

﴿He created man from a drop of sperm; then behold, he is an open adversary.﴾

﴿He created man﴾ — i.e., this species, other than its first individual ﴿from a drop of sperm﴾, an inanimate substance without sensation or movement, fluid, that retains neither shape nor form.

﴿Then behold, he is﴾, after creation, ﴿an adversary﴾, eloquent and disputatious, contending on his own behalf, combating opponents, ﴿open﴾, clear in his argument and skilled in it. This is more fitting to the context of bestowing favor, by giving him the capacity to reason through this to the power and oneness of God, Exalted is He. Or [he is] a contender against his Creator, denying Him, saying, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?" This is more fitting to the context of enumerating the blunders of the disbelievers.

It is narrated that Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a decayed bone and said: "O Muhammad, do you think God, Exalted is He, will give life to this after it has decayed?" Then it was revealed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 5:

﴿And the cattle (al-an'am)﴾: these are the eight pairs (al-azwaj al-thamaniyah) of camels, cattle, sheep and goats. Its being in the accusative (intisab) is by means of an implied verb (bi-mudmar) which is explained by His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿He created them﴾; or it is by coordination (bi-al-'atf) with "man" (al-insan), and what follows it is an explanation of that for which it was created, and what comes after it is a detailing of that. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for you﴾ is either attached (muta'alliq) to "created them", and His saying: ﴿in them﴾ is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and His saying: ﴿warmth (dif')﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and it is that with which one is warmed, so it protects from the cold. And the clause is a circumstantial (hal) of the object. Or the first adverbial phrase (al-zarf al-awwal) is the predicate of the aforementioned subject, and "in them" is a circumstantial of "warmth", for if it were delayed it would be a qualifier (sifah). ﴿And benefits (manafi')﴾ are their milk, their riding, their carrying, tilling with them, and other than that. He expressed it with "them" (biha) so that it would encompass all of this, although it is the more fitting for the context of bestowing favors (maqam al-imtinan bi-al-ni'am). And the placing of "warmth" before "benefits" is in observance of the style of ascending to the higher. ﴿And from them you eat﴾: i.e., you eat what is eaten from them of meats, fats and other things. The change in arrangement (taghyir al-nazm) is to indicate that they do not remain when eaten, as in what precedes and what follows, for warmth, benefits and beauty are obtained from them while they remain in their state, and for this reason they were made places (mahall) for these, unlike eating. And the fronting of the adverbial phrase (taqdim al-zarf) is to announce that eating from them is the customary and principal means of livelihood (al-ma'ash), because eating from other than them, such as chickens, ducks, and game of land and sea, belongs to the category of enjoyment (al-tafakkuh). Together with this there is observance of the fawasil (verse endings). It is also possible that the meaning of "eating from them" is eating what is obtained by means of them, for the grains and fruits that are eaten are acquired by hiring out camels, by the increase of their offspring, and by their milk and hides.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 6:**

﴿And for you in them﴾ — along with the various kinds of essential benefits that have been detailed — ﴿is beauty﴾, meaning adornment in the eyes of people and prestige in their sight, ﴿when you bring them home﴾, i.e., you return them from their pasturing grounds to their resting place (*marah*) in the evening, ﴿and when you send them out﴾, i.e., you lead them out in the morning from their pens (*hazair*) to their grazing grounds (*masarih*). The object is omitted from both verbs for the sake of preserving the rhyme (*fawasil*, the rhymed endings of verses). The specifying of these two times is because what the matter of beauty revolves around — the adorning of courtyards and their surroundings with them, and the echoing of their lowing and bleating — occurs only at their coming and going during these two times. As for when they are in the pastures, their sensory attribution to their owners is cut off, and when they are in the pens no observer sees them or looks upon them. The mention of bringing home before sending out is due to the precedence of arrival over departure, and because it is more evident in producing the beauty mentioned, and more complete in bringing about delight and pleasure, since in it there is presence after absence and approach after withdrawal, in the best state, with bellies full and udders raised.

It was also read: (*hinan turihunna*) and (*hinan tasrahuna*), with both verbs being descriptive of *hinan* (a period of time), meaning: "you bring them home during it" and "you send them out during it."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 7:

﴿And they carry your loads﴾ is the plural of thiql (ثَقَل), which is the belongings of the traveller (matā' al-musāfir). It is also said: athqālukum means your bodies (ajrāmukum).

﴿To a land﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: it refers to Yemen, Egypt, and Syria. Perhaps he considered that these are the trading places of the people of Makkah. 'Ikrimah said: it refers to Makkah. Perhaps he considered that their loads and burdens on the return journey from their trade are greater, and their need for beasts of burden is more pressing. The apparent meaning is that it is general, applying to every distant land.

﴿You would not have been able to reach it﴾ arrival there, reaching it by yourselves, stripped of the loads, were it not for the camels.

﴿Except with great hardship to yourselves﴾ let alone taking your loads along with you. It is also read with a fatha on the shin (شِقّ / شَقّ), and both are two dialects (lughatān), meaning hardship and difficulty. It is also said that the one with fatha is a verbal noun from shaqqa al-amr 'alayhi shaqqan (it was hard upon him), and its real meaning goes back to the shaqq (شَقّ), which is the split, while the one with kasra means half. As if he loses half his strength due to the exertion he encounters. The attribution to "the souls" (al-anfus) is then figurative, or there is an elided noun, i.e., "except with the shaqq of the powers of the souls." This is an exceptive construction of the incomplete type (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of things, i.e., you would not have been able to reach it by anything except with the shaqq of the souls. Perhaps the change of the preceding noble structure, which indicates that the cattle are the source of the previous blessings, to the verbal sentence which conveys mere occurrence, is to indicate that this blessing is not general in terms of its origin and its object, and in terms of encompassing all times and the regular occurrence at the customary times, in the manner of the earlier blessings. For in terms of its origin it is specific to camels, and in terms of its object it concerns those who travel through the land, moving about in it for trade and other purposes, at times that are not regular. As for the rest of the enumerated blessings, they exist in all kinds of livestock and are general to all the addressees always, or at all times.

﴿Indeed your Lord is Kind and Merciful﴾ and for this reason He has bestowed upon you these magnificent blessings and made the arduous matters easy for you.

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 8:

﴿And the horses, and the mules, and the donkeys, that you may ride them﴾ "al-khayl" (horses) is a collective noun (ism jins) for the horse, having no singular form derived from its own word, like "al-ibil" (camels). It is conjoined (ʿatf) to "al-anʿam" (the cattle), meaning: He created the horses, the mules and the donkeys ﴿that you may ride them﴾, which is a causal clause (ta'lil) stating its principal benefit; otherwise, benefiting from them by carrying loads is also undoubtedly real. ﴿and as an adornment﴾ is conjoined to the position (mahall) of "li-tarkabuha" (that you may ride them). Its being stripped of the preposition "li-" (for/that) is because it is an act of the agent of the causal clause and not of the first, and its being placed later is because riding is more important than it. Or it is a verbal noun (masdar) of an omitted verb, meaning: "and you adorn yourselves with them as an adornment." It is also read without the conjunction "wa", meaning: He created them as an adornment, that you may ride them. It may also be a verbal noun standing in the position of a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of "tarkabuha" or its object, meaning: adorning yourselves with them, or they being adorned with them.

﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾ meaning: He creates in this world other than what has been enumerated of the kinds of blessings for you and for your benefit, which you do not know the essence of nor the manner of its creation. The shift to the future form (istiqbal) indicates continuity and renewal, or to bring the scene vividly to mind. Or He creates for you in Paradise, other than the worldly blessings mentioned, what you do not know, meaning what it is not within your capacity to know. This is what was alluded to by the Prophet (ﷺ) relating from Allah, the Exalted: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." It is also possible that this is an announcement that He, glorified is He, creates among creatures what we have no knowledge of, as a proof of His dazzling power which necessitates monotheism, like His inner and outer blessings.

Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) reported: that to the right of the Throne there is a river of light, as large as the seven heavens, the seven earths and the seven seas. Jibril (peace be upon him) enters it every dawn and bathes, and he increases in light upon light, beauty upon beauty, and greatness upon greatness. Then he shakes himself, and Allah, the Exalted, creates from every drop that falls from his feathers so-and-so thousands of angels. Of them, seventy thousand enter the Bayt al-Ma'mur every day, and seventy thousand enter the Ka'bah, and they do not return to it until the Day of Resurrection.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 9:**

﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the path﴾. Al-qasd is a verbal noun (masdar) used in the sense of the active participle. It is said: sabil qasd wa qasid, meaning "straight." This is by way of metaphor, or by way of attributing to the path the state of the one who travels it, as if it "aims at" the way that the traveler intends and does not deviate from it. That is, it is binding upon Him, glorified and exalted, by the requirement of His mercy and His inevitable promise, to explain the straight path that leads whoever follows it to the truth, which is monotheism (tawhid). He does this by setting up proofs, sending the messengers, and sending down the scriptures to call people to it. Or it is a masdar meaning "establishing" and "making upright" (al-ta'dil), as Abu al-Baqa' said. That is, it is upon Him, mighty and majestic, to make it upright and to balance it, that is, to make it such that whoever travels it reaches the truth, but not after it had been in itself deviating from it. Rather, its origination from the beginning is in this manner, in the line of his saying: "Glory be to the One who made the mosquito small and the elephant large." Its reality returns to what was mentioned of setting up proofs, and He has done that, in that He originated these marvels, each one of which is (p-99) a clear road guided by its beacon, and a sign illuminated by its fire. He also sent messengers as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down to them scriptures, among which is this revelation that speaks the reality of the truth, examining every secret, great or subtle, guiding to the way of reasoning by those proofs that lead to the landmarks of guidance, removing one from the wastelands of misguidance and the precipices of perdition. Do you not see how He first clarified the transcendence of the majesty of His presence and His exaltedness, in essence, above any trace that could suggest association (shirk) coming near Him? Then He clarified the secret of sending down revelation to the prophets, peace be upon them, and the manner of commanding them to warn the people, call them to monotheism, and forbid them from associating partners with Him. Then He returned to clarifying His exaltedness above that, in terms of actions, guiding to the method of reasoning. He began with His action concerning the center and circumference of the physical world, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth; exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾. Then He detailed His actions related to what lies between them, beginning with His action concerning the selves of those addressed, then mentioned what is related to what they must have in their livelihoods, then clarified His power to create what the knowledge of humans does not encompass, by His saying: "﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾." All of that, as you see, is a clarification of the way of monotheism after a clarification, and an upright balancing of it in the fullest sense. So the meaning of "the path" in the first interpretation is the genus (jins), as is shown by the attribution of the direction (qasd) to it. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and among them﴾, is in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), either with regard to its content, or by way of an implied described noun, as in His saying, exalted is He: "and among us are those below that." This has already been discussed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among the people are those who say: We believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, and so on. That is, some of the path, or some of the path. For it is both feminine and masculine in form.

﴿deviating﴾, that is, inclining away from the truth, turning aside from it, not leading its traveler to it. These are the roads of misguidance, whose number cannot nearly be counted, all of which fall under "the deviating." In the second interpretation, it is the straight path itself, and the pronoun in "among them" refers back to it, with an implied noun, that is, "and of its genus," because of what you have come to know: that the balancing and making upright of the path is its origination from the beginning in the manner of uprightness and justice, not its making upright after its deviation. In any case, there is nothing in the noble text of a change of style (iltifat) for the sake of some desired matter, as has been said. For that happens only where the apparent arrangement requires a specific structure. Rather, one departs from that for a purpose more important than it, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Who feeds me and gives me drink﴾, ﴿and when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾. For the apparent requirement would be to say: "Who makes me ill and cures me." But it was changed to what the noble text has, to avoid attributing to Him, glorified is He, what the soul dislikes. The purpose of stating the direction of the path is not merely to inform that it is straight, such that attributing deviation to it would be correct and would require an excuse for its absence. Moreover, even if that were intended, there would be no purpose for changing the style. This has been explained in countless places. Rather, the purpose is the setting up of proofs mentioned earlier, to guide people to Him. It is not possible to attribute something of that kind to Him, exalted is He, with regard to the deviating road, such that one would say: "and its deviator," and then the composition of the structure be changed from that for a stronger reason. Rather, the phrase "and among them the deviating" is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradiyya), brought in to show the need for clarification and balancing, and to display the grandeur of the blessing in that. The meaning is: upon Allah, exalted is He, is the clarification of the straight path that leads to the truth, and its balancing by what was mentioned, namely the setting up of proofs, so that people may travel it by their own choice and reach the goal. This is the guidance explained as indicating what leads to the desired end, not the guidance that necessarily entails actual being guided, for that is not binding upon Allah, exalted is He, neither by His essence nor by His mercy. Rather, it would contradict His wisdom, since it would require equating the doer of good and the doer of evil, the obedient and the disobedient, according to their readiness. To this He alluded by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had He willed, He would have guided you all﴾. That is, had He willed to guide you to what was mentioned of monotheism with a guidance that definitely leads to it and necessarily entails that you all are guided, He would have done so. But He did not will it, because His will follows wisdom, which calls for it, and there is no wisdom in such a will, since that upon which the orbit of moral responsibility (taklif) turns, and to which reward and punishment are attached, is only partial choice (al-ikhtiyar al-juz'i), upon which the actions by which recompense is attached are based. This is what the context requires and what the good ordering of the composition demands. The statement that the direction of the path is upon Him, exalted is He, has been interpreted as meaning that it ends with Him, in the manner of uprightness. The use of the particle of elevation ('ala, "upon") instead of the particle of ending (ila, "to") is to emphasize uprightness in a figurative way, without there being any elevation of something over Him, glorified is He, exalted far above that, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is a straight path﴾. So "al-qasd" is a masdar in the sense of the active participle. The intended "path" is the genus, as already explained. His saying, exalted is He, "and among them the deviating," is conjoined to the first sentence, and the meaning is that the direction of the path reaches Him by uprightness, while some of it deviates from Him. Had He willed, He would have guided you all to the first. You know that this is true in itself, but it has no connection to any purpose that would justify placing it between the arguments for monotheism that came before and what follows. And since the scriptural way to monotheism was clarified in a general manner, and some of its proofs related to the conditions of animals were detailed, and this was followed by clarifying the underlying secret for it, as a stimulus for the addressees to reflect on what came before, and as an incitement to receive well what follows, there was added after that the mention of what indicates it from the conditions of plants, and so it was said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 10:

﴿He it is Who sends down﴾ by His overpowering power, ﴿from the sky﴾, that is, from the clouds, or from the direction of the sky, ﴿water﴾, that is, a kind of it, which is rain. Its being placed after the prepositional phrase is due to what has passed many times, that the intended meaning is the information that He sent down from the sky something that is water, not that He sent it down from the sky. The secret in this is what has preceded, that when something that by right should be placed first is delayed, the mind remains awaiting it and longing for it, so that when it arrives it settles there with far greater firmness.

﴿For you there is from it a drink﴾, that is, that which you drink. It (i.e., "a drink") is either raised by the first adverbial phrase, or is a subject (mubtada'), with "huwa" (it) as its predicate. The clause is a qualifier of "water". The second adverbial phrase is put in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl) from "sharāb" (drink), and "min" is partitive (tab'īḍiyyah). There is no implication in placing it first that the drink is restricted to it, such that one would need to excuse it by saying there is no harm in it, because the waters of springs and wells are also from it, according to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So He caused it to flow as springs in the earth﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We made it settle in the earth﴾. It has also been said: the first adverbial phrase is connected to "anzala" (sent down), and the second is the predicate of "sharāb". The clause is a qualifier of "water". You know well that what this contains of inserting the accusative between the two prepositional phrases, and inserting the second of them between the water and its qualifier, is not becoming to the eloquence of the arrangement of the sublime revelation.

﴿And from it is trees﴾: "min" here is inceptive (ibtidā'iyyah), i.e., from it there comes into being trees on which the livestock graze, and what is meant by it is whatever grows from the earth, whether it has a stalk or not. Or it is partitive metaphorically, because when its irrigation was from the water, it was made as if it were from it, like the saying: "the humps of the camels in its rain (rabāb)", meaning by it the rain by which the pasture grows that the camels eat, so that their humps become fat. And in the hadith of 'Ikrimah: "Do not eat the price of trees, for it is unlawful gain (suḥt)", meaning: the pasture.

﴿In it you pasture [your livestock]﴾: "tusīmūn" means you graze, from "sāmat al-māshiyah" (the livestock grazed) and "aṣāmahā ṣāḥibuhā" (its owner sent it to graze), and its root is "al-sawmah", which is the mark, because it leaves marks upon the earth by grazing.

﴿Yunbitu﴾ (He causes to grow): that is, Allah, exalted and majestic is He. It is also read with the nun (﴿Nunbitu﴾).

﴿Lakum bihi﴾ (for you by it): by means of what He sent down from the sky.

﴿Al-zar'a wa al-zaytūna wa al-nakhīla wa al-a'nāba﴾ (the crops, the olives, the date palms, and the grapes): an explanation of the bounties poured out upon them from the earth, by way of resumption (isti'nāf, a new sentence that resumes the discourse). The choice of the present tense (ṣīghat al-istiqbāl) indicates renewal and continuity, and that this is His constant custom throughout the ages. Or it is to bring to mind the image of growth. The placing of the two adverbial phrases (al-ẓarfayn) before the direct object is for what has passed just before, together with the concern for them that comes from first bringing in the pleasure. The crops are placed before the rest because they are the root of foods and the pillar of livelihood. The olive is placed forward for the nobility it possesses, in that it is a condiment from one aspect and a fruit from another. The date palm is placed before the grape for the evident primacy and permanence of its roots. The grapes are put in the plural to point to the various kinds it contains. The specific mention of these named kinds, though they are included under His saying ﴿And of all the fruits﴾, serves to draw attention to their excellence. The trees are placed before them, although they are fodder for livestock, because they come about without human effort. Or it is to guide toward noble character, for its requirement is that a person's concern for what is under his hand should be greater than his concern for himself. Or because most of those addressed are owners of livestock who have no crops or fruit. It has also been said: the intent is to place first what is pastured (the livestock), not to place first its food, since it is an animal food for humans, and it is the most noble of foods.

It is also read as (yanbutu) from the triliteral form, with the subject being the crops and what is joined to them.

﴿Inna fī dhālika﴾ (Indeed, in that): that is, in the sending down of water and the growing of what has been detailed, ﴿la-āyatan﴾ (is a sign), a great one, indicating His singularity in divinity, because it comprises the perfection of knowledge, power, and wisdom, ﴿li-qawmin yatafakkarūn﴾ (for a people who reflect). For whoever reflects on how the seed or the pit falls into the earth, and moisture reaches it and penetrates it, so that its lower part splits, and roots emerge from it spreading into the depths of the earth, and its upper part splits, even though it was upside down at its falling, and a stalk emerges from it and grows, and leaves, blossoms, grains and fruits emerge from it, comprising bodies of differing shapes, colors, properties and natures, and a seed capable of producing its like in the same pattern without end, while the materials are united and the relation of the lower natures and the upper influences is equal to all of them, he knows that One whose acts and effects are such cannot have anything resembling Him in any of the attributes of perfection, much less share with Him the least of things in His most specific attribute, which is divinity and the entitlement to worship. Exalted is He above that, to a great height. And since the pursuit of this path requires arranging intellectual premises, the noble verse ends with "reflect" (al-tafakkur).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 12:

﴿And He subjected to you the night and the day﴾, succeeding one another in alternation, for your sleep and your livelihood, and for the setting and ripening of fruits. ﴿And the sun and the moon﴾ continue diligently in their courses and in their light, both primarily and in succession, and in their regulating of what their well-being depends upon among the created beings, of which are those things that were detailed and those that were summarized. All of that is for your benefits and your advantages.

The meaning of their being subjected for you is not that you are empowered to dispose of them however you wish, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿Glory be to Him who subjected this to us﴾ and its like. Rather, it is His Exalted disposing of them in whatever manner their benefits and advantages result from. It is as if that is a subjection for them, and a disposal on their part according to their will. The expression of that disposal as subjection indicates the difficulty of handling the subjected things relative to the addressees. The choice of the past tense form indicates that this is one continuous matter, even though its effects are renewed. ﴿And the stars are subjected by His command﴾: it is a subject and predicate, meaning that all the stars, in (p-102) their movements and their configurations, such as trine and quadrature and the like, are subjected to God Exalted, or to that for which they were created, by His will and His purpose. Since the return of the benefits of the stars to them is not as evident as that of the two luminaries and the two moons mentioned before, their subjection was not attributed to them with the particle of specification; rather it was mentioned in a manner that indicates that they are under His Exalted dominion without indication of anything else. For this reason, one turned away from the verbal sentence, which indicates occurrence, to the nominal sentence, which indicates permanence and continuity.

It was also read: with the nominative for "the sun and the moon" too. And it was read: with the accusative for "(the stars)", as the first object of an implied verb indicated by the mentioned verb, and "(subjected)" is its second object. That is: and He made the stars subjected by His command. Or it is coordinated with the preceding accusatives. "Subjected" is a circumstantial state of all of them, and the governing element is what is in "subjected" of the meaning of "benefited", that is: He benefited you through them in a state where they are subjected to God, who created them and arranged them as He wills; or for that for which they were created by His bringing them into being and His decree; or for His judgment; or it is a verbal noun of the mimi type, pluralized because of the difference of kinds, that is: kinds of subjection. As for what has been said, that in it there is an announcement of the answer to what might be said: that the influence in the formation of plants is the movements of the stars and their configurations, to which it is answered: that even if this is granted, there is no doubt that these are also matters whose essence and attributes are possible, and that they fall upon some of the possible modes; therefore they necessarily require a specifying, chooser, necessarily existent originator, in order to avert circularity and infinite regress. Its foundation is the reckoning of what has been mentioned as proofs for the existence of the Creator, Exalted is He, and His power and His choice. And you know that the matter is not thus, for it is not something the opponent disputes, nor does he hesitate in accepting it. God Exalted said: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon, they would surely say: God. Then how are they turned away?﴾ And God Exalted said: ﴿And if you asked them who sends down water from the sky, and with it revives the earth after its death, they would surely say: God﴾ ... the verse. Those are only proofs of tawhid, in that one whose matter is such is not imagined to have anything share with Him in anything, let alone that inanimate matter should share with Him in divinity. ﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is: in what has been mentioned of subjection, related to what has been mentioned, summarily and in detail, ﴿are signs﴾, manifest and abundant, ﴿for a people who reason﴾. And since these heavenly effects are multiple, and the indication of what is in them of great power, knowledge and wisdom toward oneness is more apparent, the word "signs" was made plural, and it was tied to mere reason without need for contemplation and reflection. It is permissible that the meaning be: for a people who understand that; so the referent then is the marvels of the subtle details deposited in the heavenly matters, indicated by the subjection, which only the skilled masters among the pillars of the scholars of wisdom undertake to know. And there is no doubt that their need for reflection is greater.

﴿Wa-ma dhara'a﴾ (and what He created) is conjunctive (ʿaṭf) with His words, exalted is He, "and the stars" (al-nujūm), in both the nominative and accusative cases, as its object (mafʿūl) governed by "jaʿala" (He made), meaning: "and what He created."

﴿Lakum fī al-arḍi﴾ (for you on the earth) of animals and plants, while it is ﴿mukhtalifan alwānuhu﴾ (of diverse colours), meaning its kinds (aṣnāf). Their difference is generally by difference in colour, subjected (musakhkhar) to God, exalted is He, or to what they were created for of properties (khawāṣṣ), states (aḥwāl) and qualities (kayfiyyāt). Or that was made of diverse colours, meaning kinds, so that you may enjoy from them whichever kind you wish. It has been conjoined to what precedes it of the accusative objects, and it was objected that mentioning their creation for you makes mentioning their subjection unnecessary. It was answered that the first does not necessarily entail the second by rational necessity, since what was created for you may be of noble aim and difficult attainment.

It was said: it is governed by a verb implied (muqaddar), meaning: He created and caused to grow, with His words "mukhtalifan alwānuhu" being a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of its object.

﴿Inna fī dhālika﴾ (indeed in that), which was mentioned of subjections and the like, ﴿la-āyatan﴾ (is surely a sign) clear in its indication that whoever has this characteristic is one, having no peer and no opposite. ﴿Li-qawmin yadhdhakkarūn﴾ (for a people who reflect), for that does not need anything beyond recalling what might be overlooked of the necessary (ḍarūriyya) sciences. As for what is said, that their difference in natures, forms and appearances is nothing but the work of a wise Maker, its basis is what we have hinted at, namely reckoning what was mentioned as evidence for establishing the Maker, exalted is He. You have known the reality of the matter, for the presentation of what indicates His, glory be to Him, being described by what was mentioned of attributes of perfection is not by way of inference (istidlāl) to Him, but rather from premises already accepted; it was brought forward to infer from it what necessarily requires His oneness, exalted is He, and the impossibility that anything should share with Him in divinity.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 14:

﴿And it is He who subjected the sea﴾ This begins the enumeration of the blessings connected with the sea, following the detailed account of the blessings connected with the land, both animal and plant. That is: He made it such that you are able to benefit from it by riding upon it, diving into it, and hunting in it.

﴿that you may eat from it fresh flesh﴾ This refers to fish. The expression "flesh" (laḥm) is used for it even though it is an animal, to hint that its benefit is confined to eating. Describing it as "fresh" (ṭarī) indicates its delicacy and alerts to the necessity of hastening to eat it, lest decay quickly overtake it, as is indicated by the sea being made the subject of the verb "eat" (the sentence structure of "from it" placed first). It also signals the perfection of God's power, may He be exalted, in creating from salty water something sweet and fresh. Based on the application of the term "flesh" to it, Malik and al-Thawri held that whoever swears not to eat meat breaks his oath by eating it. The answer is that oaths are based on custom ('urf), and there is no doubt that "flesh," when used without qualification, is not understood as referring to fish. For this reason, if someone instructs his servant to buy meat and he brings fish, he has not carried out the order. Do you not see that God, may He be exalted, called the disbeliever a beast (dābba) when He said: ﴿Indeed, the worst of beasts in the sight of God are those who disbelieve﴾? And one who swears not to ride a beast does not break his oath by riding it.

﴿and that you may extract from it ornaments﴾ such as pearls and coral ﴿which you wear.﴾ In a context of favour, He expressed the women's wearing of them as the men's wearing, since they are part of them, or because their wearing is for their sake.

﴿And you see the ships﴾, meaning the vessels, ﴿plowing through it﴾, meaning running through it, advancing, turning back, and crossing with one wind, cleaving it with their prows, from al-makhr, which is the cleaving of water. It is also said that it is the sound of the ships' running.

﴿And that you may seek﴾ is coordinated with "that you may extract," and what is coordinated is linked to it, while what lies between them is a parenthetical clause preparing the principles of seeking and averting the assumption that it is by extracting ornaments. Or it is connected to a deleted cause, that is: so that you may benefit from that and seek, as Ibn al-Anbari mentioned. Or it is connected to a deleted verb, that is: and He did that so that you may seek ﴿of His bounty﴾, from the abundance of His provision, by riding them for trade; ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾, that is, you will recognise the rights of His great blessings and carry them out through obedience and monotheism. The specific linking of this blessing with gratitude is because in it there is the crossing of a long distance with heavy loads in a short time, without undertaking the means of travel, indeed without any movement at all, and yet it lies among perils. The absence of an intervening mention of attaining the sought-after object between seeking and gratitude indicates that it is needless to state it explicitly, and that both occur together.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 15:

﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾, i.e., immovable mountains. Its verification has already passed in the beginning of Surah al-Ra'd.

﴿Lest it should sway with you﴾: lest it incline with you and be agitated; or "so that it does not sway with you." For the earth, before the mountains were created in it, was a light, simple-natured sphere, and it was fitting that it should move in a circular motion like the celestial spheres, or be moved by the slightest moving cause. When the mountains were created, its edges became uneven, and the mountains, by their weight, tended toward the center and became like tent-pegs. It is also said: When God Most High created the earth, it began to heave, so the angels said: "No one can remain settled upon its back." Then in the morning it had been anchored with the mountains.

﴿And rivers﴾, i.e., and He placed in it rivers, because in "alqa" (cast) there is the meaning of "placing." ﴿And roads, that you may be guided﴾ by them to your destinations.

[Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 16]

﴿And landmarks﴾: landmarks (ma'alim) by which travelers (al-sabila) are guided during the day, by a mountain, a watering place, or a wind. It has been reported that a group of people would smell the dust and by it recognize the roads.

﴿And by the star they are guided﴾: by night, in deserts and seas, where there is no sign other than it. The word "star" (al-najm) here refers to the genus. It was also said that it refers to the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), the two bright stars (al-Farqadan), the Banat al-Na'sh, and the Pole Star (al-Jadi). It has been read as "nujum" with two dammas, and with a damma and a sukun, and it is a plural like "ruhn" and "ruhun." It was said that the first reading is by way of dropping the waw from "nujum" for lightness. Perhaps the pronoun refers to the Quraysh, for they were frequent travelers for trade, well known for being guided by the stars on their journeys, and the composition is turned away from the usual forms of address. The placing of "the star" first, and the insertion of the pronoun, are for specification, as if it were said: "And by the star, especially these, especially they are guided." Therefore the lesson to be drawn from this, and the thanks for it, are obligatory for them and binding upon them.

﴿Is He then who creates﴾ these great created things and performs those wondrous acts, or who creates everything, ﴿like one who creates nothing﴾ at all? This is a rebuke to the disbelievers and a refutation of their associating partners with God and their worship of idols, by denying what their practice entails of similarity between them and Him, exalted is He, after enumerating what clearly calls for that denial. The placing of the interrogative particle (al-hamza) before the particle of consequence (al-fa') directs the denial to the supposed similarity mentioned, given the great, manifest matters that are exclusively His, exalted is He, as is well known even among them, as indicated by what we have recited of the words of the Exalted: ﴿And if you asked them...﴾ (the two verses). The restriction to mentioning creation among them is because it is the greatest and most evident of them, and because it entails the others; or because each of them is a particular kind of creation. That is: after the evident proof that He, exalted is He, alone holds the origin of these clear affairs, which point to His oneness, His being singular in divinity, and His exclusive entitlement to worship, could a similarity be imagined between Him and what is utterly devoid of that, as your association (of partners) demands and is founded upon? Although it is a comparison of a non-creator to the Creator, the comparison, since it is a relation that subsists between those being related, the noble wording was chosen out of regard for the priority of possession (malaka) over non-existence ('adam), and to avoid placing the non-existence of the latter between it and its detailed particulars mentioned before it, and to alert to the complete ugliness of what they did, insofar as that is not merely removing the idols from their place, but a degrading of the station of lordship to the rank of inanimate objects, and there is no doubt that this is uglier than the former. By "one who creates nothing" is meant everything of this nature, whatever it may be; and the expression of it by what is specific to rational beings is for the sake of harmony (al-mushakala), or it refers to rational beings specifically, and the state of others is known from it by the indication of the text (dalalat al-nass), for if the one who creates is not like the one who creates nothing, and he is among the rational beings, then what do you suppose about inanimate matter? In any case, the inclusion of the idols under the ruling of non-similarity and non-equivalence is either by way of their being subsumed under the general relative pronoun, or by way of their being understood through the indication of the text according to the demonstrative method, not that they are the sole intended referents of the relative pronoun. ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ That is: do you not reflect, so that you would then remember that? For it is so evident that it requires nothing beyond remembrance.

(p-105) ﴿And if you were to count the favour of Allah﴾ is a general reminder of His blessings, exalted be He, after enumerating a portion of them. The apparent course would have been to mention it immediately after them, as a completion of them, in the manner of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾. Perhaps the separation between the two by His saying, exalted be He: "﴿Is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then remember?﴾" is for the sake of hastening to establish the proof and to set the stone (of argument) right after detailing the acts that have been detailed, which are proofs of God's oneness, along with a secret that you will come to understand, and their indication of it. Although (these acts) are not confined to the aspect of creation, since their indication (of God's oneness) is evident also from the aspect of bestowing blessings, yet, since these were consequences of the first aspect, the explicit mention of them was dispensed with, and their state was clarified in summary. That is: if you were to count His bestowed favour upon you from what has been mentioned and what has not been mentioned, as indicated by His saying, exalted be He: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾, ﴿you cannot enumerate it﴾, i.e., you cannot manage to limit it or fix its number, even in summary, let alone give thanks for it. We have already discharged the obligation of verifying this in Surah Ibrahim, by the grace of Allah, glorified be He.

﴿Indeed Allah is Most Forgiving﴾, in that He covers up what has passed from you of disbelief in them and neglect in fulfilling their rights, and does not hasten punishment upon you for that; ﴿Most Merciful﴾, in that He bestows them upon you although you deserve being cut off and deprived because of what you do and leave undone of kinds of disbelief, among which is failing to distinguish between the Creator and other than Him. Each of these is a favour, and what a favour it is! The sentence is an explanation for the ruling of the impossibility of enumeration. The mention of the attribute of forgiveness before the attribute of mercy is because clearing away (what is undesirable) precedes adorning (with what is desirable).

Qur'an 16:19: "And Allah knows what you conceal (tusirrun)."

Tusirrun: you hold secretly, meaning you keep within yourselves of beliefs and deeds.

"And what you disclose (tu'linun)": that is, what you make apparent of those two. The returning pronoun (al-'a'id) has been omitted for the sake of the rhyming endings (al-fawasil), meaning: your secret and your open conduct are equal in relation to His all-encompassing knowledge. In this there is a warning, and an indication of His, glorified be He, exclusive possession of the attributes of divinity, which is not hidden.

The mention of the secret before the open is, as we have explained in Surat al-Baqara and Surat Hud, for the sake of establishing equality between His two knowledges related to them in the most eloquent manner, as if His knowledge of the secret, exalted be He, were prior to His knowledge of the open. Or, because everything that is made open was previously concealed in the heart, so the relation of His knowledge to its first state is prior to its relation to its second state.

﴿And those whom they invoke﴾ begins the demonstration that the idols are wholly undeserving of worship. Its clarification, so that no trace of doubt remains, comes through enumerating their attributes and states, which clearly contradict such desert. Although these states need no explanation, they are spelled out to alert the reader to the complete foolishness of their worshippers, who would not recognize this except through explicit statement. That is: the gods that the unbelievers worship ﴿besides God﴾, glorified is He. It is also read in the passive form (*yu-dʿawna*, "are invoked") and in the second person (*tadʿūna*, "you invoke").

﴿They create nothing﴾ of things at all, that is, it is not within their nature to do so. Since there is no necessary connection in meaning (*mafhūm*) between denying the capacity to create and being created, although the two are necessarily connected in truth (*ṣidq*), the text affirms this for them explicitly, saying: ﴿and they are created﴾. That is: their condition and the requirement of their essence is being created, because they are contingent beings (*mumkinah*), dependent in both their quiddities and their existences upon the one who brings them into being. The verb is put in the passive form to establish the opposition and contrast between what is affirmed for them and what is negated of them, namely the attributes of being created and being a creator (*khāliqiyyah*). It also signals that there is no need to specify the agent, since the act's exclusive belonging to its agent, exalted is His majesty, is evident. It is also permissible to take the second "creating" to mean carving and shaping, in keeping with the parallelism between it and the first, and as an exaggeration of their being made by their worshippers and incapable of helping them. It also signals the utter feebleness of their minds, since they associated with their Creator something that is itself created. As for taking the first "creating" also to mean this, as some have done, there is no basis for it, since the power to create in that sense is not at all what worship is grounded upon. And since affirming createdness for them does not require negating life from them, given that some created beings are living, he states this explicitly, saying:

﴿Amwat﴾ (dead) is a second predicate (khabar) of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those"), not of the pronoun (al-damir) as has been said. Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'). Since some of the dead may later or earlier be possessed by life, such as the bodies of animals and the sperm drops that God Most High brings into being as animals, this was guarded against by saying: ﴿not living﴾, meaning that life never possesses them at all. So they are dead in the absolute sense. As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they do not perceive when they will be raised﴾, meaning that those idols do not perceive when their worshippers will be raised, this is in the manner of mockery toward them, because the perception of inanimate matter regarding even apparent matters is obviously impossible in the view of everyone. How then could it be with what none knows except the All-Knowing, the All-Aware? It also contains an announcement that resurrection is a necessary consequence of moral responsibility (al-taklif), and that knowing its time is something indispensable to divinity (al-uluhiyyah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 22:

﴿Your God is one God.﴾ He has no partner in anything. This is an explicit statement of the claim (al-mudda'a), and a clear conclusion (tamhid li-l-natijah) reached after establishing the proof.

﴿As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ and its conditions, of which the resurrection mentioned is one, and what follows it of recompense, which entails their punishment and humiliation,

﴿their hearts are deniers﴾ of the Oneness (al-wahdaniyyah), rejecting it, or [deniers] of the signs (al-ayat) that point to it.

﴿And they are arrogant﴾ in refusing to acknowledge it, or [arrogant] toward the signs that point to it. The "fa" (fa, "so/therefore") indicates that their persistence in denial and their continued arrogance occurred as a consequence (natijah) of the manifest proofs and the dazzling demonstrations. The meaning is: it has been established, through the arguments and clear evidences that have been set forth, that divinity belongs exclusively to Him, glorified is He. So their persistence in the aforementioned denial and arrogance is a result of that. The placing of the judgment upon the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) signals that it is caused by what lies within the relative clause (silah), for disbelief in the Hereafter, and in what it contains of resurrection and of recompense that varies between reward for obedience and punishment for disobedience, leads to restricting one's view to the immediate, and to turning away from the auditory and rational proofs. This necessarily gives rise to denying them and denying what they convey, and to arrogance in following the Messenger (ﷺ) and affirming him. As for belief in the Hereafter and in what it contains, it inevitably calls one to reflect upon the signs and proofs, with desire and fear, and this produces certainty in the Oneness and submission to the command of God Most High.

**Surely** (*laa jarama*): that is, truly. Its verification has already been discussed in Surah Hud.

﴿Surely Allah knows what they conceal﴾ of the denial in their hearts, ﴿and what they reveal﴾ of their arrogance, and their saying about the Qur'an that it is ﴿legends of the ancients﴾, and other of their ugly deeds, so He will requite them for that. ﴿Indeed, He does not love the arrogant﴾. This is a reason for what the speech implies of threat, meaning: He does not love those who are arrogant toward *tawhid* (the affirmation of God's oneness), or toward the signs that point to it, or He does not love the category of the arrogant at all, so how much more so one who is arrogant toward what has been mentioned? (p-107)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (*Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*) on surah 16, verse 24:

﴿And when it is said to them﴾ i.e., to those deniers, the arrogant ones. This is an explanation of their misguidance after the explanation of their error.

﴿"What has your Lord sent down?"﴾ The speakers are the delegations who came to them, or the Muslims, or some of them, in the manner of mockery. "Mada" (*mā*, "what") is in the accusative, governed by what follows it, or in the nominative, meaning: "What thing did He send down?" or "What is it that He sent down?"

﴿They say: "Fables of the ancients."﴾ i.e., what you claim was sent down. What is sent down, in mockery, is the tales of the ancients and their falsehoods, which have nothing to do with sending down at all. It is said: these speakers are the *muqtasimun* (those who divided up the approaches), who divided up the entrances to Makkah, deterring people from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when the delegations of pilgrims asked about what had been revealed to him (ﷺ).

﴿That they may bear﴾ is connected to *qalu* (they said), meaning: they said what they said so that they would bear ﴿their own burdens﴾, namely the burdens of their own misguidance, ﴿in full﴾, with none of them being expiated by some calamity that befell them in this world, as the burdens of the believers are expiated by such calamities. ﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾ is the time-expression (*zarf*) for ﴿they may bear﴾. ﴿And some of the burdens of those who mislead them﴾ refers to a portion of the burdens of those who were led astray through their misleading, namely the burden of misguiding others. This is because the two are partners: one misleads and the other follows, so they both share the burden.

The *lam* in *li-yahmilu* is the lam of causation (*lam al-ta'lil*) in reality (*nafs al-amr*), not in the sense of an intended purpose. The form of the future (*sigha al-istiqbal*), in *yudillun*, indicates the continuation of misguidance, or it is considered from the standpoint of the time of their saying, not the time of the bearing.

﴿Without knowledge﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the subject: that is, they mislead them while not knowing that what they call to is the path of misguidance. As for interpreting it to mean "not knowing that they will bear on the Day of Resurrection the burdens of misguidance and misleading," so that the governing verb of the circumstantial clause is *qalu*, and supporting this with His Exalted words that follow, ﴿and the punishment will come upon them from where they do not perceive﴾, on the basis that whoever bears the mentioned burdens of misguidance and misleading is among those to whom punishment comes from where they do not perceive, this is refuted by the fact that the bearing mentioned is on the Day of Resurrection, while the punishment mentioned is the punishment of this world, as you will come to understand.

Or it is a circumstantial clause referring to the object: that is, they mislead those who do not know that they are misguided. The purpose of restricting it with this condition is to indicate that their deception does not succeed with a person of intellect; it is only the foolish and ignorant who follow them. It also draws attention to the fact that such ignorance on their part is not an excuse, since it was incumbent upon them to inquire and to distinguish between the one who is rightly guided and worthy of being followed and the one who is in falsehood.

﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾, that is: how wretched is the thing they bear, namely what has been mentioned.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 26:

﴿Those before them had already plotted.﴾ This is a warning to them that the harmful consequences of their scheming would return upon themselves, just as it did for those earlier nations who came before them, upon whom the swift punishment befell. That is, they prepared snares with which they intended to deceive God Most High's messengers. ﴿Then God's command and judgment came upon their building﴾ (and it was read as "their house" and "their houses") ﴿from its foundations﴾, which are the pillars that support it, or its base, so its supports were weakened, ﴿and the roof fell down on them from above them﴾. That is, the roof of their building collapsed upon them. Since it is inconceivable for it to stand once its foundations have been destroyed, the state of those scheming deceivers, in their preparing of plots and snares by which they intended to ensnare God's messengers, and in God's nullifying of those stratagems and plots and making them causes of their own destruction, is likened to the state of a people who built a structure and supported it with pillars, so that the structure was attacked through its pillars, its supports were weakened, the roof fell upon them, and they perished. It was also read as ﴿the roofs fell down on them﴾ with two dammas.

﴿And the punishment came to them﴾, that is, the destruction and ruin, ﴿from where they did not perceive﴾, not from the direction they expected, but rather they anticipated the arrival of the opposite of what they wished for and desired. The meaning is that these schemers, who say that the Great Qur'an is "tales of the ancients," will be struck by a punishment like the one that struck them, and they do not expect it. What is meant by this is the swift punishment, due to His, glorified be He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 27:

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them﴾. It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon an implied element (muqaddar) to which the discourse extends, i.e., "this which was understood from the parable concerning the punishment of those people," or something more general than it, and of what was mentioned concerning the punishment of those others, their recompense in this world. "And on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them," i.e., He will humiliate them with the punishment of disgrace (khizy) before the eyes of the witnesses. The origin of khizy is a humiliation that causes one to feel shame. The "then" (thumma) indicates the disparity between the two recompenses along with what it implies of temporal remoteness. The change of construction by fronting the adverbial phrase is not to restrict disgrace to the Day of Resurrection, as is apparent from making the adverbial phrase dependent on the verb; rather, because the report of their recompense in this world signals that they have an otherworldly recompense, the soul remains anticipating its arrival, asking what it will be, even while being certain that it is in the Hereafter. So the discourse is arranged in a manner that signals that the purpose of mention is their being disgraced, not merely that it occurs on the Day of Resurrection. The pronoun refers either to those who slandered the noble Qur'an, or to them and to those among the deceivers whom they were likened to, as has been indicated. Restricting it to "they" (hum) is rejected by both the preceding context (siyaq) and the broader context (sibaq), as you will see. ﴿And He will say﴾ to them, for exposure and rebuke, so it is ... etc., an explanation of the disgrace. ﴿"Where are My associates?"﴾ He attributed them to Himself, Glorified is He, as a narration of their false ascription, so in it is rebuke upon rebuke along with mockery of them.

﴿"Concerning whom you used to dispute"﴾, i.e., you used to contend with the prophets and the believers regarding them, claiming they were true partners, when they (the prophets and believers) made clear to you their falsehood. The intent of the interrogative is to summon them for intercession, or as a challenge in the manner of mockery and reproach. Inquiring about their whereabouts does not necessarily entail their actual absence, so as to be excused by saying that they might be placed between them and their worshippers at that time so that they could check on them in an hour in which they had hung their hope upon them, or because they had not benefited them. Rather, it suffices for that the non-presence of them in the capacity they used to claim, that they possessed a divine quality, so there are no partners there, nor their places. Moreover, His saying "so that they may check on them" is not accurate, for the matter had already become clear to them at that time, so they retracted that false claim; how then can checking on them be conceived of from them? It is also read with a kasra on the nun (nunation), i.e., "you contend with Me," on the basis that contending with the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, and the believers, especially in a matter connected to Him, Glorified and Exalted, is contending with Him, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Those who were given knowledge said﴾, from among the people of the station, and they are the prophets and the believers who were given knowledge through the proofs of monotheism, and who used to call them in the world to monotheism, so they would argue with them and act arrogantly toward them. That is, as a rebuke to them, and to display gloating at them, and as an affirmation of what they used to admonish them, and a confirmation of what they threatened them with. The choice of the past tense form indicates its certainty and the inevitability of its occurrence, as is customary in His, Glorified and Exalted, reports, as in His saying: ﴿And the companions of the Garden called out﴾, ﴿And the companions of the Heights called out﴾.

﴿Indeed, disgrace﴾: the exposure, humiliation, and abasement.

﴿Today﴾ is in the accusative governed by "disgrace," according to the view of those who hold that a verbal noun introduced by the preposition lam operates, or by "being settled" within the adverbial phrase. In this there is a separation between the governor and the governed by the conjunction, but this is excused in adverbial phrases. Its mention indicates that they had previously been in might and defiance.

﴿And evil﴾, i.e., the punishment, ﴿upon the disbelievers﴾ in God, Exalted is He, and in His signs and His messengers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 28:

﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾, with the verb in the feminine form (*tatawaffahumu*, "they take"). It is also read with the verb in the masculine form (*yatawaffahumu*), and with the assimilation (*idgham*, merging of two identical consonants) of the *ta'* into the *ta'*. The shift to the present-tense form (*mudari'*, imperfect) is to bring before the mind the image of their being taken in death, because of the terror it contains. The relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) is in the genitive position as an attribute (*na't*) of "the disbelievers," or as an apposition (*badal*) to it, or it is in the accusative or nominative position, as a term of censure (*dhamm*). Its purpose is to restrict the disgrace and evil to those whose disbelief persisted until the time of death, excluding those among them who believed, even at the end of their lives. That is, [the verse refers to] the disbelievers who persisted in disbelief until the angels take them in death.

﴿while they were wronging themselves﴾, that is, while they were persisting in disbelief. This is a wrong they did to themselves, and what a wrong it is, since they exposed themselves to the everlasting punishment, and they altered the natural disposition (*fitrah*) of God into something else.

﴿Then they will offer submission﴾, that is, they will [then] offer it. The shift to the past-tense form (*madi*) is to indicate the certainty of its occurrence. It is coordinated (*'atf*) with the Most High's words: ﴿And He will say, "Where are My partners?"﴾. What lies between them is a parenthetical sentence (*jumlah i'tiradiyyah*), brought in to confirm the disgrace that befell them before all witnesses. That is, they will make submission, abandon opposition, and relinquish the arrogance and fierce obstinacy they had in the world, saying: ﴿We did no evil﴾ in the world, ﴿[no] wrong﴾, that is, [no] polytheism. They said this denying that it proceeded from them, as in their saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾. They expressed it as "evil" only in acknowledgment that it is evil, not in denial that it is such while acknowledging that it proceeded from them. It may also be that it is an explanation of "submission," on the understanding that what is meant by it is the speech that indicates it. In either case, this is an answer to the Most High's words in surah al-An'am, "Where are My partners?" and not an answer to the words of those possessed of knowledge, as a claim that they do not deserve what overtook them of disgrace and evil.

﴿Yes indeed﴾: a response to them from the side of those possessed of knowledge, and an affirmation of what they denied. That is, yes indeed, you were doing what you were doing.

﴿Indeed God is All-Knowing of what you were doing﴾, so He will repay you for it, and this is its time.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 29:**

﴿So enter the gates of Hell﴾. That is, each kind (enters) its own gate that was prepared for it. It was also said that its gates are the kinds of its punishment, so "entering" is an expression for being immersed in and enduring (it).

﴿Abiding therein﴾. If by "entering" is meant its occurrence, then the circumstantial clause (hal) is anticipated (muqaddarah), and if what is meant is the mere state of being therein, then it is concurrent (muqarinah).

﴿How wretched is the abode of the arrogant﴾, (arrogant) toward monotheism, as God the Exalted says: ﴿Their hearts deny, and they are arrogant﴾. Mentioning them under the title of arrogance indicates that it is the cause of their abiding therein. The object of the blame (al-makhsus bi-al-dhamm) is omitted, i.e., Hell. The interpretation of their words: ﴿We did no evil﴾ is that we were not doing that in our belief, (saying so) out of a desire to maintain that there was no lying. There, it is refuted by the rejoinder mentioned. As for what is in surah al-An'am, God the Exalted's words: ﴿Look how they lied against themselves﴾.

(p-110) ﴿And it will be said to those who were mindful of God﴾, that is, the believers. They are described as "mindful of God" to indicate that the answer they gave arose from their God-consciousness (taqwa).

﴿"What has your Lord sent down?" They said, "Goodness."﴾ They followed the form of the question in their answer, without hesitation and without altering its shape. The meaning is: "He has sent down goodness." This is an answer that corresponds to the question and accords with the reality that is established in itself. As for the disbelievers, may God forsake them, they altered the answer away from the path of the truth, which has no repeller, and changed its form, deviating from the pattern of the question when they said "myths of the ancients" out of obstinacy, given what had passed concerning their denial of the revelation. It is narrated that the tribes of the Arabs would, during the season of the pilgrimage, send someone to bring them news of the Prophet (ﷺ). When the envoy arrived, the partitioners (al-muqtasimun) would confront him and order him to leave, saying: "If you do not meet him, it will be better for you." Then the envoy would say: "I am the worst envoy if I return to my people without investigating the matter of Muhammad and seeing him for myself." So he would meet the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), may God be pleased with them, and they would inform him of the true state of affairs. These are the ones who said "goodness."

﴿For those who did good﴾, that is, in their deeds, or who performed good, ﴿in this﴾ ﴿world, there is good﴾, that is, a good reward, a recompense in it, ﴿and the abode of the Hereafter﴾, that is, their reward therein, ﴿is better﴾ than what they were given in this world of reward, or it is better absolutely, so the attribute of being better may be ascribed to the abode of the Hereafter itself. ﴿And excellent indeed is the abode of the mindful﴾, that is, the abode of the Hereafter, the noun being omitted because of what preceded it as an indication. This is a new (independent) statement with which God praised the mindful, and counted their answer as reported among their good deeds, and promised them with it the reward of both this world and the Hereafter.
