Therefore it has no place in terms of grammatical analysis (i'rab); or it is a substitute for "goodness" (khayran), or an explanation of it, meaning: what He sent down was goodness, namely this comprehensive statement that they uttered as an encouragement to the inquirer.

﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾ is the predicate (khabar, the comment on the subject) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the topic), or else a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, meaning "for them are gardens." It is also permissible that it be the object of praise (al-makhsus bi'l-madh), in which case the phrase is understood as the specified subject of a praise. ﴿They enter it﴾ is a qualifier (sifah) of ﴿gardens﴾ on the assumption that ʿAdn is indefinite, and likewise ﴿rivers flow beneath them﴾. Alternatively, both may be circumstantial clauses (hal), on the assumption that ʿAdn is a proper name (ʿalamiyyah). ﴿For them therein﴾, meaning in those gardens, ﴿is whatever they wish﴾. The first adverbial phrase (al-zarf al-awwal) is the predicate (khabar) of the particle mā, and the second is a circumstantial clause (hal) from it. The governing element (al-ʿamil) is mā in the first case, or the first adverbial phrase is attached to it. The meaning is: there will be for them therein whatever they desire of kinds of things that are craved. Its being placed first serves to prevent the misunderstanding that it is connected with the act of wishing, or, as has been noted many times, because delaying what should be placed first causes the soul to anticipate it, so that when it arrives it is firmly established in the soul with greater firmness.

﴿Thus﴾ is like that great recompense. ﴿God rewards the God-fearing﴾. The definite article in al-muttaqin (the God-fearing) is for the genus (lam al-jins), meaning everyone who guards himself against polytheism and sins. Those mentioned as God-fearing are included in it in the first instance, and it contains an exhortation to others to be God-fearing. Alternatively, the article is for a specific reference (lam al-ʿahd), in which case it contains a rebuke to the disbelievers.

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾ is a qualifier (na't, a descriptive adjective) for "the God-fearing." His words, Exalted is He, ﴿in a state of goodness﴾ mean: pure from the filth of wronging their own souls. It is a circumstantial clause (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject) referring back to the pronoun (damir) in "takes them." Its purpose is to inform that the essence of God-consciousness (taqwa) is purity from what has been mentioned, up until the time of their death. This contains an exhortation to the believers to persist in this, and to others to attain it. It has also been said: "joyful and content of soul at the angels' good tidings to them of Paradise," or "in a state of goodness through the taking of their souls, because their souls were wholly turned toward the presence of holiness."

﴿Saying﴾ is a circumstantial clause describing the angels, meaning: saying to them, ﴿"Peace be upon you."﴾ Al-Qurazi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: When the soul of the believer is summoned, the Angel of Death, peace be upon him, comes to him and says: "Peace be upon you, O friend of Allah. Allah sends you His greetings, and gives you the good news of Paradise." ﴿"Enter the Garden"﴾: the definite article (al-) is for specific reference, meaning: the Gardens of Eden, and so on. For this reason it is stripped of a qualifier. What is intended is their entry into it at that very time, for this is a great good news, even if what was promised is delayed. What is intended is not entry into the grave, which is one of its gardens, since the good news of it is not equal to the good news of entering Paradise itself. ﴿"For what you used to do"﴾: because of your steadfastness in God-consciousness and obedience, or "for that which you used to do of such." It has also been said: what is intended by "taking" is the taking for the Gathering (on the Day of Resurrection), because the command to enter is then fully realized.

﴿Do they then await﴾ meaning: do the disbelievers of Makkah, whose mention has passed, await ﴿anything but that the angels come to them﴾ to take their souls with punishment? They are treated as those who await this, but how far apart is that from awaiting it not because it will certainly befall them, as an expected matter does, but because they engage in its causes, which necessitate it and lead to it. It is as if they intend its coming and watch for its arrival. It is also recited with the verb feminine-marked, ﴿or that the command of your Lord comes﴾. Mentioning the attribute of Lordship (rububiyyah) together with its addition to his pronoun (ﷺ) indicates that his coming is a kindness to him (ﷺ), even though it is a punishment for them. By "the command" is meant the worldly punishment, not the Resurrection. But this is not because waiting for it would be compatible with waiting for the coming of the angels, so that the conjunction "or" would be unsuitable; rather, it is because it is not explicit in denial, since it is permissible to regard the prevention of emptiness as the meaning, and its mention is intended to show that each of the two matters suffices for their punishment. Rather, it is because the words of the Exalted in what follows, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾, ﴿so there befell them﴾ ... the verse, are explicit that what is meant by it is the punishment of this world that befell them. ﴿Thus﴾ meaning: like the conduct of these people in polytheism (shirk), wrongdoing, denial and mockery, ﴿did those who came before them﴾ of the nations ﴿do﴾, ﴿and Allah did not wrong them﴾ by what will be recounted of their punishment, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾ by the vile deeds they persisted in, which necessitated that. It would have been apt to say, ﴿but they were themselves the wrongdoers﴾, as in Surat al-Zukhruf. But the noble composition chose what it has, to convey that the harm of their wronging returns to them and its consequence is confined to them. And the restriction of each person's wronging to himself entails, in terms of occurrence, its restriction to him in terms of origin. Its verification has passed in Surat Yunus.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 34:

﴿So the evil consequences of what they did struck them﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿those before them did [the same]﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtiraḍ) to explain that their doing that was a wronging of themselves. ﴿Sayyiʾāt mā ʿamilū﴾ means: the requitals (ajziyat) of their evil deeds, following the figure of speech of naming the effect (musabbab) by the name of its cause (sabab), as a declaration of its atrocity (fazaʿah), and not by way of eliding a modifier (ḥadhf al-muḍāf), for that would give the impression that they had deeds other than their evil deeds.

﴿And there encompassed them﴾, that is: there surrounded them, from ḥayq, which is the encompassing of evil (iḥāṭat al-sharr). It is more intensive than iṣābah (striking) and more dreadful: ﴿what they used to mock﴾, namely the punishment.

(p-112) ﴿And those who associated partners [with God] said﴾: that is, the people of Makkah. This explains another aspect of their disbelief. The shift from the pronoun to the relative noun (alladhina) serves to rebuke them with what is contained in the relative clause and to censure them for it from the outset.

﴿If God had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him﴾: that is, if He had willed that we not worship anything other than Him, as you would say, "we would not have worshipped that." ﴿Neither we nor our fathers,﴾ whom we follow in our religion, ﴿nor would we have prohibited anything besides Him﴾ such as the sawa'ib (freed camels), the bahair (slit-eared she-camels), and others. They said this only to deny the Messenger (ﷺ) and to attack prophethood entirely, holding fast to the view that whatever God Most High wills must come to pass, and whatever He does not will is impossible. So if He had willed that we affirm His oneness, not associate anything with Him, and not prohibit anything of what we have prohibited, as the messengers say and convey from God, glory be to Him, then the matter would be as He willed, with regard to monotheism, the negation of associating partners, and what follows from them. Since this is not the case, it is established that He did not will any of that, and that the messengers say it on their own accord. He is answered with the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like that shameful act, ﴿did those before them do﴾ from among the nations, that is, they associated partners with God, made lawful what He had made unlawful, rejected His messengers, and argued with them falsely when they warned them of error and guided them to the truth.

﴿So is there upon the messengers﴾ who convey the messages of God and the resolute commands and prohibitions of His ordinance ﴿except the clear conveyance?﴾ That is, their duty is nothing but to convey the message plainly, or clearly explained, and to make clear the path of truth and to manifest the rulings of revelation. Among these rulings is the necessity that God's will be linked to the guidance of whoever directs his capacity and choice toward attaining the truth, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our ways.﴾ As for compelling them to that, and enforcing their word upon them whether they will or refuse, as the implication of their argument requires, that is not part of their duty, nor does it belong to the wisdom upon which the matter of moral obligation (al-taklif) turns in any way. Thus one cannot infer from the absence of its effects either the non-reality of the messengers or the non-linkage of His will, exalted is He, to that. For what entails reward and punishment among the acts of servants must, for God's will to be linked to its occurrence, proceed from their voluntary exertion and the directing of their partial choice toward achieving it; otherwise reward and punishment would be compulsory. The particle fa' (فـ) here indicates causation, as if it were said: thus did their predecessors act. And that is false, for the messengers' task is only to convey the commands and prohibitions of God Most High, not to realize their content or to enforce their consequences upon people by coercion and compulsion. The use of the word ʿalā (على, "upon") indicates that they are under obligation in this matter, or that what they convey is a right owed to people from them, which they must fulfill. By this it becomes clear that interpreting their words, ﴿If God had willed﴾ ... etc., as mockery does not fit the answer. And God knows best what is correct.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 36:

﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger﴾ This establishes how God's will (mashi'ah) relates to the actions of His servants, after clarifying that compulsion (al-ilja', forcing someone to act) is not among the functions of the messenger (risalah), nor is it of the kind of will connected to what reward and punishment depend on, namely voluntary actions performed by them. That is: We sent in every one of the past nations a messenger specifically to them.

﴿saying, "Worship God alone and avoid taghut (false deities, here the Devil and everything that calls to misguidance)"﴾ The word ﴿أنْ﴾ (an) may be explanatory (mufassirah), clarifying the sense of speech implied in the sending, or it may be verbal-source (masdariyyah), meaning: We sent him with the command "worship God alone."

﴿Then among them﴾, that is, among those nations, the particle ﴿الفاء﴾ (al-fa', here explained as fasihah, introducing an elliptical clause) indicates: so they conveyed what they were sent with, the command to worship God alone and avoid taghut, and then they divided. ﴿Among them are those whom God guided﴾ to the truth, which is worshipping Him and avoiding taghut, after their capacity and their partial choice were directed toward attaining it.

﴿And among them are those upon whom misguidance was justly due﴾, that is, it became necessary and was established for them, until death, because of their obstinacy and persistence in it and their failure to direct their capacity toward attaining the truth. The shift in phrasing indicates that this is due to their bad choice, like His saying: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾ [26:80]. Thus neither the will of guidance nor the will of its absence operated except in accordance with what arose from them of turning toward the truth or not turning toward it, and not by way of coercion and compulsion, so that the absence of both is used as evidence that God's will is not connected to their worshipping Him alone.

﴿So travel﴾, O assembly of Quraysh, ﴿through the earth and observe﴾ in its regions ﴿how was the end of the deniers﴾ such as 'Ad and Thamud, and whoever followed their way among those upon whom misguidance was justly due, ﴿that perhaps you may reflect﴾ when you witness, in their dwellings and homelands, the traces of destruction and punishment. The ordering of travel upon the mere report that misguidance was established over them, without mention of the descent of punishment, signals that this is too evident to need explanation, and that report is not like seeing. The ordering of observation after travel is because it comes after it, and because the decisive factor in that end was denial. Their pretext that "had God willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him" is also refuted by this.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 37:

﴿If you are eager﴾ is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is also read with a fatha on the ra' (taḥrаṣ → taḥraṣ), which is a dialectal variant (lughayya).

﴿for their guidance﴾ meaning: if you seek their guidance with all your effort. ﴿Surely Allah does not guide those who go astray﴾ meaning: know that He, exalted is He, does not create guidance by compulsion and force in one in whom He creates misguidance due to his own evil choice. The intended people here are the Quraysh. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is placed in the position of the pronoun (al-damir) to specify that they are among those upon whom misguidance has been decreed, and to indicate the cause of the judgment. It is also permissible that what is mentioned is the cause (ʿilla) of the omitted apodosis (jaza' mahdhuf), meaning: if you are eager for their guidance, then you are not capable of that, because Allah does not guide the one whom He misguides, and these are among them. It is read as (lā yuhdā) in the passive voice, meaning: no one can guide the one whom Allah, exalted is He, misguides. It is read as (lā yahaddī) with a fatha on the ha' and the assimilation of the ta' of yahtadī into the dal, and it is permissible that yahdī means yahtadī (is guided). It is read as (yaḍillu) with a fatha on the ya'. It is also read: lā hādiya li-man yuḍillu wa-li-man aḍalla.

﴿And they have no helpers﴾ who would help them with guidance, or ward off the punishment from them. The plural form of "helpers" (al-nāṣirīn) is in accordance with the plurality in the pronoun, since matching plural with plural requires the distribution of units to units, not because the intended meaning is the negation of some group of helpers from each of them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 38:**

﴿And they swore by Allah﴾ This begins the explanation of another kind of their falsehoods, namely their denial of resurrection (al-ba'th).

﴿With their most emphatic oaths (jahd aymanihim)﴾ This is a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal), meaning: striving in their oaths.

﴿Allah does not raise up one who dies﴾ Allah, exalted is He, gave them the most eloquent refutation with His true words: ﴿Yes (bala)﴾, meaning: yes, He will raise them up.

﴿As a promise (wa'dan)﴾ This is a verbal noun emphasizing what is indicated by "yes" (bala), for that is a promise from Allah, glorified is He. Or it is an omitted verb, meaning: He promised this with a promise.

﴿Incumbent upon Him (alayhi)﴾ This is an attribute of "promise," meaning: a promise firmly binding upon Him to fulfill, because He does not break His promise, or because resurrection is among the requirements of wisdom.

﴿As a truth (haqqan)﴾ This is another attribute of it, or it is in the accusative of the verbal noun, meaning: it is truly established as a truth.

﴿But most people﴾ Because of their ignorance of the affairs of Allah, mighty is His affair, concerning knowledge, power, wisdom, and the other attributes of perfection, and concerning what is permissible for Him and what is not, and because they do not comprehend the secret of creation and its ultimate purpose, nor that resurrection is among what wisdom requires, which is His, glorified is He, customary practice to observe, ﴿they do not know﴾ that He will raise them up, so they pronounce definitively that it will not happen, or that it is a promise binding upon Him and true, so they deny it, saying: ﴿Indeed, we and our fathers were promised this before; this is nothing but the fables of the ancients.﴾

**Verse:** ﴿That He may make clear to them﴾ is the purpose (ghayah) of what the word "Yes" (bala) indicates, namely the resurrection (al-ba'th). The pronoun refers to those who die, since the clarification also encompasses the believers. Although they already know this, when the reality of the situation is directly witnessed, the matter becomes clear and their knowledge reaches the level of *ʿayn al-yaqin* (the certainty of direct sight). That is: He will raise them so that He may make clear to them, through what they experience of the conditions as they truly are, and through witnessing them in their real forms.

﴿Concerning which they differ﴾: this refers to the truth, which encompasses everything that opposes what the clear law (al-shar' al-mubin) has brought. The resurrection is included in this first and foremost. ﴿And that those who disbelieved﴾ in God, the Exalted, by associating partners with Him, by denying the resurrection, and by denying His true promise, ﴿may know that they were liars﴾ in everything they say, especially in their statement: ﴿God will not raise up those who die.﴾

The expression of the truth by a relative clause (al-mawsul) serves to show its grandeur, and to indicate that what is mentioned in the relative clause is the cause of the clarification. The phrase joined to it makes both of them the purpose of the resurrection previously referred to. This is because the verse comes in the context of rebutting the opponents and refuting the stubborn people's claim, which calls for addressing what will deter them from opposition and compel them to submit to the truth. When disbelievers know that the realization of the resurrection is in order to show that it is true, and so that they may know they were lying in denying it, this is more effective in deterring them from denying it and more conducive to their acknowledging it. This is necessarily so, because it indicates the sincerity of the resolve to bring it about, as when you say to someone who denies that you pray: "I will surely pray, in spite of your nose, and to expose your lie."

Also, the repetition of purposes (ghayat) indicates more strongly that the action qualified by them will occur. Otherwise, the original purpose of the resurrection, considered in itself, is the recompense, which is the ultimate purpose of creation, qualified by knowing Him, the Mighty and Majestic, and worshipping Him. That was not mentioned because it is repeatedly mentioned in other places and is well known.

The knowledge of the disbelievers regarding their lying was not placed under the clarification by saying: "Indeed, those who disbelieved were liars." Rather, the form of knowledge was used, because that is not among the things to which clarification applies. Clarification is the disclosure of what was previously ambiguous, by informing about it so that people then differ concerning it, like the resurrection which the Qur'an declared, and concerning which the differing people differed. But the lying of the disbelievers is not of this kind. What is related to it is a necessary knowledge they have from their own selves. Its realization has already been discussed in Surat al-Tawbah, at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until it becomes clear to you who are truthful﴾ (9:43).

The attribution (al-isnad) was specifically restricted to them (the disbelievers) and not stated as "and that the disbelievers..." etc. This is because the believers' knowledge of that is also already present beforehand.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 40:

﴿Our saying is only﴾ is a resumptive clause (istinaf) explaining how creation takes place in general, both in origination and in return, after the warning about the immediacy of the Resurrection. From this, its manner becomes clear. Thus "ma" is a restrictive particle (kaffah, a "ma" that neutralises the governing particle), and "qawluna" ("Our saying") is the subject (mubtada').

His words ﴿to a thing﴾ mean: any thing whatever, of what is great or small. It is connected to the saying, with the lam being of communication (tabligh), as in your saying: "I said to him: stand up, and he stood." Al-Zajjaj (Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj) took it to be causal, meaning "for the sake of a thing," but this is not clear. The expression "thing" is used here with regard to its existence at the moment when the Exalted's will is directed toward it, not because it was a thing before that.

﴿when We intend it﴾ is an adverbial clause (zarf) modifying "qawluna," meaning: at the time of Our intending its existence.

﴿that We say to it, "Be"﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of the subject.

﴿and it is﴾ is either a conjunction (atf) upon an implied element that the "fa" reveals and that the discourse extends to, meaning: "so We say that, and it is," like His saying, exalted is He: "When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is" (cf. 36:82). Or it is the answer (jawab) to an omitted condition, meaning: "So when We have said that, it is," and there is no saying, nor one addressed, nor command, nor one commanded, such that it could be said that this entails one of two impossibilities: either addressing what does not exist, or obtaining what is already obtained.

Or it may be said: what this requires is the restriction of His exalted saying, "Be," and it does not follow from this that the causes of creation are restricted to it, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: "His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be,' and it is" (36:82). The intended meaning of "command" is the affair, which includes both speech and act. Necessarily, its restriction to the word "Be" does not restrict all of its causes to it in an absolute sense. Rather, this is only an image of the ease with which things within the scope of power come about according to the connection of His exalted will to them, and a depiction of the speed with which they occur, by means of what is a known matter concerning the obedience of the one commanded to the command of the one who commands and is obeyed. The meaning is: Our bringing a thing into being, when Our will is connected to it, is that We bring it into being in the swiftest manner. And since He expressed it by the command, which is a particular kind of saying, it was necessary to express the absolute act of bringing into being by the absolute saying. So reflect.

In this noble verse there is such grandeur and eloquence that minds and intellects are bewildered by it.

It is also read with the accusative "yakuna" (﴿فيكونَ﴾), as a conjunction upon "naqula" (﴿أن نقولَ﴾), or as making it analogous to the answer of a command (jawab al-amr).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 41:

﴿And those who emigrated for God's sake﴾ i.e., in the cause of God Most High, seeking His good pleasure, for His right, and for His countenance.

﴿after they had been wronged﴾ Perhaps they are those of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) whom the people of Mecca wronged and drove out of their homes, so they emigrated to Abyssinia (al-Habasha). Then God Most High settled them in Medina (al-Madina), as He promised in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good place﴾, i.e., a good dwelling (mabaa'a hasana), or a good settling (tabwi'a hasana), as Qatada said. This is the most fitting view given what is well known, that the surah, except its last three verses, is Meccan. As for what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that it was revealed concerning Suhayb, Bilal, 'Ammar, Khabbab, 'Abis, Jubayr, and Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl, whom the polytheists seized and began to torture in order to turn them away from Islam: as for Suhayb, he said to them, "I am an old man; if I am with you, I will not benefit you, and if I am against you, I will not harm you," so he ransomed himself from them with his wealth and emigrated. When Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, saw him, he said, "The sale has profited, O Suhayb!" And 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said, "Suhayb is an excellent servant; if he did not fear God, he would not disobey Him." This accords only with what is related from al-Asamm, that the entire surah is Medinan. And what is reported from Qatada, that this verse through to the end of the surah is Medinan, so what we have related from him about the revelation of the verse concerning the people of the two emigrations is to be understood as its being revealed in Medina between the two emigrations. As for making the Messenger of God (ﷺ) one of them, the structure of the revelation does not support it, nor does his exalted station. It is read: (la-nuthawwiyannahum), and its meaning is: a good abode, or: We will settle them in the world in a good station, which is: victory over those who wronged them from the people of Mecca, and over the Arabs entirely, and the people of the East and the West altogether.

﴿And the reward of the Hereafter﴾ i.e., the recompense for their deeds mentioned, in the Hereafter, ﴿is greater﴾ than what is hastened for them in this world. It is reported from 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, that when he gave a man from among the emigrants a gift, he would say to him, "Take it; may God Most High bless it for you. This is what God Most High promised you in this world, and what is stored up in the Hereafter is better."

﴿if they only knew﴾ The pronoun refers to the disbelievers, i.e., if they knew that God Most High gathers for these emigrants the good of both abodes, they would agree with them in the religion. It has been said that it refers to the emigrants, i.e., if they knew that, they would increase in striving, or they would not be pained by what befell them of emigration and its hardships.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 42:

﴿Those who are patient﴾ under the hardships, such as the harm inflicted by the disbelievers, the separation from family and homeland, and other things. Its position (i'rab, grammatical case) is accusative (nasb), or nominative (raf') by way of praise (al-madh).

﴿And upon their Lord alone﴾ ﴿they rely﴾, severing their attachment to Him, the Exalted, turning away from anything other than Him, and entrusting to Him the whole matter. The clause is either conjoined (ma'tufah) to the relative clause (sillah), and the fronting of the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) indicates the restriction (qasr) of reliance (tawakkul) to Allah, the Exalted. The use of the present-tense form (sighat al-istiqbal) indicates the continuity (dawam) of reliance; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "sabaru" (they were patient).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 43:

﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed⦆ — and it is read with the yā' (as yūḥā ilayhim, in the passive voice), and this is a refutation of the Quraysh when they said: "God is too exalted to have a messenger from among mankind," just as their statement is structured: ﴿If God had willed, we would not have worshipped⦆ ... etc. That is: the divine custom has proceeded, as wisdom requires, that He sends for the general call none but men to whom He reveals, through the intermediary of the angel, His commands and His prohibitions, so that they may convey them to the people. Since the intended address to the Messenger of God ﷺ was to alert the disbelievers to its content, the address was turned toward them, and it was said: ﴿So ask the people of the Reminder⦆, i.e., the People of the Book, or the scholars of reports, or everyone who is mentioned for knowledge and verification, so that they may teach you that.

﴿If you do not know⦆ — its answer is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it. In it is an indication that He did not send an angel for the general call. The words of the Exalted: ﴿Who made the angels messengers⦆ mean: messengers to the angels, or to the messengers. Nor a woman, nor a child; and the prophethood of Jesus, upon him be peace, does not contradict this, for he was in the cradle; because prophethood is more general than messengerhood. It also points to the obligation of referring to the scholars in matters that are not known.

﴿with the clear proofs and the Scriptures﴾: with the miracles and the books. The particle "bāʾ" (bi-, "with") is connected to an implied verb that stands as an answer to a question of the form: "With what were they sent?" So it is said: they were sent with the clear proofs and the Scriptures. Or it is connected to "bimā ursil-nā" (with what We sent), falling under the exception together with "rijālan" (men) according to those who permit this, meaning: We sent none but men with the clear proofs, like your saying: "I struck none but Zayd with the whip." Or it is connected to a fronted position before the exception particle "illā" (except), meaning: We did not send before you, with the clear proofs and the Scriptures, except men, according to those who permit the relative clause of "mā" (what/none) to come after "illā" and be placed after what follows it. Or "bi-" is a descriptive phrase qualifying the excepted noun, meaning: except men who are associated with the clear proofs. Or it is connected to "nūḥī" (We reveal) as an objective complement (object), or as a circumstantial complement (ḥāl) from the deputy of the subject of "yūḥā" (is revealed), which is "ilayhim" (to them), with the understanding that His saying, exalted is He, "fa-s'alū" (ask), is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ). Or it is connected to His saying "lā taʿlamūn" (you do not know), with the conditional clause serving as a rebuke, like the words of the hired worker: "If I have worked for you, then give me my due."

﴿And We sent down to you the Reminder﴾: that is, the Qur'an. It was named "the Reminder" because it is a reminding and an alert for the heedless.

﴿so that you might make clear to the people﴾: all of them, and the people of Makkah enter among them first and foremost.

﴿what was sent down to them﴾: in that Reminder, of the rulings and laws and other matters, and of the conditions of the peoples who were destroyed with various kinds of punishment, according to their deeds that brought this about, explained in detail with a sufficient explanation. This is indicated by the form of the verb "tafʿīl" (causative form) in both verbs, especially after the second occurs. Or it is in the form "ifʿāl" (another causative form). Because "tabyīn" (clarification) is more general than explicit statement of the intended meaning, and than guidance to what indicates it, it encompasses analogical reasoning (qiyās) in general, whether in the legal rulings or otherwise. Perhaps His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿and perhaps they will reflect﴾ points to that (p-117), that is, the aim that they should contemplate, so that they become alert to the realities and to the lessons contained in it, and guard against what would lead to the like of the punishment that befell the earlier peoples.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 45:

﴿Do those who devised evil plots feel secure﴾ They are the people of Makkah who plotted against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and sought to block his Companions from faith, may Allah be pleased with them, not those who schemed for the destruction of the prophets, as has been said. Nor is it one that encompasses both groups, because the intent is to warn these people against suffering the like of what befell those others of the various kinds of punishment that were recounted. And "al-sayyi'at" (the evil deeds) is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun (masdar), i.e., "they plotted" (makaru). The plots are the evil deeds that were related about them. Or it is the direct object of the verb mentioned, on the basis of its being construed with the sense of "doing" (i.e., "they did evil deeds"). Then His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿that Allah cause the earth to swallow them﴾ is the object of "feel secure" (amina). Or "al-sayyi'at" is an attribute of what is the object, i.e., "Do those who plot feel secure from the evil punishments?" And His saying, "that He cause to swallow..." ... etc., is a substitute for that. In any case, the "fa" (then) is for conjunction with an implied element which the noble composition extends to, i.e., "We sent down to you the Reminder so that you might make clear to them its content, of which are reports of the destroyed nations with various kinds of punishment, and that they might reflect upon it. Did they not reflect? Do those who devised evil plots feel secure that Allah cause the earth to swallow them, as was done to Qarun?" This is with the negation directed at both conjoined elements together. Or "Did they reflect, and then feel secure?" with it directed at the conjoined element, since feeling secure after reflection is something almost no one would do. It has also been said: it is a conjunction with an implied element indicated by the relative clause, i.e., "Were they plotted against, and so those who plotted feel secure...", etc.

﴿Or that the punishment come upon them from where they do not perceive﴾ without perceiving its coming, i.e., while they are heedless, or from their place of safety, or from where they hope the arrival of what they desire, as was related earlier concerning what befell those who plotted.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 46:

﴿Or He seizes them in their going to and fro﴾, i.e., in the state of their going to and fro in their journeys and their trade.

﴿Then they cannot escape﴾, i.e., they cannot prevent it, or they cannot escape by fleeing and running away, as the state of going to and fro and traveling might suggest. The "fa'" (the particle "fa", here "then") is either to give the reason for the seizing, or to indicate that the non-escaping follows from it, signifying the continuance of the negation, not the negation of continuance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 47:

﴿Or He seizes them while they are in fear.﴾ That is: in apprehension and caution against destruction and punishment, by destroying a people before them, so that they become fearful and the punishment seizes them while they are in a state of fear. Since the two states, of turning about (taqallub) and of fear (takhawwuf), are a presumed occasion for flight, the striking of the punishment during them is expressed by "seizing" (al-akhdh), and its striking them in a state of heedlessness, which indicates stillness, is expressed by "coming" (al-ityan). It has also been said: takhawwuf means diminishing (tanaqqus). One of them said:

Ghayr: The traveler's saddle became fearful of her, a bald-backed, mangy camel, as the bow-wood of the nab'a tree is worn down by the scraper.

That is: He seizes them by diminishing them little by little in their persons and their wealth, until they are destroyed.

The purpose of mentioning the three conditions is to show God's power, may He be glorified, to destroy them in any manner whatsoever, not to restrict it to these.

﴿Indeed your Lord is Kind and Merciful﴾, in that He does not hasten to punish you, and forbears from you despite your deserving it.

(p-118) ﴿Awa-lam yaraw﴾ is an interrogative of denial (istifham inkari). It is also read in the second-person form (ʿala sighat al-khitab). The waw is for coordination (al-ʿatf) upon an implied element required by the context, meaning: "Have they not looked, and have they not seen while turning [their attention]," ﴿to what God has created of a thing﴾, that is, of every thing, ﴿whose shadows turn about﴾, that is, return little by little as dictated by the will of the Creator, may He be exalted, for tafayyu' (the turning about of shadows) is the intransitive form (mutawiʿ) of ifa'ah (causing to return). It is also read with the verb feminine (bi-ta'nith al-fiʿl): ﴿from the right and the left﴾, that is, have they not seen the things that have shadows which turn away from their right sides and their left sides, meaning from the two sides of each one of them. This usage is borrowed for them from the right and left of a human being. ﴿Prostrating to God﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the shadows, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and their shadows in the mornings and evenings﴾. What is meant by their prostration is their being disposed according to the will of God, glorified is He, and their submission to His will, may He be exalted, in lengthening, contracting and other things, without resisting Him in what He has subjected them to. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿while they are humbled﴾, that is, abased and submissive, is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿their shadows﴾. The plural is used in view of the meaning, and the form specific to rational beings is employed because humbling (dukhur) is among their characteristics. The meaning: the shadows return from one side to another by the rising and descending of the sun, or by the difference of its risings and settings, for each day of the year it moves upon a specific orbit among the daily orbits, by the determination of the Mighty, the All-Knowing, submitting to what has been decreed for it of turning about, or lying upon the earth, clinging to it in the manner of one prostrating, while its owners, the bodies, are humbled and submitting to His judgment, may He be exalted. Describing the shadows with humbling suffices in place of describing their shadows with it. Or both are circumstantial clauses from the referred-to pronoun, and the meaning: the shadows of those bodies return while being submissive to God, may He be exalted, and humbled. Thus describing them with both suffices in place of describing their shadows with both. Perhaps what is meant by the relative pronoun is inanimate things: mountains, trees and stones, whose shadows show no effect except turning about by the aforementioned rising and descending of the sun, or the difference of its risings and settings. As for animals, their shadow moves with their movement. It has been said: what is meant by "right" and "left" is the right side of the celestial sphere, which is its eastern side, because the stars appear from it rising and shining; and its left, which is its western side opposite to it. For the shadows at the beginning of the day begin from the east, falling upon the western quarter of the earth, and at noon they begin from the west, falling upon the eastern quarter of it. After explaining the prostration of the shadows and their owners among the lower bodies, whose reports are established, and their humbling before Him, glorified and exalted is He, he began to explain the prostration of the created beings that move by will, whether or not they have shadows. So it is said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 49:

﴿And to Allah prostrates﴾ i.e., to Him alone, the Exalted, submits and obeys, not to anything else, either independently or in partnership. Thus the restriction (al-qasr) encompasses both the inversion (al-qalb) and the singling out (al-ifrad), but the more fitting for the state of the addressees is the restriction of singling out (qasr al-ifrad), as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah said: Take not two gods, two.﴾

﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾ entirely, and ﴿whatever is on the earth﴾ of whatever kind, ﴿of living creature﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of what is on the earth. Its being placed first is due to its scarcity, and so that a separation does not occur between the explained and the explanation. The singular form, although the intended meaning is the plural, serves to convey the clarity of the inclusion of prostration for every single individual of the living creatures. Al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash) said: it is like your saying, "No man came to me like him," and "No men came to me like him."

﴿and the angels﴾ is coordinated (atf) upon what is in the heavens. Gabriel was coordinated upon the angels for the sake of magnification and honour. Or it is coordinated upon the intention that what is in the heavens refers to the creation called the Spirit. Or it refers to the angels of the heavens. By His saying "and the angels," it refers to the angels of the earth, among them the guardians (al-hafazah) and others.

﴿and they﴾, i.e., the angels, despite the eminence of their rank, ﴿are not proud﴾ from worshipping Him, mighty and majestic is He, and from prostrating to Him. The placing of the pronoun first is not for restriction. The clause is either a circumstantial state (hal) from the subject pronoun in "prostrates," attributed to the angels, or a resumptive statement (istinaf) in which they are informed of this.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 50:

﴿They fear their Lord﴾, i.e., the Owner of their affair. In this there is an inculcation of awe and an indication of the reason for the ruling.

﴿from above them﴾, i.e., they fear Him, exalted and high is He, with the fear of reverence and veneration, and He is above them in dominion, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾. Or [it means] they fear that He will send down upon them a punishment from above them. The clause is either a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun in ﴿they are not arrogant﴾, or an explanation of it and a confirmation, because whoever fears God, glorified is He, is not arrogant toward His worship.

﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾, i.e., what they are commanded with of acts of obedience and of governance. The use of the verb in the passive form accords with the customs of majesty, and signifies that there is no need to mention the agent explicitly, since it is impossible for it to be ascribed to anyone other than Him, glorified is He. In it [is also the indication] that the angels are obligated and balanced between fear and hope. After He had made clear that all existent things are subject to submission and natural compliance, and what is similar to it, such as the worship of the angels, since it is inconceivable that they would fail to comply with God, mighty and majestic, at all, He followed that with relating His prohibition, glorified and exalted is He, to the obligated ones against associating partners [with Him]. So it is said:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 16, verse 51:**

﴿And Allah said﴾, coordinated (*'atf*, grammatical coordination) with His statement "And to Allah prostrates…", and the subject is stated explicitly. The Divine Name *Allah* (*lafẓat al-jalala*) is mentioned specifically to signal that He alone is the one deserving of divinity (*ulūhiyya*). What is forbidden is associating partners with Him (*al-ishrāk bihi*), not the absolute taking of two gods in a way that would be satisfied by abandoning either one. That is, He said to all the responsible persons (*al-mukallafīn*): ﴿Do not take two gods﴾. The number is mentioned even though the dual form already conveys it, to show that the thrust of the prohibition is duality itself, and that duality is incompatible with divinity. Likewise, the description of God as one in His statement ﴿Indeed, He is only one God﴾ serves to show that the intended point is the affirmation of oneness (*wahdāniyya*), which is among the necessary attributes of divinity (*ilāhiyya*). As for divinity itself, it is a matter whose affirmation for Him, glory be to Him, is already accepted. This is indicated by attributing the statement to Him. Here there is an *iltifāt* (shift in grammatical person) from the first person (speech) to the third person (absence), according to the view of those who are satisfied that an *iltifāt* exists when the discourse shifted from is the proper form of speech, and who do not require that the referent have been mentioned previously in that particular form.

﴿So fear Me alone﴾: this is an *iltifāt* from the third person to the first person, to cultivate awe and cast reverence into hearts. For this reason the object was placed first and the verb was repeated. That is: if you are fearing anything, then fear Me, fear only Me, for I am that One to whom prostrates whatever is in the heavens and the earth.

**﴿And to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾** — in creation and in dominion. This establishes the cause for which everything in them submits to Him, glorified is He, exclusively, and affirms that fear is due to Him, exalted is He, alone. The placing of the adverbial phrase first serves to strengthen the sense of exclusivity contained in the *lam* (of possession). The same applies to His saying, exalted is He: **﴿And to Him is the religion﴾**, meaning obedience and submission.

**﴿Perpetual﴾**, meaning obligatory and firmly established, without any cessation for Him, since it has been established that He alone is the God who truly deserves to be feared. It was also said that *wāṣiban* derives from *al-waṣb* (hardship, toil), meaning: **and to Him is the religion, involving hardship**. It was further said that *al-dīn* here means recompense, meaning: **and to Him belongs the perpetual recompense**, such that its reward for whoever believes and its punishment for whoever disbelieves never end.

**﴿Then is it other than God that you fear?﴾** The *al-hamza* (the interrogative particle) is for denial and rebuke, and the *al-fa'* (the conjunctive particle "then") is for coordination with an implied element that the context carries along, meaning: after the establishment of the matters mentioned, namely the restriction of all existent things to prostration before Him, exalted is He, that all of this belongs to Him, and His prohibition of taking rivals, and that the religion is His perpetually, which necessitates restricting fear of God, glorified is He, to Him alone, **is it other than God, whose state is what has been mentioned, that you fear, so that you obey?**

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 53:

﴿Whatever blessing is with you﴾: that is, whatever thing attaches to you and accompanies you, of any blessing whatsoever, ﴿it is from Allah﴾, meaning it is from Allah. So "ma" (whatever) is either conditional (shart), or a relative pronoun (mawsulah) that implicitly carries the meaning of a condition with regard to the informing and not to the occurrence; for the attachment of a blessing to you is the reason for the informing that it is from Him, the Exalted, and not because it is from Him, the Exalted.

﴿Then when harm touches you﴾, touching it lightly, ﴿to Him you cry for help﴾: you humble yourselves in supplication for its removal, not to anyone else. Al-judar (crying for help) means raising the voice in supplication and seeking aid. Al-A'sha said:

؎ It alternates, of the prayers of the angels, between prostration at times and crying out at other times.

It is also read (tajjarun), with the hamzah dropped and its vowel transferred to the letter before it. Mentioning "touch" (massa), which indicates the slightest contact, and expressing it with the verbal sentence (al-jumlah al-fi'liyyah), which signifies occurrence, together with "then" (thumma), which indicates that it happens after a interval of time; the definiteness of "harm" (ad-durr) with the article of genus (lam al-jins), which conveys the slightest contact with whatever is called by that generic name; the expression of the blessing with the nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah), which indicates permanence; the expression of their attachment to the addressees with the preposition of accompaniment (ba' al-musahabah); and the use of "ma" (whatever), which indicates generality: all of this reflects a grandeur and magnificence that is not hidden. Perhaps the use of "idha" (when) rather than "in" (if) is to secure, by means of it, the certainty of the occurrence of the answer.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 54:

﴿Then, when He removes the harm from you﴾. It is also read: (kāshafa al-ḍurr, "He has removed the harm"). The word thumma (then) does not indicate that the duration during which the harm touched them was prolonged, or that the removal occurred after a lengthy interval. Rather, it indicates the remoteness of the rank of what follows from it, namely the sudden shift to associating partners with God, which is indicated by His words, glorified is He: ﴿at once a party of you associate partners with their Lord﴾. Its consequence upon that is at the furthest extreme of misguidance. Then, if the address is directed to all people, then "min" (of) is partitive (lil-tab'īḍ), and the party (farīq) is the party of disbelievers. If the address is directed to the disbelievers, then "min" is explanatory (lil-bayān), as if it were said: "when there is a disbelieving party, and they are you." It is also possible that among them there were those who took heed and were restrained, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then when He brings them safely to land, some of them are moderate﴾. So "min" is partitive here too. The mention of the attribute of lordship (rubūbiyya) serves to signal the complete ugliness of what they committed of associating partners and ingratitude.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 55:

﴿That they may deny what We have given them﴾ of the blessing of relief from them. It is as if they made their aim in associating partners with Allah the denial of the blessing and the rejection that it comes from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿So enjoy yourselves﴾ is a command of threat, and the shift to address (khitab) is to signal (li'l-i'dhan) the extremity of wrath. It is also read with the yā' (yalkafurū and yatamattaʿū, in the passive voice) as a conjunction with "liyakfurū", such that denial of the blessing and enjoyment become an aim for them from associating partners. It is permissible that the lām be the lām of command (lam al-amr) that comes for threat.

﴿But you will soon know﴾ the outcome of your affair and the punishment that will descend upon you. In it is a firm warning, indicating a severe seizing, since the object is not mentioned, to signal (ish'ar) that it is of a kind that cannot be described.

(p-121) ﴿Wa-yajʿalūna﴾ ("and they assign"): this is probably coordinated (ʿaṭf) with what precedes in meaning, as an enumeration of their offenses. That is: they do what they do of supplication (juʾār) to God Most High when harm touches them, and of associating partners with Him when it is removed; and they assign ﴿to what they do not know﴾, i.e., to what they do not know the reality of, nor its lowly worth, of the inanimate objects (jamādāt) which they take as partners to God, glory be to Him, out of ignorance and foolishness, and they claim that these will benefit them and intercede for them. (This is) on the basis that "mā" is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), and its returning pronoun is omitted. Or (it means) ﴿to what has no knowledge at all, and it is not in its nature to have that﴾. So "mā" is also a relative pronoun, and its returning pronoun is the concealed pronoun within the verb; the plural form used for rational beings (ṣīghat jamʿ al-ʿuqalāʾ) is because "mā" refers to their gods, whom they described with the attributes of rational beings. Or "mā" is a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah). The lām is for causation (taʿlīl), i.e., because of their not knowing; and the one for whom it is assigned (al-majʿūl lahu) is for the knowledge of its place.

﴿a portion of what We have provided them﴾: of the crops and livestock and other things, seeking nearness to them.

﴿By God, you will certainly be questioned﴾ with a question of rebuke and reproach ﴿about what you used to fabricate﴾ in the world, by claiming that they are true gods deserving to be drawn near to. And in beginning the sentence with the oath, and shifting the speech from the third person to the second person, which indicates the completeness of anger due to the severity of the threat, there is something not hidden.

**﴿They attribute daughters to Allah﴾**: they are Khuza'ah and Kinanah, the ones who say that the angels are the daughters of Allah. **﴿Glory be to Him﴾** is a declaration of His transcendence and sanctity, Mighty and Majestic is He, above the meaning of their saying. Or it is an expression of wonder at their audacity in uttering such a monstrous thing.

**﴿And for them is what they desire﴾**, namely of sons. The word *mā* (ما) is in the nominative position, as the subject (*mubtada'*), with the adverbial phrase preceding it as its predicate (*khabar*), and the clause is in the circumstantial position (*ḥāliyyah*). The phrase *subḥānahu* (سبحانه) is a parenthetical interjection (*i'tirāḍ*) placed in its proper location. Making *mā* accusative by coordinating it with *al-banāt* (البنات, "the daughters") is also possible, meaning: they attribute to themselves what they desire of sons. This leads to attributing the act of attribution itself, in the sense that it encompasses both the claim and the choice.

﴿When one of them is given the good news of a female⁠—﴾ that is, he is informed of her birth. ﴿his face remains darkened﴾ that is, it becomes, or remains, dark all day, ﴿darkened﴾ from grief and from shame before people. The darkening of the face is a metaphor (kinayah) for distress and disturbance.

﴿while he suppresses his rage﴾ that is, filled with seething anger and fury.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 59:

﴿Hides himself﴾, that is, he conceals himself ﴿from the people because of the evil of that which he has been given good news of﴾, on account of its evil. The expression "that which" (*ma*) is used for it in order to strip it of the rank of rational beings. ﴿Whether he will keep it﴾, that is, hesitating over his matter and debating within himself about his situation, ﴿whether he will keep it﴾ ﴿with humiliation﴾, with disgrace. It was also read as (*hawanin*).

﴿Or will he bury it﴾, concealing it ﴿in the dust﴾ by burying it alive (*wa'd*). The masculine pronoun is used in view of the wording of *ma* (*lafz ma*). It was also read with the feminine.

﴿Surely evil is what they judge﴾, in that they assign to God what is of this nature, which they regard as humiliation and contemptibility, the One exalted above having a consort or a child. Yet they shun it for themselves and choose sons for themselves. So the root of the error lies in their assigning that to God, the Glorified, while they themselves recoil from it, not in their choosing sons for themselves, nor in their not assigning it to Him, the Glorified. It is also possible that the root of the error is reversal (*ta'kis*), in keeping with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That, then, is an unfair division﴾.

(p-122) ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, of those whose vile qualities were mentioned, ﴿is the attribute of evil﴾: the evil attribute which is like a parable in its ugliness, namely the need for a son to take their place at their death, the preference for males so as to be supported by them, the burying of daughters to avoid shame, and the fear of poverty, which calls out to them. All of this indicates incapacity, deficiency, and extreme miserliness. Placing the relative pronoun in the position of the pronoun serves to indicate that the basis of their being characterized by those vile qualities is their disbelief in the Hereafter.

﴿And to Allah﴾, glory be to Him and exalted, belongs ﴿the most exalted parable﴾, i.e., the wondrous attribute which is a parable of absolute loftiness: necessary existence in Himself (al-wujub al-dhati), absolute self-sufficiency (al-ghina al-mutlaq), vast generosity (al-jud al-wasi'), and transcendence above the attributes of created beings. It also includes His exaltation above what they say, a great exaltation.

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, who alone possesses perfect power, especially in calling them to account for their sins, ﴿the Wise﴾, who does everything He does in accordance with consummate wisdom. This too is among His wondrous attributes, exalted is He.

﴿And if Allah were to take people to task for their wrongdoing﴾, meaning the disbelievers, for their unbelief and their sins, among which are the vile deeds already enumerated, ﴿He would not leave upon it﴾, that is, upon the earth (indicated by the word "people"), ﴿a single creature﴾. This is an explicit statement of what His words ﴿but He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾ imply, and a notice that the vile deeds they have committed have reached a limit beyond which there is no end. And by His words ﴿a single creature﴾, the meaning is: He would leave upon it no creature at all, but would destroy it entirely because of the ill omen of the wrongdoing of the wrongdoers. This is like His words: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike only those among you who have done wrong﴾.

It is reported from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he heard a man say: "The wrongdoer harms only himself." He said: "No, by Allah, even the great bustard (al-ḥubārā, a bird) dies in its nest because of the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer."

And it is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "The dung beetle (al-ju'al) nearly perished in its hole because of the sin of the son of Adam, or of a wrongdoing creature."

It has been said: If He were to destroy the fathers, the sons would not exist, and it would follow that there would be no creature on the earth, since creatures were created for the benefit of mankind, according to His words, glorified is He: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾.

﴿But﴾ He does not take them to task for that; rather, ﴿He defers them until an appointed term﴾, either for their lifespans or for their punishment, so that they may multiply, or so that their punishment may increase.

﴿So when their term comes﴾, the appointed one, ﴿they cannot delay it﴾ beyond that term; that is, they cannot postpone it. The form of the verb here, istif'āl (the tenth verbal form, which expresses seeking or effort), is used to indicate their inability to delay it despite their seeking to do so, ﴿even for an hour﴾, a single hour. This is a figure of speech for the shortness of the period.

﴿Nor can they advance it﴾, that is, they cannot move ahead. Its mention, although advancing is not conceivable when the term arrives, is made in order to emphasize the impossibility of delay, by placing it in the same series as what is impossible, as in His words: ﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have now repented," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers﴾. For one who dies as a disbeliever, although he has no repentance at all, is placed in the same string as those whose repentance is not accepted, to indicate that the two are alike in that respect. This has already been discussed in the commentary on Surah Yunus.

(p-123) That is: they attribute to Him, glorified is He, and they ascribe to Him, in their claim, ﴿what they dislike﴾ for themselves of what has been mentioned. This is a repetition of what preceded it, a second time for the sake of rebuke and as a preparation for His words, exalted is He: ﴿and their tongues describe the lie﴾. That is: they assign to Him, exalted is He, what they assign, and yet their tongues describe the lie, which is ﴿that theirs is the best﴾, the best outcome with Allah, exalted is He, like His words: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, surely I shall have the best with Him﴾. It has also been read as "al-Kudhub" (الكُذُبَ), which is the plural of kadhub (الكَذُوب, "habitual liar"), taken as an adjective of "the tongues."

﴿Without doubt (lā jaram)﴾ is a rejection of their statement and an affirmation of its opposite, meaning: truly.

﴿that for them﴾ in place of what they hoped for of the best.

﴿the Fire﴾, whose torment has no torment beyond it, and which is a designation for the worst abode (al-sawʼā, السَّوْأى).

﴿and that they are ones who are left behind (mufraṭūn)﴾: that is, those who are brought forward to it, from afrattuhu, meaning I sent him ahead in the search for water. It has also been said: those who are forgotten, from "afraṭtu fulānan khalfī," when you leave someone behind and forget him. It is also read with shaddah and a fatḥah on the rāʼ (فَرَّطْتُهُ, from farraṭtuhu, "I sent him ahead in search of water"), and with a kasrah on the shaddah rāʼ (مُفَرِّطُون, from tafrīṭ, "neglect") in regard to acts of obedience, and with a kasrah on the unshaddah rāʼ (مُفْرِطُون, from ifrāṭ, "excess") in regard to sins. In that case, these two readings do not then count among their conditions in the Hereafter, as they are coordinated with what precedes them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 63:

﴿By Allah, We certainly sent [messengers] to communities before you﴾ — a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he suffers from the ignorance of the disbelievers, and a warning to them for that. That is: We sent messengers to them, and they called them to the truth, but they did not respond to it.

﴿So Satan made their deeds seem fair to them﴾ — the ugly deeds — so they clung to them, persisting.

﴿He is their walī﴾ — that is, their companion (qarīn), and what an evil companion.

﴿Today﴾ — that is, the day when Satan made their deeds seem fair to them, in which case it is a narration of a past situation; or in the world; or the Day of Resurrection, in which case it is a narration of a future situation, namely their state of being punished in the Fire. The walī here means the helper (nāṣir), that is: he is their helper today, and they have no helper other than him, as an emphatic negation of any helper for them. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the idolaters of Quraysh, and the meaning is: he made the deeds of the earlier nations seem fair to them, so he is the walī of these people because they are of them. It is also permissible that there is an omitted modifier, that is: the walī of their likes.

﴿And for them﴾ — in the Hereafter — ﴿is a painful punishment﴾, which is the punishment of the Fire.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 64:

﴿And We did not send down to you the Book﴾ That is: the Qur'an.

﴿except that you may make clear﴾ This is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of the causes (al-'ilal), meaning: We did not send it down to you for any cause among the causes, except that you may make clear ﴿to them﴾, that is, to the people, ﴿that wherein they differ﴾ concerning monotheism (tawhid), predestination (qadar), the rulings on acts (ahkam al-af'al), and the states of the Return (ahwal al-ma'ad).

﴿and as a guidance and a mercy﴾ These two are coordinated (ma'tufan) with the grammatical position (mahall) of "li-tubayyina," meaning: and for guidance and mercy ﴿for a people who believe﴾. They are put in the accusative (intasaba) because they are the effects (athar) of the agent of the causally-explained verb, unlike "al-tabayyun," where it is not in the accusative because its condition is absent. Perhaps the reason for placing it before them is its precedence in existence (li-taqaddumihi fi al-wujud), and the restriction of their being guidance and mercy to the believers is because they are the ones who benefit from its effects.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 65:

﴿And Allah sends down from the sky﴾ from the clouds, or from the direction of the sky, as has passed. This is a repetition of what preceded it, for emphasis of its content, and as a preparation (tawti'a) for the proofs of monotheism (tawhid) that follow it. ﴿water﴾: a specific type of water, namely rain. The placing of the prepositional phrase (majrur) before the object (mansub) is, as has passed many times, (p-124) for the sake of creating suspense (tashwiq) toward the delayed element. ﴿And He gives life thereby to the earth﴾ by what He causes to grow in it of various kinds of plants ﴿after its death﴾, i.e., after its drying out. What the particle fa' (then) indicates of customary sequence (ta'qib 'adi) does not contradict the interval (muhla) that exists between the two conjoined elements. ﴿Indeed, in that﴾, i.e., in the sending down of water from the sky and the giving of life to the dead earth through it, ﴿is surely a sign﴾, and what a sign it is, indicating His unity, glory be to Him, His knowledge, His power, and His wisdom.

﴿for a people who hear﴾: hearing this reminder and its counterparts as hearing of reflection and contemplation. It is as if whoever is not like this is deaf.

And indeed, in the cattle there is for you a great lesson. What a lesson it is, whose depths minds are unable to fathom, and whose understanding bewilders the wisdom of the wise.

﴿We give you to drink﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) explaining what was left vague at the beginning concerning the lesson. ﴿From what is in their bellies﴾ means: in the bellies of the cattle. The masculine pronoun here is in consideration of the wording, since *an'am* is a collective noun (*ism jam'*). For this reason Sibawayh counted it among the nouns built on the pattern *af'āl*, like *akbāsh* ("rams") and *akhlāq* ("characters"). Its feminine form in Surat al-Mu'minun is in consideration of the meaning. Whoever took it to be the plural of *na'am* made the pronoun refer to some of them, since milk does not come from all of them. The first reading is according to the meaning, since what is intended is the genus.

It is also read with a *fatḥa* on the *nūn* here, and in Surat al-Mu'minun: ﴿from between dung and blood, milk﴾. *Al-farth* is the residue of the fodder that remains in the rumen after it has been partly digested, and the thick part of what remains in the intestines. It is related from Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when an animal grazes and the fodder is cooked in its rumen, its lowest part becomes dung, its middle part becomes milk, and its upper part becomes blood. Perhaps what is meant is that its middle part is the material of milk, and its upper part is the material of the blood that nourishes the body, since it is beyond doubt that milk and blood are not formed in the rumen itself. Rather, the liver draws the pure essence of the food that has been digested in the rumen, and what remains of it, its sediment, is the dung. Then the liver retains it for a while until it digests it, producing four humours along with a watery substance. The discerning faculty then separates from that watery substance what exceeds the needed amount of the two biles, yellow and black, and pushes them to the kidney, the gall bladder and the spleen. Then it distributes the rest to the organs according to their needs, giving each its due in the manner suited to it, by the decree of the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing. Then, if the animal is female, the humours in her exceed her nourishment because cold and moisture dominate her temperament. So the surplus is first directed to the womb for the sake of the foetus. When it is delivered, that surplus, or part of it, flows into the udders, where it turns white through its contact with the white glandular flesh there, its taste becomes pleasant, and it becomes milk.

Whoever reflects on the marvels of the creation of Allah, exalted is He, in what has been mentioned of these humours and milks, the numbers of their reservoirs and channels, the causes that generate them, and the powers that govern them at every moment in the manner suited to each, will be compelled to acknowledge the perfection of His knowledge, power and wisdom, and the limitless extent of His kindness and mercy.

The first ﴿مِن﴾ (*min*) is partitive (*tab'īḍiyya*), because milk is a part of what is in their bellies, since it is created from a part of the blood which is produced from the subtle particles that are in the dung, as explained. The second ﴿مِن﴾ is initial (*ibtidā'iyya*), as in the saying: "I drank from the pool," because between the dung and the blood lies the starting point of the giving to drink. It is connected to ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ﴾. Its placement before the object is, as has been noted many times, because placing before its place what should be delayed arouses in the soul a longing for the delayed element, which makes its arrival more welcome. This is especially so when the fronted element contains a description that contrasts with the description of the delayed element, as in this case, since there is a contrast and distance between the descriptions of the fronted and delayed elements, such that their fires cannot be seen from each other. This increases the longing and eager anticipation for the delayed element, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who made for you fire from the green tree﴾.

Or it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from ﴿لَبَنًا﴾ (*labanan*, "milk"), placed before it because it is indefinite, and to draw attention to the fact that this is the place of the lesson. ﴿Pure﴾ (*khāliṣan*), free from any admixture of the qualities found in the blood and the dung, by a barrier of overpowering power that prevents either of them from oppressing it, even though both surround it. ﴿Palatable to the drinkers﴾ (*sā'ighan li-sh-shāribīn*), easy to pass down their throats. It has been said that no one has ever choked on milk. It is also read as (*sayyighan*) with a doubled letter and without doubling, like *hayn* and *hayyin*.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 67:

﴿And of the fruits of the date-palms and the grapevines﴾ is connected to what the watering implies, namely the general sense of feeding that encompasses giving both food and drink, for milk is both food and drink. That is: "And We feed you from the fruits of the date-palms and from the grapevines," that is, from their juice (ʿaṣīr). And His, exalted is He, saying ﴿you take from it intoxicant (sakar)﴾ is a resumption (istiʾnāf) to explain the essence (kunh) of the feeding and to disclose it; or it is connected to His saying "you take from it," and the repetition of the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) is for emphasis; or it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada') whose qualifier is "you take," that is: "And of the fruits of the date-palms and the grapevines there is fruit from which you take [an intoxicant]." Omitting the qualified noun when the word "min" is present in the speech is permissible, as in His, exalted is He, saying ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾. The pronoun is masculine in the first two readings because it refers to the omitted annexed noun, namely "the juice" (ʿaṣīr). Or because the intended meaning is the genus, and sakar is a verbal noun (maṣdar) by which wine (khamr) is named. It has been said that it is nabidh (date or grape infusion), and it has been said that it is the taste (ṭaʿm).

﴿And a good provision (rizq ḥasan)﴾ such as dates, date-syrup (dibs), raisins, and vinegar (khall). If the verse was revealed before the prohibition of wine, it indicates its disapproval; otherwise it combines reproach and a reminder of favour (minna).

﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ manifest ﴿for a people who use reason﴾, who employ their intellects upon the signs through reflection and contemplation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 68:

﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾ That is: He caused it to know by instinct (alhama), cast into its hearts, and taught it in a manner that none knows except the All-Knowing, the All-Aware.

It is also read with two fathahs: ﴿that take⁠﴾ meaning: "that take," where "an" (that) is a verbal particle (masdariyyah, introducing a verbal noun). It may also be an explanatory particle (mufassirah) for the sense of speech (qawl) implicit in the inspiration (iha'). The feminine pronoun is used although al-nahl (the bee) is masculine, either by considering the sense (hamlan 'ala al-ma'na) or because it is a plural of nahlah (a single bee), and the feminine form is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz.

﴿Of the mountains, dwellings﴾ That is: nests, together with the cells (khalaya) in them. It is also read as (biyutan) with a kasrah on the ba'. ﴿And of the trees and of what they erect﴾ That is: what people raise (ya'rishuhu al-nas), i.e., what they elevate of vines or roofs. It has been said that what is meant is what people raise and build for the bees. The meaning is: take for yourself dwellings of mountains and trees if you have no keepers; otherwise, take what they build for you. The use of the partitive particle (harf al-tab'id) is because it does not build in every mountain, every tree, every trellis, nor in every place within them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 69:

﴿Then eat of all the fruits﴾ — of every fruit that you desire, sweet or bitter.

﴿Then follow﴾ what you have eaten of them ﴿the ways of your Lord﴾, that is, His paths which He created such that by His overpowering power He transforms the bitter nectar within your bodies into honey; or, follow the ways which He inspired you to use in making honey; or, follow, returning to your homes, the ways of your Lord which are not rough for you nor confusing. ﴿Made smooth﴾ — the plural of dhalul (ṭhalūl), which is a state (ḥāl) of "the ways," meaning: made easy, not rough, which Allah, glorified is He, made smooth and facile for you; or it is a state of the pronoun in "follow," meaning: follow, submissive to what you have been commanded.

﴿There comes forth from their bellies﴾ — a resumed statement (isti'nāf), turned away from addressing the bee, to explain what appears from them of the marvels of Allah's creation, which are the place of lesson after they were commanded with what they were commanded.

﴿A drink﴾ — that is, honey, because it is drunk. Whoever claims that bees eat flowers and fragrant leaves, which are transformed in their bellies into honey, and then regurgitate it as a store for winter, argues with this and with His saying, "eat" (kulī). And whoever claims that they pick up with their mouths small, sweet, scattered particles upon flowers and leaves and place them in their hives, so that when a great amount gathers there it becomes honey, interprets "bellies" as "mouths."

﴿Of varying colors﴾ — white, black, yellow and red, according to the difference in the age of the bee, or the season, or the source from which it took the honey.

﴿Wherein is healing for mankind﴾ — either by itself, as in phlegmatic diseases, or with other things, as in all other diseases, since there is rarely an electuary (ma'jūn) in which there is no honey. The indefiniteness (tankīr) of "healing" indicates subordination (tab'iyya), and it is permissible that it is for exaltation (tafkhīm). It is related from Qatada that "a man came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: My brother complains of his stomach. The Prophet ﷺ said: Give him honey to drink. He went and then returned and said: I have given him to drink, but it did not benefit him. He said: Go and give him honey to drink, for Allah has spoken the truth and the belly of your brother has lied. So he gave him to drink and he was cured," as if he had been released from a bond. It has also been said: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, or to what Allah, exalted is He, has explained of the states of the bee. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: Honey is a healing for every disease, and the Qur'an is a healing for what is in the breasts; so hold fast to the two healings, honey and the Qur'an.

﴿Indeed in that﴾ — what has been mentioned of the marvels of the effects of Allah's power, exalted is He, ﴿is surely a sign﴾, great, ﴿for a people who reflect﴾. For whoever reflects upon the bee's being singled out with those subtle sciences and wondrous actions, which include excellent craftsmanship and correct division, which the most skilled engineers cannot achieve except with delicate instruments, fine tools and precise observation, is certain with definite conviction that it has a Creator who is powerful and wise, who inspires it with that and guides it thereto, may His majesty be exalted.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 70:

﴿And Allah created you﴾. When He, glorified is He, mentioned some of the wonders of the states of what He had mentioned—namely the water, the plants, the livestock and the bee—He pointed to some of the wonders of the states of mankind from the beginning of his life to its end, and his transformations in between. They have fixed the stages of life in four: the first is the age of growth and increase (sinn al-nushur wa al-nama'). The second is the age of standing still, which is the age of youth (sinn al-shabab). The third is the age of slight decline, which is the age of maturity (sinn al-kuhula). The fourth is the age of great decline, which is the age of decrepitude (sinn al-shaykhukha).

﴿Then He causes you to die﴾, as His will requires, which is founded on far-reaching wisdoms, at differing terms: children, youths and old people. ﴿And among you is one who is brought back﴾ before his death, that is, he is returned.

﴿To the most abject part of life﴾, that is, its lowest and most worthless part, which is seventy-five years according to what is related from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. And ninety years according to what is reported from Qatada, may Allah be pleased with him. It was said: ninety-five. The preference for "return" (radd) over "reaching" (wusul), "attaining" (bulugh) and the like is to indicate that his attaining it and arriving at it is in reality a return to weakness after strength, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whomever We cause to live long, We reverse him in creation﴾. And there is no life worse in condition than the life of senility, which resembles childhood in the deficiency of intellect and strength.

﴿So that he does not know, after knowledge﴾ much, ﴿anything﴾ of knowledge or of (p-127) the known things; or so that he does not know anything after knowing that thing. It was said: so that he does not understand, after his first understanding, anything. ﴿Indeed Allah is Knowing﴾ of the measures of your lifespans, ﴿Competent﴾ over everything, who causes the vigorous youth to die and preserves the decrepit, perishing old man.
