In this is an admonition that the variation in terms is only by the decree of a Capable, Wise One who fashioned their structures and balanced their temperaments to a known measure; and if that were required by natures, the variation would not have reached this extent.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 16, verse 71:**

﴿And Allah has favored some of you over others in provision.﴾ That is: He made you differ in it, and gave you more of it than He gave your *mamalik* (the people your right hands possess, i.e., slaves).

﴿So those who have been favored﴾ in it over others ﴿do not return their provision﴾ which He gave them ﴿to those whom their right hands possess﴾, to their *mamalik* who are their partners in being created and in being provided for, ﴿so that they are equal in it﴾, that is, the owners and the owned (*al-mulluk wa al-mamalik*) are equal in it, that is, in provision. ﴿So that they are equal in it﴾ means that they do not give it back to them in such a way that they become equal in disposing of it, or share in managing it. The *fa'* (the particle "so") in *fa-* indicates the sequence of equality upon the returning. That is: they do not return it to them with a return that results in equality. They only return to them a small portion of it. Since they are not pleased for their *mamalik* to be equal to themselves, although they are alike to them in being human and created, and the provision that Allah, mighty is His authority, gives is not specific to them but encompasses them and their *mamalik*, and they are equal with them in its entitlement, then what is wrong with them that they associate with Allah, glorified and exalted is He, in what befits none but Him, namely divinity and the worship specific to His Essence, exalted is He, some of His creatures, which is far beyond the level of consideration? This, as you see, is an example struck to illustrate the utter ugliness of what the polytheists do, as a rebuke to them, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you have among those whom your right hands possess any partners in what We have provided you, so that you are equal in it?﴾ ... the verse.

﴿Then do they deny the favor of Allah?﴾ That is, in that they do what they do of associating partners with Him, for this requires that they attribute the favors of Allah, glorified is He, which overflow upon them, to their partners, and deny that they come from Allah, exalted is He. Or it means: in that they reject such compelling proofs after Allah has bestowed them upon them. The *ba'* (the particle "with") is for *tadmin* (implying a meaning), where denial (*al-judud*) is given the meaning of disbelief (*al-kufr*), as in His saying: ﴿and they denied them﴾. The *fa'* is for coordinating with an implied clause, and it is included in meaning in relation to the verb. That is: "Do they associate partners with Him and thereby deny His favor?" It is also read as *tajhadun* (with the second person), meaning: "Are the masters not the ones returning the provision to their *mamalik*? Rather, I am the One who provides for them and for those whom they own, so let them not think that they give them anything. It is only My provision which I cause to flow through their hands. Thus they are all equal in this, and the masters have no superiority over their *mamalik*." Do they not understand this, so that they deny the favor of Allah? This is a rejection of the claim of those who favored (themselves), or of their action which indicates that claim. Or it means: "Are those who are favored not returning some of their excess to their *mamalik*, so that they become equal in it all? Yet favoring them is only so that He may test them: whether they will be grateful or disbelieve?" Do they not know this, so that they deny the favor of Allah, exalted is He? It is as if it were said: "So they did not return it to them." The nominal sentence (*al-jumla al-ismiyya*) indicates the continuation of their failure to return it.

It is related from Abu Dhar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "They are your brothers, so clothe them with what you wear, and feed them with what you eat." After that, his slave was never seen except that his cloak was his cloak, and his lower garment was his lower garment, without any difference.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 72:

﴿And God has made for you, from your own selves,﴾ (p-128) that is: from your own kind, ﴿spouses﴾ so that you may find comfort in them, and by that establish all your interests, and so that your children may be like you. It has also been said: this refers to the creation of Hawwa' (Eve) from the rib of Adam, upon him be peace. ﴿And has made for you, from your spouses,﴾ the apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun, to signal that what is meant is that He made for each of you, from his own spouse, and not from the spouse of another.

﴿sons﴾ and that the outcome of spouses is procreation. ﴿And grandchildren (hafadah)﴾ is the plural of hafid, who is one who hastens in service and obedience. From this is the saying of the devout (al-qanit): "And to You we hasten and serve (nahfid)," meaning: He made for you servants who hasten in your service and obedience. It has been said: what is meant by them is the children's children. It has also been said: the daughters, and He expressed them by this to signal the aspect of favour, since they serve the houses with the most complete service. It has also been said: the children of the wife from a previous husband. It has also been said: the sons, and the conjunction is because the two descriptions differ. It has also been said: the sons-in-law (al-akhtan) over the daughters. The placing of the accusative (mansub) after the genitive (majrur) in both positions is for the sake of the suspense (al-tashwiq) mentioned earlier, and the placing of the genitive with the preposition "li" before the genitive with "min" signals from the outset that the benefit of the making returns to them, as a support for the suspense and a strengthening of it. That is: He made for your benefit, from what suits you, spouses, and He made for your advantage, from a direction suitable to you, sons and grandchildren.

﴿And provided for you from the good things﴾ from delights, or from the lawful things. The "min" here is partitive, since what is provided in this world is a model of what is in the Hereafter. ﴿Will they then believe in falsehood?﴾ namely, that the idols benefit them, and that the bahira and the like are forbidden. The "fa" (then) in meaning is attached to the verb, and it serves as a conjunction upon an implied premise, meaning: Will they disbelieve in God, Who is characterised by this, and so believe in falsehood? Or, after the certainty of what has been mentioned of God's blessings, will they believe in falsehood rather than in God, glorified is He? ﴿And in the blessing of God﴾ the Exalted, which overflows upon them from what has been mentioned and from what the scope of exposition cannot encompass ﴿they disbelieve﴾, in that they attribute it to the idols. The placing of the relative complement before the verb is for emphasis, or to suggest exclusivity as an intensification, or for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawasil). The shift to the third person (al-iltifat ila al-ghaybah) signals that their condition deserves turning away from them, and the address is turned to others among the listeners, marvelling at them for what they have done.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 73:

﴿And they worship besides Allah﴾ This is probably a conjunction with "they disbelieve" (yakfurun), falling under the reproachful rhetorical denunciation. That is: "Do they disbelieve in the blessing of Allah and worship besides Him?"

﴿that which possesses no provision for them from the heavens and the earth, any [amount]﴾ If al-rizq (provision) is taken as a verbal noun (masdar), then shay'an (any [amount]) is in the accusative as its object, meaning: it has no power to provide them with anything, neither rain from the heavens nor vegetation from the earth. If al-rizq is taken as a name for the thing provided, then shay'an is in the accusative as a substitute for it (badal), in the sense of "a little." Min al-samawat wal-ard (from the heavens and the earth) is a qualifier of rizqan, meaning: existing from them both. It is also permissible for it to be an emphasis of la yamliku (it does not possess), meaning: it does not possess any provision, any portion of dominion.

﴿And they are not able﴾ to possess it, since they have no ability at all, for they are lifeless matter with no movement in them. So the pronoun refers to the idols. It is also permissible for it to refer to the disbelievers, in the sense that they, despite being living beings who dispose of affairs, are not able to do any of that; how then [could one expect it] of inanimate matter that has no perception?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 74:

﴿So do not strike forth similitudes for Allah﴾. This is a shift to direct address, to signal the importance of the prohibition. That is, do not associate anything with Him. Expressing this by "striking similitudes" aims at the prohibition of associating anything with Him, exalted is He, in any of His affairs, for the basis of striking a similitude (darb al-mathal) is comparing one state with another and one story with another. That is, do not liken any of His affairs to anything else. The "lam" here is like it in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah strikes a similitude for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah﴾, ﴿and Allah strikes a similitude for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh﴾, but not like it in His saying: ﴿and strike for them a similitude: the people of the town﴾, and its like. The "fa" (so) indicates that the prohibition follows from the blessings enumerated that overflow upon them from Him, glory be to Him, and that what they associate with Him is far from possessing for them any provision whatsoever from the regions of the heavens and the earth, let alone what has been detailed of the blessing of creation, the preference in provision, and the blessing of spouses and children.

﴿Indeed, Allah knows﴾: this is the reason for the aforementioned prohibition and a warning against what is forbidden. That is, He, the Exalted, knows the true nature of what you do and what you leave, and that it is of utmost magnitude and ugliness, ﴿while you do not know﴾ that, for otherwise you would not have done it. Or, He, the Exalted, knows the true nature of things, while you do not know it; so leave your opinions and stand in positions of obedience to what has come to you of commands and prohibitions. It is also possible that the meaning is: "So do not strike similitudes for Allah; indeed, Allah knows how similitudes are to be struck, while you do not know that, so you fall into what you fall into of the abysses of ruin and error." Then He taught them the manner of striking similitudes in this matter, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 75:

﴿God strikes an example﴾, i.e., He mentions and presents something (*mathal*, an example or parable) from which one may infer the vast difference in condition between His exalted Majesty and what they associate with Him, and the distance between the two, such that it loudly proclaims the corruption of what they have committed. ﴿A slave owned, who has no power over anything﴾ is an apposition (*badal*) to *mathalan* and an explanation of it. The *mathal* is in reality his condition that befalls him of being owned and of complete incapacity. In accordance with this, He struck himself as the example. He described the slave as "owned" to distinguish him from the free person, since both are servants of God, glorified is He, and it is implicitly included that all are His servants, exalted is He. He described him as having no power to distinguish him from the *mukatab* (a slave contracted to purchase his freedom) and the *ma'dhun* (a slave licensed to trade), who have some disposal in general. The beginning with an ambiguous example and then its explanation by what is mentioned conveys a grandeur and eloquence that is not hidden.

﴿And one whom We have provided﴾: *man* is a qualifying relative, coordinated with *'abdan*. That is, We have provided him by way of ownership. The shift to the first person plural (*iltifat*, a shift in grammatical person) serves to indicate the difference between the two states: the striking of the example and the provision.

﴿from Us﴾: from Our great and exalted presence, ﴿a good provision﴾: lawful and pure, or praiseworthy and approved by people. ﴿So he spends from it﴾ out of grace and kindness. The *fa'* (then) indicates the sequence of spending upon provision, as if it were said: "And one whom We have provided with a good provision from Us, and so he spent." The choice of the nominal sentence with a verbal predicate, as in the noble composition, is to indicate the constancy and continuity of spending, renewed over time.

﴿secretly and openly﴾: i.e., in the state of secrecy and openness, or spending in secret and spending openly. The purpose is to show the generality of his spending across all times, and the inclusiveness of his bounty toward those who shun accepting it openly. It also points to the various kinds of God's outward and inward blessings. The placement of "secretly" before "openly" signals His favor upon him. The departure from matching the two counterparts by saying "and a free man who owns wealth," although this would have indicated more clearly the difference in condition between him and his counterpart, is to aim at establishing the truth that free persons too are under the yoke of His servitude, glorified and exalted is He, and that their ownership of what they possess is only by God, exalted is He, granting it to them without any contribution on their part. This is with an effort to intensify the indication of what the example was meant to show, namely the difference in condition between the two compared parties. For if the owned slave is not like the owning slave, then what is your opinion of the inanimate?! And of the Owner of the Kingdom, the Creator of the worlds.

﴿Are they equal?﴾ The pronoun is in the plural to indicate that what is mentioned refers to those who possess the described qualities from the two mentioned categories, not to two specific individuals from them. That is: are the slaves and the free persons who possess the mentioned attributes equal? Yet both groups are equal in being human and created by God, glorified is He, and what the free persons spend is not something in whose creation or ownership they have any part; rather it is something God, exalted is He, has given them. Since the two groups are not equal, what then is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds, when you associate with Him that which has no humiliation more abject than itself, namely the idols?

﴿Praise be to God﴾: i.e., all praise belongs to Him, because He is the source of all blessings, and no one other than Him deserves it, even if it appears through the hands of some intermediaries, let alone the deserving of worship. In this is guidance to what is true: that whatever appears through the hand of one who spends from what has been mentioned is traced back to God, glorified is He, as His saying, "We have provided him," alluded to. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ what has been mentioned, so they attribute God's blessings to others and worship them on account of these blessings. The negation of knowledge from most of them indicates that some of them do know this, but they do not act upon its requirement out of obstinacy, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They recognize God's blessing, then they deny it, and most of them are disbelievers﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 76:

﴿And Allah strikes a parable﴾ That is: another parable, which indicates what the previous parable indicated, but in a clearer and more manifest manner. Having left this vague, so that the soul would await its coming and anticipate it until it settles firmly within it upon its arrival, He explained it, saying: ﴿two men, one of them dumb﴾, meaning one who was born mute, ﴿who has no power over anything﴾ of the things related to himself or to others, whether by guesswork or by insight, due to the scantiness of his understanding and the poorness of his perception.

﴿And he is a burden﴾, a weight and a dependent, ﴿upon his master﴾, upon the one who supports him and takes charge of his affairs. This is an explanation of his inability to manage his own interests, after mention of his inability over anything at all. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿wherever he directs him﴾, that is, wherever his master sends him on some matter, is an explanation of his inability to accomplish his master's interests, even if they are a minor interest. It was also read in the passive voice, and in the form of the past tense of "tawajjaha" (to turn/direct).

﴿He brings no good﴾, no success and no sufficiency in any important matter whatsoever.

﴿Is he equal﴾ together with what he has of the aforementioned attributes ﴿and one who commands justice﴾, that is: one who is articulate, so he is a person of sound opinion, sufficiency and right guidance, who benefits people by urging them to justice, which gathers all the virtues, ﴿and he﴾ in himself, together with what has been mentioned of his general benefit to the particular and the general.

﴿Upon a straight path﴾. The contrasting of the aforementioned attributes with these two descriptions is because they lie at the very core of what opposes them: the sum of the aforementioned attributes is the lack of deserving to be commanded, and the essence of these two is the deserving of complete commanding authority, which entails the possession of all good qualities together. The change of style, in that He did not say "and the other commands justice," etc., is to observe the suitability between it and what is intended, namely the explanation of the contrast between the two comparisons. Know that neither of the two verbs is meant to narrate a past striking of a parable; rather, what is meant is the creation of it through what is mentioned after it. It is not far-fetched to say that Allah, exalted is He, struck a parable by creating the two groups as they are, so their creation was as such in order to infer, from their non-equality, the impossibility of equality between Him, glorified is He, and what they associate with Him. Thus each of the two verbs would be a narration of a past striking.

(p-131) ﴿And to Allah﴾ exclusively, not to anyone else, either independently or in partnership, belongs ﴿the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾. That is, the matters hidden from the knowledge of all created beings, such that there is no way for them to reach it, neither by witnessing nor by inference. The sense of the idafa (annexation) to them both is connection to them, either in terms of occurring within them, whether presently or eventually, or in terms of being absent from their inhabitants. The purpose is to show that the unseen is exclusive to Him, Exalted, in respect of knowability, as the title "the unseen" indicates, not in respect of creatureliness and being owned, although the matter is so in reality as well. In this there is an indication that His, glorified be He, knowledge is ḥuḍūrī (presential, direct). For the actualization of the unseens in themselves is knowledge in relation to Him, Exalted. For this reason, it did not say, "And to Allah belongs the knowledge of the unseen of the heavens and the earth."

﴿And the matter of the Hour﴾, which is the greatest of the unseens connected to them both about which disputes have arisen, in terms of its being hidden from their inhabitants, or in terms of the appearance of its effects in them at the time of its occurrence. For the exact time of its occurrence is among the unseens specific to Him, glorified be He, although its being instantaneous is among the unseens for which proofs have been established. That is, its matter in speed of coming is ﴿nothing but like the blink of an eye﴾, that is, like the return of the glance from the top of the pupil to its bottom, ﴿or it is nearer﴾, that is, rather its matter in what has been mentioned is ﴿nearer﴾ than that, and quicker in time, by occurring within a part of its time. For that, although it is shorter than an instantaneous motion which has a continuous identity coinciding with a time that has an identity, is likewise divisible into parts which are also times. Rather, it occurs in an indivisible instant of that time, which is the instant of the beginning of that motion. Or, its matter is nothing but like the thing which is regarded as near, and it is said, "It is like the blink of an eye," or "It is nearer." In any case, this is a figure of speech for the swiftness of its coming, as it was expressed at the opening of the noble surah with the word "coming": ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾. And among things is that He brings it as swiftly as possible, so He is capable of that. Or, the matter of the establishment of the Hour, whose essence and modality are among the unseens specific to Him, glorified be He, is the causing of the living to die and the raising of the dead from the first and the last, and the transformation of the forms of all existence. The deniers have denied it and have regarded it as among what does not fall within possibility in speed of occurrence and ease of accomplishment, except "like the blink of an eye," or "it is nearer," according to the two aspects already mentioned. ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾, so He is capable of that without doubt.

It has also been said: "The unseen of the heavens and the earth" is an expression for the Day of Resurrection itself, because His knowledge of its particulars is hidden from their inhabitants. So He placed "the Hour" in the place of the pronoun to strengthen the content of the sentence.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 78:

﴿And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah made for you from yourselves spouses﴾, and it is aligned with it in the string of proofs for monotheism (tawhid), along with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah sent down water from the sky﴾, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah created you﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has favoured some of you over others﴾. And "al-ummahat" (the mothers) is with a damma on the hamza. It has also been read with a kasra, as the plural of "al-umm" (the mother), with a hා added to it, just as the hа was added in "ahraqa" (to spill) for "araqa" (to spill), and its addition in the singular is anomalous, as in the verse:

﴿Ummahati Khindif wa-l-Yas abi﴾ (My mother is Khindif, and al-Yas is my father).

﴿You know nothing﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: not knowing anything at all.

﴿And He made for you hearing, sight and hearts﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "akhrajakum" (He brought you forth). It does not indicate that the mentioned making was after the bringing forth, because the implication of the particle "wa" (and) is mere togetherness in general, not sequence. Moreover, the effect of that making does not appear before the bringing forth. That is, He made these things for you as instruments through which you obtain knowledge and understanding, by your senses perceiving the particulars of things, and by your hearts (af'idah) comprehending them, and by your becoming aware of the agreements and differences among them through repeated sensation; thus there arise for you self-evident knowledges (ʿulum badihiyya), by considering which you are able to acquire acquired knowledges (ʿulum kasbiyya). The "af'idah" is the plural of "fu'ad": it is the middle of the heart, and it stands to the heart as the heart stands to the breasts, and it is among the plurals of paucity (jumu' al-qilla) which have taken the place of the plurals of abundance. The fronting of the prepositional phrase over the objects (al-manṣubat) is, as already explained, to signal from the outset that what was made is beneficial to them, and to arouse the soul's longing for what is delayed, so that it settles more firmly upon arrival.

﴿So that you may give thanks﴾: so that you may recognise the blessings bestowed upon you, one state after another, and thus give thanks for them. The fronting of hearing over sight is because it is the means of receiving revelation; or because its perception is earlier than the perception of sight. Its being singular is in view of it being a verbal noun (masdar) in origin.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 79:

﴿Have they not seen﴾. It is also read with the ta' (as "Have you not seen," tara).

﴿At the birds﴾, the plural of ṭā'ir (bird), i.e., have they not looked at them, ﴿made subservient﴾, made submissive to flying by means of the wings created for them and the causes that assist them in it. There is an intensification here, in that the meaning of taskhīr (subjugation, taskhir) is making a thing compliant to another which disposes of it as it wishes, like the subjugation of the sea, the ship, and the beasts for man. What occurs here is the subjugation of the air to the birds, so that they fly in it as they wish, whereas the natural disposition of the bird would be to fall. So God, exalted is He, subjected them to flying. In this there is a reminder that flying is not the natural disposition of the bird, but rather that it is by God's subjugation, exalted is He.

﴿In the expanse of the sky﴾, i.e., in the air that is distant from the earth; and the ṣukāk (the heavens of the fixed stars) and the tablet (al-lawḥ) are further away than it. Its being attributed to the sky is because it is on its side from the viewpoint of the observer, and to display the perfection of power.

﴿Nothing holds them up﴾ in the air when they fold their wings, spread them, and remain poised.

﴿Except God﴾, mighty and majestic, by His vast power, for the heaviness of their bodies and the thinness of the substance of the air would require their falling; there is no support from above them, nor prop from beneath them. This (phrase) is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the hidden pronoun in ﴿subservient﴾, or from the birds, or it is a resumptive (independent) statement.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, which was mentioned of the subjugation of the birds to flying, in that He created them with a nature by which they are enabled to do it, in that He made for them light wings and similarly tails, and made their bodies so light that when they spread their wings and tails, the heaviness of their bodies would not be borne by the thin-substanced air beneath them, and they pierce the air in front of them, because they do not meet it with a large mass.

﴿Are signs﴾, manifest, ﴿for a people who believe﴾, i.e., it is fitting for them to believe. He specified this for them only because they are the ones who benefit from it.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 80:

﴿And God has made for you﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to what preceded. The placing of ﴿for you﴾ before what follows, namely the prepositional phrase and the object, serves to indicate from the outset that this is for their benefit and advantage, and to arouse the soul's eagerness for what is to come. The words of the Exalted: ﴿from your houses﴾, that is, from your familiar houses which you build of stone and clay, specify that thing which was vaguely mentioned as made, and emphasize the eagerness mentioned before. ﴿Shelter﴾ (sakan) is an noun in the sense of a passive participle (fa'al bi-ma'na maf'ul), meaning a place in which you dwell at the time of your residence. Or [it means] that you find rest in it without it moving from its place, that is, He made some of your houses such that you find rest in them and are at peace with them.

﴿And He made for you from the hides of cattle houses﴾, that is, other houses different from your familiar houses, namely tents, domes, pavilions, and tent-cloths, ﴿which you find light﴾, that is, you find them light and easy to handle.

﴿On the day of your departure﴾, that is, at the time of your travelling, in dismantling, loading, and transporting. It is also read with the letter ʿayn vowelled with a fatha (ẓaʿnikum). ﴿And on the day of your settling﴾, that is, at the time of your alighting, in pitching and erecting. ﴿And from their wool, their fur, and their hair﴾ is conjoined to the words of the Exalted: ﴿from the hides﴾. The pronouns refer to the cattle in a way of classification, that is, He made for you from the wool of sheep, the fur of camels, and the hair of goats, ﴿furnishings﴾, that is, household goods. Its root meaning is abundance and gathering; from it comes "thick hair" (sha'r athif).

﴿And provision﴾, that is, something enjoyed in every kind of enjoyment, ﴿for a time﴾, until you fulfil your needs from it, or until it wears out and perishes, for it is subject to decay and extinction. It has been said: until you die. The discussion of the ordering of the objects is like what has passed before.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 81:

﴿And Allah has made for you, of what He has created, shade﴾ (made) without any effort on your part, ﴿shade﴾: things under which you seek shade from the heat, such as clouds, trees, mountains and other things. He, glorified is He, bestowed this favour because those lands are predominantly hot. ﴿And He has made for you, among the mountains, shelters﴾: places to dwell in, such as caves, cavities and clefts. The discussion of the order between the objects (mafa'il) is like that which has passed more than once. ﴿And He has made for you garments﴾: the plural of sirbal, which is anything worn; that is, He made for you clothing of cotton, linen, wool and other materials, ﴿that protect you from the heat﴾. He specified heat by mention, being content with mentioning one of the two opposites over mentioning the other; or because protection from it is the most important to them, as has passed just before. ﴿And garments﴾ of coats of mail and body armour, ﴿that protect you from your violence﴾; that is, the violence that reaches some of you from others in war, from striking and thrusting. Allah, glorified is He, has indeed bestowed His favour upon us by mentioning all His bounties overflowing upon all the groups, beginning with what concerns the resident, when He said: ﴿And Allah has made for you, from your houses, a dwelling﴾. Then with what concerns the travellers who have the ability to obtain tents and the like, when He said: ﴿And He has made for you, from the skins of livestock﴾... etc. Then with what encompasses those who are not able to do that and for whom only shade shelters, when He said: ﴿He has made for you, of what He has created, shade﴾... etc. Then with what is indispensable for everyone, when He said: ﴿And He has made for you garments﴾... etc. Then with what is indispensable in wars, when He said: ﴿And garments that protect you from your violence﴾. Then He said: ﴿Thus﴾; that is, like that complete perfection ﴿He completes His favour upon you, that you may submit﴾; that is, in order that you may reflect upon what He has bestowed upon you of favours, the apparent, the hidden, the those within yourselves and those of the horizons, so that you know the right of the One who bestows them, and thus believe in Him alone, abandon what you were associating with Him, and submit to His command. The singular "favour" is either because what is meant by it is the verbal noun, or to show that this, in relation to the majesty of His side, is a small thing. It is also read "you may be safe" (taslamun); that is, you may be safe from punishment or from polytheism. It has been said: from wounds, by wearing armour.

"﴿Then if they turn away﴾ is a past-tense verb used in the manner of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), and turning the address away from them to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is a consolation to him. That is: if they turn away from Islam and do not accept from you what has been delivered to them of clear proofs, lessons and admonitions, ﴿then upon you is only the clear conveyance﴾, that is: there is no shortcoming on your part, since your duty is conveyance that is made plain, or clear. You have done it to the fullest extent, so this is of the kind of placing the cause in the position of the effect (wad' al-sabab mawdi' al-musabbab)."

(p-134) ﴿They recognize the blessing of Allah﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining that their turning away and their aversion from Islam is not due to their being wholly ignorant of the blessings of Allah Most High that have been enumerated, for they do recognize them and acknowledge that they come from Allah Most High. ﴿Then they deny it﴾ through their deeds, in that they worship other than its Bestower, or through their saying that it is by the intercession of our gods, or that it is due to such-and-such a cause. It has also been said: the blessing of Allah Most High is the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ); they recognized it through the miracles, as they recognize their own sons, and then they denied it out of obstinacy. The meaning of "then" (thumma) is to express the improbability of denial after recognition, because the due response of one who has known a blessing is to acknowledge it, not to deny it. The attribution of recognition, and of the denial that follows from it, to the pronoun of the polytheists in an unrestricted manner belongs to the category of attributing the state of some to all, like their saying: "The sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," when the killer is only one of them; for some of them are not like this. This is confirmed by His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿and most of them are the disbelievers﴾, that is, those who deny in their hearts, not those who acknowledge what has been mentioned. The judgment against them as disbelievers in an absolute sense, which indicates completeness in terms of quantity, does not contradict the completeness of the first group in terms of quality. This is it. It has been said that the mention of "most" is either because some of them did not recognize (it) due to deficiency of intellect, or negligence in reflection, or because the proof had not been established against them, since they had not reached the age of legal responsibility. So reflect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 84:

﴿And on the Day We raise up from every nation a witness﴾ who bears witness for them with faith and obedience, and against them with disbelief and disobedience; and this witness is their Prophet. ﴿Then permission will not be given to those who disbelieved﴾ to make excuses, since they have no excuse. And "thumma" (then) indicates that their being tested by being prevented from making excuses, which indicates total despair, is, when it is said to them, ﴿Be gone into it, and do not speak to Me﴾, more severe and more grievous than their being tested by the testimony of the prophets, peace be upon them, against them.

﴿Nor will they be made to seek to please [their Lord]﴾: yastaʿtabūn means they will be asked to be pleased, i.e., it will not be said to them, "Satisfy your Lord," since the Hereafter is the abode of recompense, not the abode of action. The accusative of the time-adverb (al-zarf) is governed by an implied verb whose estimated form is "remember," or "warn them of the Day when We raise up ... etc." Or [it is governed by] "on the Day We raise up," [meaning] there will befall them what befalls them, of that which cannot be described. Likewise the saying of the Most High:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 85:

﴿When those who did wrong see the punishment﴾ which they deserve for their wrongdoing, namely the punishment of Jahannam (Hell), ﴿it will not be lightened for them﴾ in that, ﴿nor will they be given respite﴾; that is, they will not be granted a reprieve. Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, it will come upon them suddenly, and it will confound them﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 86:

﴿And when those who associated partners (with Allah) see their partners⁠—﴾ those whom they used to worship in the world, and they are either the idols or the devils who shared with them in disbelief by inciting them to it, and accompanied them in error and misguidance.

﴿They will say: "Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to call upon besides You."﴾ That is: we used to worship them or obey them. Perhaps they said this hoping to distribute the punishment among them, as indicated by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Then they will throw at them the word: "Indeed, you are liars."﴾ That is, their partners. Their denial of what they said is only for self-defense and to escape the harm of its implication. They denied them although they had been worshipping them and obeying them, because the idols were not pleased with their worship of them. So it is as if their worship was not worship of them, as the angels, peace be upon them, said, but rather they were worshipping the jinn, meaning that the jinn were the ones who were pleased with their worship, not us. Or they denied them in calling them partners and gods, to glorify Allah, exalted is He, above having a partner. And the devils, although they were pleased with being worshipped by them, did not compel them to it by force or coercion, as Iblis said: ﴿And I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me.﴾ So it is as if they were saying: "You did not truly worship us; rather you were only worshipping your own desires."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 87:

﴿And they will proffer submission﴾, that is, those who associated partners (with God), ﴿to God on that day﴾, ﴿the submission﴾, meaning surrender and submission to His mighty, dominant judgment, after their arrogance toward it in the world. ﴿And what they used to fabricate will be lost to them﴾, that is, it will perish and become void: [the claim] that God, glory be to Him, has partners, and that these would help them and intercede for them. This will be when [those partners] deny them and disown them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 88:

﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ within themselves, ﴿and bar﴾ others ﴿from the way of Allah﴾ by preventing them from Islam and driving them toward disbelief, ﴿We shall increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾ which they deserved because of their disbelief. It has been said: in the increase of their punishment there are serpents like the Bukht camels (Bukht: a large breed of camel with long necks), and scorpions like mules, one sting of which makes its victim feel its venom (ḥummah) for forty autumns. And it has been said: they will be brought out of the Fire to the Zamharir (an extreme cold), and out of the intensity of the cold they will hasten back to the Fire.

﴿Because they used to spread corruption﴾ is connected to His saying: "We shall increase them," meaning: We shall increase their punishment because of their persistence in corruption, which is the barring mentioned.

﴿And [mention] the day We raise up⁠﻿ ﴾ repeats what has already been mentioned, reinforcing the warning, ﴿in every nation a witness against them﴾, that is, a prophet.

﴿from among themselves﴾, that is, of their own kind, to cut off their excuse. The words ﴿against them﴾ indicate that the testimony of their prophets over their nations will take place in their presence. ﴿And We bring you﴾: the word *ji'na* (we bring) is chosen over *ba'atha* (we raise up) to show full concern for his (ﷺ) status, and the past tense form is used to indicate that the event is certain to occur.

﴿a witness over these﴾: over the nations and their witnesses, as in His saying: ﴿How then, when We bring from every nation a witness, and We bring you as a witness over these?﴾ It has been said that it means over your nation. The adverbial phrase (*zarf*) has an omitted governing verb, as mentioned earlier. What is meant is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And We sent down to you the Book﴾, the complete Book in its quality as a book, deserving to be designated by the generic name (*ism al-jins*). This clause is either a new sentence (*isti'naf*) or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) with *qad* implied.

﴿an explanation﴾: an eloquent explanation ﴿of all things﴾ that relate to the affairs of the religion. Among these are the circumstances of the nations with their prophets, peace be upon them, so that it serves as evidence that he (ﷺ) is a witness over them. Likewise, among its contents is what this noble verse reports about the raising of the witnesses and the raising of him (ﷺ) as a witness over them, peace and blessings be upon them.

*Tibyan* is like *tilqa'* in having a kasra on its first letter (*tibyan* with a kasra, like *tilqa'*). Its being an explanation of all things of the religion's affairs is understood in the sense that it contains explicit statements on some of them and refers others to the Sunnah (the prophetic practice), since he was commanded to follow the Prophet (ﷺ) and obey him. It has been said concerning this: ﴿nor does he speak from [his own] desire﴾. It also encourages *ijma'* (scholarly consensus). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) approved for his community following his companions when he said: "My companions are like the stars; whichever of them you follow, you will be guided." They exerted effort (*ijtihad*), applied analogy (*qiyas*, reasoning by analogy), and trod the paths of *ijtihad*. Thus the Sunnah, the consensus, and analogy are all grounded in the explanation (*tibyan*) of the Book. What is somewhat obscure in some parts does not detract from its being an explanation, for the intensive form (*mubalaghah*) is with respect to quantity, not quality. As it has been said concerning His saying: ﴿and I am not one who wrongs the servants﴾, that it is from your saying: "So-and-so is a wrongdoer to his servants" and "a great wrongdoer to his servants." From it is His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿and the wrongdoers have no helpers﴾.

﴿and guidance and mercy﴾ for the worlds. The deprivation of disbelievers from the benefits of its effects arises from their own neglect, not from the Book itself.

﴿and good tidings for the Muslims﴾ specifically, or all of that is specific to them, since they are the ones who benefit from it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 90:

﴿Indeed, Allah commands﴾ i.e., in what He sent down as an exposition of everything, and as guidance, mercy and good tidings for the Muslims. The use of the present-tense form here, and in what follows, is to convey renewal and continuity.

﴿justice﴾ by observing the mean between the two extremes of excess and deficiency. It is the head of all virtues, under which falls the virtue of the rational faculty, the angelic (malakiyyah) faculty, namely wisdom (hikmah), which is the mean between cunning (al-harmazah) and dullness (al-baladah); and the virtue of the appetitive faculty, the bestial (bahimiyyah) faculty, namely chastity (iffah), which is the mean between profligacy (al-khala'ah) and torpor (al-khumud); and the virtue of the irascible faculty, the predatory (sab'iyyah) faculty, namely courage (shaja'ah), which is the mean between recklessness (al-tahawwur) and cowardice (al-jubn). Among the doctrinal wisdoms is tawhid, which is the mean between denial (al-ta'til) and associating partners (al-tashrik). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that justice is tawhid. And the doctrine of acquisition (kasb), which is the mean between compulsion (jabr) and predestination (qadar). Among the practical wisdoms is worship through performing the obligations, which is the mean between idleness (al-batalah) and monasticism (al-tarahhub). Among the moral wisdoms is generosity, which is the mean between miserliness (al-bukhl) and extravagance (al-tabdhir).

﴿and excellence (ihsan)﴾ i.e., doing what He has commanded in the proper manner. This is either in terms of quantity, such as voluntary supererogatory acts, or in terms of quality, as indicated by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Ihsan is that you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you."

﴿and giving to the kinsfolk﴾ i.e., giving relatives what they need. This is a specification after a generalisation, out of concern for its importance.

﴿and He forbids indecency﴾ excess in following the appetitive faculty, such as fornication, for example.

﴿and wrongdoing﴾ what is deemed reprehensible by the Shari'ah or by reason, from excess in displaying the effects of the irascible faculty.

﴿and transgression (al-baghy)﴾ haughtiness and domination over people, and tyrannising over them. It is among the effects of the satanic illusory faculty, which results from the two vices of the aforementioned faculties, the appetitive and the irascible. There is no evil among human beings except that it falls under these categories, proceeding from them through these three faculties. For this reason Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It is the most comprehensive verse in the Qur'an for good and evil, and had there been no other in it but this noble verse, it would have sufficed for it being an exposition of everything, and guidance."

﴿He admonishes you﴾ by what He commands and forbids. This is either a resumptive clause, or a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronouns in the two verbs.

﴿that you may take heed﴾ as a hope, meaning: that you may be admonished by that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 91:

﴿And fulfil the covenant of God﴾ is: the pledge of allegiance (bay'ah) to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), for it is a pledge of allegiance to God, glorified is He, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to God﴾.

﴿When you have made a covenant﴾ means: observe the limits of what you have covenanted with God, and pledged to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

(p-137) ﴿And do not break oaths﴾ which you swear at the time of the covenant.

﴿after their confirmation﴾, as is customary during covenants, not that the prohibition is restricted to and specific to confirmation. ﴿And you have indeed made God your surety over you﴾, meaning a witness and an overseer, for the surety (kafil) takes account of the state of the one for whom he stands surety and safeguards it. ﴿Indeed God knows what you do﴾ of breaking oaths and covenants, and so He will requite you for that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 92:

﴿And do not be⦆ in what you do of breaking (the oath), 

﴿like her who unravelled her yarn﴾ i.e., what she spun, the noun being used in the sense of the object (spun), ﴿after it had been made strong﴾: the phrase is connected to "unravelled", i.e., like the woman who unravelled her yarn after its twisting and firm binding.

﴿into threads﴾: strands whose twist had been undone. It is the plural of nikth (a broken strand). Its accusative case is either as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "her yarn", or as a second object of "unravelled", since the verb carries the sense of "made", and the intent is to disparage the state of breaking (the oath) by comparing the one who breaks it to this foolish, witless woman. It is said that she was Rayta bint Sa'd ibn Taym, a simple-minded woman who took a spindle about the length of a forearm, and a small whorl (sinnara), like a finger, and a large round weight (falaka) suited to her size. She and her maidservants would spin from dawn until noon, then she would order them, and they would unravel what they had spun.

﴿Taking your oaths as a means of deceit among you﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "do not be", or from the prepositional phrase that stands in the place of the predicate, meaning: being like a woman of such a condition, while you take your oaths as a corruption and a deceit among you. The root of dakhal is what enters into a thing and is not part of it.

﴿That one community should be more numerous﴾: i.e., that a group should be ﴿more in number﴾, i.e., greater in number and more abundant in wealth,

﴿than another community﴾: than another group. That is, do not break faith with a people because of your numbers or their small numbers, or because of the numbers and strength of those who oppose them, as the Quraysh did: when they saw strength among the enemies of their allies, they broke their covenant and allied with their enemies.

﴿Indeed, Allah tests you thereby﴾: i.e., by the fact that one community is more numerous than another. That is, He deals with you by that as one who tests you, to see whether you hold fast to the cord of fidelity to the covenant of Allah and the pledge to His Messenger (ﷺ), or whether you are deceived by the numbers and strength of the Quraysh and the weakness of the believers, judging by outward appearance.

﴿And He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that about which you used to differ﴾: when He recompenses you for your deeds with reward and punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 93:

﴿And if Allah had willed﴾ a willing of compulsion and coercion, ﴿He would have made you one community﴾ agreed upon Islam. ﴿But﴾ He does not will that, because it would conflict with the requirement of wisdom. Rather, ﴿He sends astray whom He wills﴾ by leading him astray, i.e., He creates misguidance in him according to how He directs his partial choice (ikhtiyar juz'i, the particular volition of the servant) toward it, ﴿and guides whom He wills﴾ to guidance according to how He directs his choice toward attaining it. ﴿But you will surely be questioned﴾ all together on the Day of Resurrection ﴿about what you used to do﴾ in the world. This is an allusion to the acquisition (kasb, the human acquisition of actions) that was hinted at, upon which the matter of guidance and misguidance turns.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 94:

(p-138) ﴿And do not take your oaths as a means of deception among yourselves﴾ is an explicit prohibition of it, after the implicit one, as emphasis, as an exaggeration in explaining the ugliness of what is forbidden, and as a preparation for His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿lest a foot slip﴾ from the highway of truth ﴿after it had been firm﴾ upon it, and steadfast in it through faith. The singling out of "foot" and its indefiniteness serve to indicate that the slipping of a single foot, whatever foot it may be, whether honored or disgraced, is a great danger. So how much more so [the slipping of] many feet?! ﴿And you would taste evil﴾, that is, the worldly punishment.

﴿Because you hindered﴾ by your own turning away, or by your hindering others, ﴿from the way of Allah﴾, which encompasses the fulfilling of covenants and oaths, for whoever breaks the pledge of allegiance and apostatizes makes that a precedent for others. ﴿And for you﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿is a great punishment﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 95:

﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah﴾ That is: do not take, in exchange for the covenant of Him, exalted is He, and the pledge of allegiance to His Messenger (ﷺ), or His verses that clearly enjoin the keeping of covenants and oaths, ﴿for a small price﴾. That is: do not substitute for them a trifling goods, namely what the Quraysh used to promise the weak among the Muslims, and stipulate for them in return for apostasy, of the debris of the worldly life.

﴿Indeed, what is with Allah﴾, mighty and majestic is He, of victory, booty, and the reward of the Hereafter, ﴿is better for you﴾ than what they promise you, ﴿if you should know﴾. That is: if you are among the people of knowledge and discernment. And this is a justification of the prohibition in the manner of verification, just as the saying of the Exalted:

﴿What is with you﴾ is a justification for the claim of superiority, presented as a resumptive statement (istiʾnaf). That is, what you enjoy of the delights of this world, however great, [is what you enjoy]. Rather, the world and all that is in it, altogether, ﴿will pass away﴾, however vast its number, and will come to an end, however long its term. ﴿And what is with Allah﴾ of the treasures of His mercy, both worldly and otherworldly, ﴿is lasting﴾, with no passing away for it. As for the otherworldly [mercy], this is evident. As for the worldly [mercy], since it is connected to the otherworldly and follows from it, it is included in the string of "the lasting good deeds." The choice of the nominal form over the present-tense verb indicates permanence, which is obvious. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and We will surely reward﴾, with the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama), by way of iltifāt (a shift of grammatical person, "turning" from the third person to the first), repeats the promise derived from His statement, ﴿What is with Allah is better for you﴾, in the manner of an oath-based emphasis, exaggerating in urging [people] to steadfastness in the religion. The iltifāt away from what the apparent situation would require, namely saying "and We will surely reward you your wage for the best of what you used to do," serves to draw attention to their deeds and to signal that these deeds are the cause of the reward. That is, by Allah, We will surely reward ﴿those who were patient﴾ under the harm of the polytheists and the hardships of Islam, among which is fulfilling covenants, and poverty. It is also read with the yāʾ (third person) without iltifāt. ﴿Their wage﴾ is the second object of "we will reward," that is, We will surely give them their particular wage in return for their patience in the matters mentioned that they were afflicted with.

﴿For the best of what they used to do﴾: that is, We will surely reward them for what they used to do of the aforementioned patience. The word "best" (aḥsan) is attached to it only to indicate the perfection of its excellence, as in His statement, glory be to Him, ﴿and the excellent reward of the Hereafter﴾. It is not intended to restrict the reward to the best part of it to the exclusion of the good part, for that does not occur to anyone, especially after His statement, "their wage," or "We will surely reward them according to the best of their individual deeds mentioned," meaning: We will give them, in return for the lesser instance of their mentioned deeds, what We give in return for the superior instance of them, of abundant reward. It does not mean that We give the reward according to their varying instances in degrees of excellence, by rewarding the good among them with a good reward and the best with the best. In this there is, as is not hidden, a beautiful promise of forgiveness for whatever may befall them within the course of patience of some distress, and their inclusion within the thread of beautiful patience. Or [it means]: We will surely reward them with a reward better than their deeds. As for interpreting it as referring to those of their deeds whose performance is preferred, such as obligatory and recommended acts, or those whose abandonment is also preferred, such as prohibited and disliked acts, [this is unacceptable], since this indicates that these are the basis for reward rather than what is equal in its performance and abandonment, such as permissible acts. This does not fit the context of urging steadfastness in the good deeds in which they are engaged, and encouraging the attainment of their fruits. Rather, it would be a restriction of the vast mercy at a time when its protected domain is being broadened, by excluding some of their deeds from being a basis for reward.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 97:

﴿Whoever does righteous deeds﴾, i.e., a righteous deed (ʿamalan ṣāliḥan). Whatever kind it may be. This is the beginning of exhorting all the believers to every righteous deed, after encouraging a particular group among them to persist in the specific righteous deed they are already engaged in, to repel the misconception that the abundant reward is restricted to them and to their aforementioned deed. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿whether male or female﴾, is an emphasis in declaring that it encompasses everyone. ﴿And he is a believer﴾: He restricted it with this because deeds of disbelievers are not counted toward deserving reward or lightening punishment, owing to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾. The choice of presenting it in a nominal, circumstantial clause rather than arranging it within the relative clause is to convey that it is obligatory for it to continue and to accompany the righteous deed.

﴿We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ in this world: he lives a good life. As for one who is wealthy, this is evident; as for one who is poor, his life is made good by contentment, acceptance of the allotment, and expectation of the great reward, like the fasting person whose day is made pleasant by contemplating the bliss of his night. This is unlike the wicked person: if he is poor, it is evident (that his life is hard); and if he is wealthy, greed and fear of loss do not leave him to enjoy his life.

﴿And We will surely reward them﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿with their reward according to the best of what they used to do﴾, in accordance with how We treat the patient, so there is no trace of repetition in it. The use of the plural in the pronouns referring to the relative pronoun is to observe the sense, just as the singular in what preceded is to observe the wording. The choice of the reverse is because the occurrence of the reward through the mode of collectivity suits plurality, while what falls within the relative clause and what follows from it through the mode of separation and succession suits the singular. Since the matter has reached the point that the basis of the mentioned reward is the goodness and excellence of the deed, the guidance toward what makes the righteous deed excellent and purifies it from the admixture of corruption has been arranged upon it with "fa" (then). So it was said:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 98:**

﴿So when you recite the Qur'an﴾: i.e., when you intend to recite it. He expressed this by the intention, using the metonymy of naming the effect by its cause (*ism al-musabbab 'ala al-sabab*, the naming of a result for its cause), to indicate that what is meant is the intention connected with the recitation.

﴿then seek refuge in Allah﴾: ask Him, whose protection is mighty, to protect you ﴿from the accursed Satan﴾ from his whisperings and his incitements, so that he does not whisper to you during the recitation, for he has an aspiration in that regard. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he wished, Satan cast [something] into his wish...﴾ ...the verse. The address being directed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the singling out of the recitation of the Qur'an from among the righteous deeds for seeking refuge when one intends it, is to alert that this is for others than him (ﷺ); and in all other righteous deeds (p-140) it is more important. For since he (ﷺ) was commanded to do this when reciting the Qur'an, which falsehood does not reach from before it or behind it, then what do you suppose about anyone other than him (ﷺ)?!

As for deeds other than recitation, the command is for recommendation (*nadb*, the recommended status of an act), and this is the position of the majority (*jumhur*, the majority of scholars). According to 'Ata', it is for obligation (*wujub*). He took the apparent meaning of the noble wording, and so Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), Malik, Ibn Sirin, Dawud, and Hamzah, among the reciters, sought refuge immediately after recitation.

From Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): "I recited to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and I said: I seek refuge in the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan. He (ﷺ) said: Say, I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan." Thus Jibril (peace be upon him) recited it to me from the Pen, from the Preserved Tablet.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 99:

﴿Innahu﴾ The pronoun refers either to the matter (al-sha'n, the pronoun of the situation) or to Satan.

﴿Laysa lahu sultan﴾ means dominion (tasallut) and authority (wilaya) ﴿over those who believe and upon their Lord they rely﴾, that is: to Him they entrust their affairs, and in Him they seek refuge in everything they do and everything they leave undone. For his whispering does not affect them, and his call is not answered by them.

The choice of the past tense form in the first clause (al-sadd al-mādī, "those who believe") indicates certainty (al-tahaqquq), just as the choice of the future/present form in the second, ﴿yatawakkalun﴾, indicates continuous renewal (al-istimrar al-tajaddudi). In mentioning the attribute of Lordship (wasf al-rububiyya) there is a noble promise by repeating the word "those who rely" (al-mutawakkilin). The clause is a justification (ta'lil) for the command to seek refuge, or for its implied answer (jawabihi al-manwi), meaning: "He will protect you" or something similar.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 100:

﴿Verily, his authority﴾ means: his domination and his dominion through his call, which is followed by compliance, not his authority by compulsion and coercion. For that is negated concerning both groups, as stated in His words, glorified is He, quoting him: ﴿And I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me﴾. This is made explicit by His words, exalted is He: ﴿over those who take him as an ally﴾, meaning: who adopt him as a patron, respond to his call, and obey him, for the one who is compelled is far removed from all of that. ﴿And those who are, because of Him﴾, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿associators﴾, or, because of Satan, are associators, since it is he who drove them to associate others with God, glorified is He. The restriction of his authority to them, following its negation regarding the believers who put their trust [in God], is evidence that there is no intermediary in external reality between trusting in God, exalted is He, and taking Satan as an ally, even though there is an intermediary in concept. Whoever does not put his trust in Him, exalted is He, is included among those who take Satan as an ally without realizing it, since by this the reasoning is completed. Therefore there is emphasis in urging trust [in God] and warning against its opposite. The choice of the verbal nominal sentence in the first relative clause, to indicate continuous renewal as previously mentioned, and the choice of the nominal sentence in the second, to indicate permanence, is similar. The repetition of the relative pronoun is to guard against the assumption that the second clause is circumstantial, implying that non-polytheist allies of Satan do not come under his authority. The first clause is placed before the second, which corresponds to the first clause earlier, in order to observe the comparison between them and what corresponds to them of trust in God, exalted is He. Had the earlier order been observed, each of the two connecting phrases would have been separated from what corresponds to it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 101:

﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another verse﴾ That is: when We send down a verse of the Qur'an in place of a verse of it, and make it a replacement for it, by abrogating it (naskh) with it.

﴿And Allah knows best what He sends down﴾ at first and at last, and that each of these, wherever it is revealed, is revealed only in accordance with what wisdom (hikmah) and benefit (maslahah) require, for every time has its own requirement, different from the requirement of another time. How many a benefit at one time turns into a harm at another time, and vice versa, because of the changing of the circumstances that call for it. Sacred laws (shara'i') are nothing but benefits for the servants in this life and the Hereafter, turning as the benefits turn. The clause is either parenthetical (mu'taridah), serving to rebuke the disbelievers and to alert them to the corruption of their opinion. In the shift to the third person (al-iltifat ila al-ghaybah) with the report attributed to the Majestic Name, which comprises all the attributes, there is a clear inculcation of awe and a confirmation of the meaning of the parenthetical clause. Or it is a circumstantial clause (haliyyah).

It is also read with the lighter form from inzal (tukhfif min al-inzal): ﴿They say﴾ That is: the disbelievers, who are ignorant of the wisdom of abrogation, ﴿Indeed you are only a fabricator (muftari)﴾ That is: one who invents lies against Allah the Exalted, commanding something and then, when a new view appears to you, forbidding it. The reporting of this saying from them here serves to indicate that this disbelief arises from the prompting of the devils, and that they are their ally.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾ That is: they do not act upon anything at all; or they do not know that in abrogation there are far-reaching wisdoms. The attribution of this judgment to most of them is because some of them know it, but deny it out of obstinacy.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 102:**

﴿Say: He has sent it down﴾: that is, the Qur'an, which is indicated by the verse.

﴿the Holy Spirit﴾ means Gabriel, peace be upon him; that is, the Spirit purified from human impurities. The attribution of "the Spirit" to "the Holy" (al-Quds), which is purity, is like the attribution of Hatim to generosity (al-Jud), where it is said "Hatim of generosity," for the sake of emphasizing that quality, as if it were his very nature. The form of the verb (taf'il) in both places indicates that gradualness in the revelation is something required by perfect wisdoms. ﴿from your Lord﴾: in the attribution of the Lord to his pronoun, peace and blessings be upon him, there is an indication of establishing the outpouring of the effects of lordship upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, which is not present in attributing it to the first-person pronoun "ya" (of the speaker), which is built upon pure instruction.

﴿with truth﴾: that is, accompanied by the established truth which accords with the wisdom that requires it, in such a way that it never departs from it, whether in revelation or abrogation. In this there is an indication that abrogation (naskh) is true.

﴿to strengthen those who believe﴾ in faith, by [the knowledge] that it is the speech of Him, the Exalted. For when they hear the abrogating (nasikh) text and reflect upon what it contains of the consideration of interests appropriate to the situation, their beliefs become firmly established and their hearts are reassured. It has been read as (li-yuthbita), from the form of if'al.

﴿and as guidance and good tidings for those who submit﴾ to His command, the Exalted; these two are conjoined to the grammatical position (mahall) of li-yuthabbita, that is: as firm establishment, guidance, and good tidings. In this there is an allusion to the occurrence of the opposites of the aforementioned matters for those other than them among the disbelievers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 103:

﴿And We know that they say﴾ other than the hideous saying reported from them.

﴿Only a human teaches him﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿a human being﴾, in a categorical manner, although it is evident that the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus) sent it down to him, peace be upon him. The sentence is adorned with various forms of emphasis (funun al-ta'kid) to confirm the threat it contains. The use of the present-future form (sigha al-istiqbal) indicates the continuity of the knowledge in accordance with the renewed continuity of its object, for they are continually uttering that monstrous claim, meaning by it Jabr the Roman, the slave of Amir ibn al-Hadrami. It was said: Jabr and Yasir, who were making swords in Mecca and reading the Torah and the Gospel, and the Messenger ﷺ would pass by them and hear what they were reciting. It was said: 'Abis, the slave of Huwaytib ibn Abd al-'Uzza, who had embraced Islam and who was a possessor of books. It was said: Salman al-Farisi. The name of the one they claimed was teaching him was not stated, although naming him would have been more effective in exposing their lie. This indicates that the basis of their discourse is not attributing to him, peace be upon him, learning from a specific person, but from a human being, whoever he might be, along with the fact that he, peace be upon him, was a mine of the knowledge of the first and the last.

﴿The tongue of the one they incline toward is foreign﴾. Ilhad (inclination, deviation) comes from alhada al-qabr, when one makes the digging of the grave deviate from straightness, so he digs in one side of it. The term was then borrowed for every deviation from straightness, so they say: alhada fulan fi qawlihi (so-and-so deviated in his speech) and alhada fi dinihi (he deviated in his religion). That is, the language of the man toward whom they incline the speech away from straightness is foreign and not clear. It was also read with a fath on the ya and the ha', and with the definite article on lisan. ﴿And this﴾, that is, the noble Qur'an, ﴿is a clear Arabic tongue﴾, possessing eloquence and fluency. The two sentences are resumed to refute their slander, and the explanation is this: the Qur'an is miraculous in its composition just as it is miraculous in its meaning. If you claim that a human teaches him its meaning, how could that human teach him this composition, which has rendered all the people of the world incapable? And clinging, in the midst of the slander, to the hem of such feeble fables is proof of their complete incapacity.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 104:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah﴾ That is: they do not affirm that they are from Allah. Rather, they say about them what they say, calling them at one time "fabrication" (ifira') and at another time "tales of the ancients" (asatir) "taught by a human" (mu'allamatan min al-bashar).

﴿Allah will not guide them﴾ to the truth, or to the path of salvation, with a guidance that leads to the desired goal, because He knows that they do not deserve that due to the wretchedness of their condition. ﴿And for them﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿is a painful punishment﴾. This is a threat to them and a warning concerning their disbelief in the signs of Allah the Exalted, and their ascribing to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fabrication and being taught by a human, after removing their doubt and refuting their accusation.

Only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah fabricate lies. This is a rejection of their saying, "You are only a fabricator," and a turning of the charge back on them, by showing that they are the fabricators, after rejecting the claim with the affirmation that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah through Rūḥ al-Quds (the Holy Spirit). The verse "And We certainly know..." ... was placed between the two statements because of how closely it is connected to the first rejection, as is well known. The meaning is: Allah the Exalted knows best that the fabricator is the one who denies the signs of Allah and says that they are a fabrication and something taught by a human being. That is, denying them in the manner mentioned is fabrication in the true sense, because its reality is lying. Judging that what is the speech of Allah the Exalted is not His speech, in being a lie and a fabrication, is like judging that what is not the speech of Allah the Exalted is His speech. The explicit mention of "lying" serves to emphasize its ugliness. The imperfect form (muḍāriʿ, the present/imperfect verb) is used to maintain correspondence between it and what it expresses, namely their saying, "they do not believe." It has been said: the meaning is that one who fabricates lies is fitting for one who does not believe in the signs of Allah, because he does not fear punishment for it so as to be restrained from them. As for one who believes in them and fears the punishment they speak of, fabrication can never at all proceed from him.

﴿And they﴾, those described by what was mentioned of not believing in the signs of Allah, ﴿are the liars﴾ in the true sense, or they are the most complete in lying, since there is no greater lie than denying His signs and disparaging them with such falsehoods. The secret of this is that simple lying, which is reporting the non-occurrence of what has actually occurred by the creation of Allah the Exalted, or reporting the occurrence of what did not occur in that way, is only an opposition to Allah the Exalted in His act. Denial is an opposition to Him, glory be to Him, both in His act and in His speech that reports it together. Or, "those whose habit is lying" are those whom no restraint of religion or honor holds back from it. It has been said: "the liars" refers to their saying, "You are only a fabricator."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 106:

﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah﴾, i.e., utters the word of disbelief, ﴿after his belief﴾ in Him, the Exalted. This is the beginning of a statement explaining the condition (p-143) of whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah after having believed in them, following the explanation of the condition of whoever does not believe in them at all. "Man" (من) is a relative pronoun, and its position is nominative as the subject (mubtada'), with the predicate omitted because the predicate that follows indicates it; or it is the predicate for both of them together; or it is in the accusative on the basis of censure.

﴿Except one who is compelled﴾ to that by something he fears for his own self or for one of his limbs. This is an exception connected to the ruling of wrath and punishment, or to the censure; because disbelief linguistically is completed by speech, as has been indicated. And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿while his heart is at rest with faith﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the one excepted, and its governing element is the disbelief that occurs under compulsion, not the compulsion itself; because the heart's being at rest with faith alongside the compulsion is of no benefit, whereas what is beneficial is its being alongside the disbelief that is uttered under it. That is: except one who disbelieves under compulsion from the one who compels him, and he is compelled and so disbelieves, while his heart is at rest with faith, his creed having not changed. He did not state it explicitly as an indication that it is not truly disbelief. In this is evidence that faith is assent of the heart.

﴿But whoever﴾ is not so, rather ﴿opens his breast to disbelief﴾, i.e., he believed in it and was content with it in his soul.

﴿Upon them is wrath﴾ great, whose true nature cannot be grasped, ﴿from Allah﴾. The explicit mention of the glorious Name is to cultivate awe and to strengthen the magnification of the punishment. ﴿And for them is a great punishment﴾, since there is no crime greater than their crime. The plural in the two pronouns in the genitive case is for regard of the meaning, just as the singular in the hidden pronoun in the relative clause is for regard of the wording.

It was narrated that "the Quraysh compelled 'Ammar and his parents, Yasir and Sumayyah, to apostasy. His parents refused, so they tied Sumayyah between two camels, and she was struck with a spear in her private part, and they said: 'She only embraced Islam for the sake of men.' So they killed her and killed Yasir, and they were the first two martyrs in Islam. As for 'Ammar, he gave them with his tongue what they had compelled him to say. It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, 'Ammar has disbelieved.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Never! 'Ammar is filled with faith from his head to his feet, and faith has mixed with his flesh and blood.' 'Ammar came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) weeping, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began wiping his eyes and said: 'What is wrong with you? If they return to you, then return to them with what you said.'"

This is evidence for the permissibility of uttering a word of disbelief under an overpowering compulsion, although it is better to avoid it in order to honour the religion, as his parents did. It was narrated that "Musaylimah the liar seized two men, and said to one of them: 'What do you say about Muhammad?' He said: 'He is the Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'What do you say about me?' He said: 'You too.' So he released him. And he said to the other: 'What do you say about Muhammad?' He said: 'He is the Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'What do you say about me?' He said: 'I am deaf.' He repeated it three times, and he repeated his answer. This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'As for the first, he took the concession; as for the second, he proclaimed the truth.'"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 107:

﴿That﴾ is a reference to disbelief after faith, or to the threat mentioned earlier, ﴿because﴾ on account of the fact that ﴿they preferred (istahabbu) the worldly life﴾, chose it ﴿over the Hereafter﴾, ﴿and that Allah does not guide﴾ to faith, and to what necessitates steadfastness in it, with a guidance of compulsion and coercion, ﴿the disbelieving people﴾ in His all-encompassing knowledge, so He does not protect them from deviation and what leads to it of anger and great punishment. ﴿And had it not been for one of the two matters﴾: either the preference of the worldly life over the Hereafter, or Allah the Glorified not guiding the disbelievers with a guidance of compulsion, [namely], that they preferred the Hereafter over the world, or that Allah the Exalted guided them with a guidance of compulsion, ﴿that would not have been the case﴾. But the second is contrary to wisdom, and the first is not among the things that fall within the realm of occurrence. And to this He alluded with His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Those﴾, i.e., those characterized by the abominations mentioned, ﴿whose hearts, hearing, and sight Allah has sealed﴾, so that they refuse to perceive the truth and to reflect upon it.

﴿And those are the heedless﴾, i.e., the complete ones in heedlessness, for there is no greater heedlessness than heedlessness of considering the consequences.

Translation:

﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they are the losers﴾ because they squandered their lives and spent them on that which leads to nothing but everlasting punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 110:
