﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated﴾ to the abode of Islam, and they are ʿAmmar and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, meaning: for them, with guardianship and victory, not against them, as the apparent state of their previous deeds would necessitate. So the prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa-al-majrur) is the predicate of "inna" (indeed). It is also permissible for its predicate to be omitted, the subsequent predicate indicating it. It is also permissible that this be its predicate, with the second "inna" being an emphasis of the first. And "thumma" (then) is for indicating the great distance between the rank of their present state and the rank of their state that is conveyed by the exception from merely leaving the judgment of wrath and punishment, by way of allusion, not the rank of the state of the disbelievers.

﴿After they had been tried﴾, meaning: they were tortured for apostasy and uttered what would satisfy them, while their hearts were at rest with faith. It is also read with the verb in the active voice, meaning: they (the disbelievers) tortured the believers, like the Hadrami whose master forced him by compulsion until he apostatized, then he embraced Islam and emigrated. ﴿Then they struggled﴾ in the way of Allah ﴿and were patient﴾ over the hardships of struggle. ﴿Indeed your Lord, after it﴾, after the emigration, the struggle, and the patience, is a clarification of what the construction of the judgment upon the relative pronoun conveyed of the causal relation of the relative clause to it, or, after the aforementioned trial, it is for explaining that this does not disrupt the judgment.

﴿Surely He is Forgiving﴾ of what they did before, ﴿Merciful﴾, bestowing favours upon them as a reward for what they did afterward. In the mention of the title of Lordship in both places there is an indication of the cause of the judgment. In the attribution of the Lord to his pronoun, peace be upon him, while the effect is manifest in the aforementioned group, there is a showing of the perfection of kindness toward him, peace be upon him, and an indication that the outpouring of the effects of lordship upon them, of forgiveness and mercy, is through him, peace be upon him, and because they are his followers.

**﴿The Day when every soul comes﴾** is in the accusative, governed by **raḥīm** (the Merciful) in the verse, or by what is ordered after it, or by **al-dhikr** (the mention). The Day in question is the Day of Resurrection, **﴿the Day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾**.

**﴿pleading for itself﴾**: on its own behalf. It strives to secure its own deliverance through excuses, not caring about the affairs of others, so it says: "Myself, myself!"

**﴿and every soul will be paid in full﴾**: that is, it will be given in full and complete measure **﴿for what it did﴾**, meaning the recompense for what it did. This is an instance of **majāz mursal** (metonymy), using the name of the cause for the effect, to indicate the complete connection between the recompenses and the deeds. The use of the explicit noun instead of a pronoun (**iẓhār** instead of **iḍmār**) serves to increase the emphasis, and to signal that the time of the pleading and the time of the full payment differ, even though both occur on the same day.

**﴿and they will not be wronged﴾**: their rewards will not be diminished, or they will not be punished without cause, and their punishment will not be increased beyond their sins.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 112:

﴿And Allah sets forth a parable: a town﴾ It has been said: ḍarb al-mathal (striking a parable) means making it and fashioning it (ṣun'uhu wa'timāluhu). Its verification has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah. It does not transitively take more than one object, and it is only made to take two because it includes the meaning of ja'l (making/rendering). The postponement of "qaryatan" (a town), although it is the first object (mafʿūl awwal), is so that the second object does not come between it and its attribute and what follows from it, since postponing it from the whole is detrimental to the interlocking of the parts of the composition and its mutual responsiveness. Also, postponing what by right should be placed first produces in the soul an anticipation of its arrival and a longing for it, especially when the preceding part contains something that calls to it. For a parable calls to preserving the details of the states of that which is the parable, so the postponed element, upon its arrival, settles in them with greater firmness. "Qaryah" (town) is either a specific one among the bygone peoples, or one that is supposed (muqaddarah), meaning: He made it a parable for the people of Makkah specifically, or for every people upon whom Allah the Exalted bestowed blessings, and the blessing made them insolent, so they did what they did, whereupon Allah the Exalted replaced their blessing with retribution. The people of Makkah entered among them by primary entry.

﴿It was secure﴾ possessing security from every fear, ﴿tranquil﴾ nothing disturbing its people, ﴿its provision came to it﴾ the sustenance of its people. This is a second attribute of "qaryah"; the change of its construction from the first attribute is because the coming of its provision is renewed, whereas its being secure and tranquil is established and continuous. ﴿abundantly﴾ widely, ﴿from every place﴾ from its various quarters. ﴿Then it denied﴾ i.e., its people denied ﴿the favours of Allah﴾ i.e., His blessings, the plural of ni'mah with the ta' dropped in counting, like dir' and adru', or the plural of nu'm, like bu's and ab'us. What is meant by them is the blessing of provision and continuous security. The choice of the plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah) is to signal that the denial of a small blessing, since it required this punishment, then what do you think of denying many blessings? ﴿So Allah made it taste﴾ i.e., made its people taste ﴿the garment of hunger and fear﴾. The effect of hunger and fear, and their harm encompassing them, is likened to a garment covering the one who wears it, so its name is borrowed for it, and the tasting (idhāqah), borrowed for the general meaning of reaching, is attributed to it, indicating the intensity of the affliction, with what it contains of the combination of the perceptions of touch and taste, by way of tajrīd (abstraction). Because of the prevalence of its use in that sense and its frequent circulation on tongues, it has become like a literal usage, as in the verse of Kuthayyir:

"Abundant of mantle; when he smiles laughing,
The necks of wealth are shackled by his laughter."

For ghamr (abundance), although in reality it is one of the states of abundant water, when it was frequently used of the good (ma'ruf) likened to abundant water, it took the status of a literal usage, so its attribution to the mantle, borrowed for goodness, becomes tajrīd. Or it likened their effect and harm, in terms of encompassing them and their aversion to them, at one time to the garment covering the wearer, suitable for fear by the common factor of encompassing and necessity, a likeness of an intelligible to a sensible, so its name is borrowed for it by explicit metaphor (isti'ārah taṣrīḥiyyah); and at another time to the taste of bitter, repellent bitterness, suitable for the hunger arising from the loss of provision, by the common factor of aversion. So it was indicated by attaching to it the tasting, borrowed for the conveying of harms, indicating the intensity of the affliction, with what it contains of the combination of the perceptions of touch and taste. The placing of hunger, arising from the loss of provision mentioned, before fear, which follows the loss of the security mentioned earlier before the coming of provision, is because it is more suitable to tasting, or to observe the contrast between it and the coming of provision. It has also been read with fear placed first, and also with its accusative case, as a conjunction upon the genitive-attached noun, or as a substitute standing in place of an omitted genitive, its original being: "and the garment of fear."

﴿with what they used to do﴾ before, or in the sense of continuity. This is the denial mentioned. He attributed that to the people of the town to verify the matter after attributing the denial to it, and placing the tasting upon it, intending exaggeration. In the form of the verb "ṣun'ah" (making/doing) there is an indication that the denial of a blessing had become a firmly established craft for them and a practiced custom.

﴿وَلَقَدْ جاءَهُمْ﴾ (And certainly there came to them) is part of the parable. It is brought to show that what they did, namely their ingratitude for the blessings, was not merely an affront to the matter of reason alone, but was also an opposition to God's proof upon creation. That is: certainly there came to the people of that town ﴿a messenger from among themselves﴾, meaning one of their own kind, whom they knew by his lineage and descent. He informed them of the obligation to give thanks for the blessing, and warned them of the evil outcome of what they did and what they neglected.

﴿Then they denied him﴾ in his mission, or in what he informed them of among the matters mentioned. The "fa'" here is the *fa' fasiha* (the "fa'" of eloquent expression, which indicates an implied omitted condition), and the omission of the object of the denial signals that they hastened to deny him without any hesitation.

﴿So the punishment seized them﴾, the one that uproots their root, after they had tasted a portion of that.

﴿While they were wrongdoers﴾, meaning while they were in the state of being entangled in the wrongdoing they were upon, which is the ingratitude for God's blessings and the denial of His Messenger, not refraining from it despite having tasted its preceding deterrents. This indicates their persistence in disbelief and obstinacy, and their transgression of every customary limit in this. The arrangement of the punishment upon the denial of the Messenger proceeded according to God's practice, as His saying, glorified is He, indicates: ﴿And We never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾. With this the parable is completed, for the condition of the people of Mecca, whether the parable was struck for them specifically or for all who follow their course, corresponds exactly to the condition of the people of that town, step for step, with no difference between them, even in a single distinct trait. How could it not be so, when they were in a secure sanctuary, ﴿while people were being snatched away from around them﴾, and not a shadow of fear passed through their minds, and the fruits of everything were brought to them? Indeed a messenger came to them from among themselves, and what a messenger, before whose exalted rank the intellects are bewildered (ﷺ). Through the alternation of the south wind and the north wind (a line of poetry, "what the south wind and the north wind have not altered"), they disbelieved in God's blessings and denied His Messenger (ﷺ), so God made them taste the garment of hunger and fear. This happened when He afflicted them in response to his supplication (ﷺ), by his saying: "O God, help me against them with seven years like the seven years of Joseph." There befell them a severe drought and a famine that consumed everything, until they were compelled to eat carrion, dead dogs, burnt bones, and *al-'ilhiz* (a term for the hair of camels or similar animals treated with blood, eaten in extreme hunger). The earth became too narrow for them despite its vastness, because of the expeditions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), for they used to raid their livestock, their caravans, and their trade convoys. Then on the day of Badr He inflicted upon them the punishment that He inflicted. This is what the context requires and what the good arrangement of the discourse calls for. As for what most of the commentators have agreed upon, that the pronoun in His saying, exalted is He, "And certainly there came to them" refers to the people of Mecca, since He mentioned their condition explicitly after mentioning their parable, and that by "the Messenger" is meant Muhammad, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and by "the punishment" is meant what befell them of drought and the battle of Badr, then this is far from verification, how could it not be, when His saying, glorified is He:

﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾ ? It is a consequence drawn from the result of the parable (tamthil), and a deterrence for them from what would lead to a similar end. The meaning: Since the condition of those who disbelieved in the blessings of Allah, denied His Messenger, and what befell them because of that of the calamities, both worldly and otherwise, first and last, has become clear to you, then desist from what you are upon of ingratitude for blessings and denial of the Messenger (ﷺ), lest there befall you the like of what befell them. Recognize the due of Allah's blessings, obey His Messenger (ﷺ) in his command and prohibition, and eat from the provision of Allah being ﴿lawful and good﴾, and leave what you fabricate of forbidding the baheera and the like. ﴿And give thanks for the blessing of Allah﴾: recognize its due, and do not meet it with ingratitude. The "fa" (so) in meaning falls upon the command to give thanks, and it was introduced upon the command to eat because eating is a means (dhari'a) to thanks. So it is as if it were said: give thanks for the blessing of Allah after eating it, lawful and good. The prohibition against claiming prohibition has been embedded (idmaj) within it. There is no doubt that this is only conceivable when the uprooting punishment was still expected, its beginnings having been laid down. But after what has occurred has occurred, who is it that would forbid, and who is it that would be commanded to eat and give thanks? Interpreting His words, ﴿So the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers﴾, as information about that before it occurred is refuted by the undertaking of their reform through command and prohibition, and by directing the address of the command to eat to the believers (p-147), although what follows of the address of prohibition is directed to the disbelievers, as al-Wahidi did when he said: "So eat, you, O assembly of believers, of what Allah has provided you of the spoils," which is not fitting to the dignity of the noble revelation.

﴿If you are indeed those who worship Him﴾, i.e., obey Him; or, if your claim that you intend by worshipping the gods the worship of Him, exalted is He, is true.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 115:

﴿Indeed, He has forbidden you only carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which any name other than Allah's has been invoked.﴾ This is a justification (ta'lil) for the permissibility of what He commanded them to eat from what He had provided for them. That is: He has forbidden only these things, not what you claim to be forbidden, such as the baha'ir (she-camels whose ears were slit), the sawa'ib (animals released for the idols), and the like.

﴿Then whoever is compelled﴾ by the necessity that befalls him and so consumes some of that, ﴿neither desiring it nor transgressing﴾, that is, [neither desiring it] over another compelled person.

﴿Nor exceeding﴾, that is, going beyond the measure of necessity, ﴿indeed your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, that is, He will not hold him to account for that. Its cause has been put in place of it (fa-uqima sababuhu maqamahu). The mention of the attribute of Lordship (al-rububiyya) hints at the reason for the ruling, and the addition of the pronoun referring to him (ﷺ) shows the perfection of gentleness toward him (ﷺ). The opening of the sentence with innama (indeed... only) serves to restrict the prohibited things to the four categories, except what is joined to them, such as beasts of prey and domestic donkeys. Then he emphasised this by forbidding forbidding and permitting according to their own whims, saying:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 116:**

﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely,﴾ "al-lam" (the lam) is a redundant particle (silah), like its use in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead"﴾. That is, do not say, concerning what your tongues describe of the livestock as lawful and unlawful, in your saying: ﴿What is in the wombs of these cattle is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives﴾, without that description being based on observation and reflection, let alone being grounded in revelation or in an analogy built upon it. ﴿The lie﴾ is in the accusative governed by "do not say." His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"This is lawful and this is unlawful"﴾, is an apposition (badal) to it. It is also permissible that it be connected to "describe" (tasif), with the implied meaning of "saying": that is, "Do not say concerning what your tongues describe, so that it says, 'This is lawful, and this is unlawful.'" It is also possible that the implied saying is a circumstantial clause (hal) from their tongues, meaning: "saying, 'This is lawful...' etc." It is also permissible that "the lie" be in the accusative governed by "describe," and that "This is lawful... etc." be connected to "do not say." In that case "al-lam" is for causation (ta'lil), and ma is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). That is: "Do not say, 'This is lawful, and this is unlawful,' because of your tongues' description of the lie," meaning: do not make lawful or unlawful merely because your tongues describe the lie and portray it in an attractive form and adorn it to the ears, as if their tongues, being the source of falsehood and the wellspring of false speech, were a person who knows its reality, encompasses its truth, and describes it to people, defining it in the clearest description and most manifest definition, by way of metaphor expressed through metonymy (isti'arah bil-kinayah), as one says: "His face describes beauty," and "His eye describes magic." It has also been read with the genitive (bil-jarr) as a qualifier (sifah) of ma together with what follows it, as if it were said: "Because of their describing the lie," in the sense of "the lying one," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with false blood﴾. The intended meaning of "description" is their tongues' describing the livestock as lawful and unlawful. It has also been read as "al-Kudhub," the plural of "kadhub," in the nominative as a qualifier of "the tongues," and in the accusative as a term of abuse (shatm), or in the sense of "false words" (al-kalim al-kawadhib). Or it is the plural of "al-kaddhab" from their saying "kadhaba kadhiban," as mentioned by Ibn Jinni.

﴿So that you may fabricate against Allah the lie﴾ (p-148). For the basis of lawfulness and unlawfulness is nothing but the command of Allah, exalted is He. Thus, ruling on lawfulness and unlawfulness is an attribution of lawmaking and prohibiting to Allah, glory be to Him, without it originating from Him. "Al-lam" is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah).

﴿Indeed, those who fabricate against Allah the lie﴾ concerning any matter of affairs ﴿will not prosper﴾, meaning they will not attain their aims for which they committed the fabrication in order to attain them.

"A little enjoyment" is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: their benefit in what they are upon of the deeds of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) is a little benefit.

"And for them" in the Hereafter "is a painful punishment" whose true nature cannot be fathomed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 118:

﴿And for those who were Jews﴾, specifically, to the exclusion of others, from among the earlier and the later peoples, ﴿We forbade what We have related to you﴾, i.e., by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We forbade every animal with claws, and of the cattle and sheep We forbade them their fat﴾ ... the verse.

﴿Before﴾ is connected either to ﴿related﴾ or to ﴿forbade﴾. It confirms what preceded concerning the restriction of the prohibited things to what was detailed, by refuting the Jews' fabrication that contradicts it and their denial of it in this regard. For they used to say, "We were not the first to whom it was forbidden; it was only forbidden to Noah, Abraham, and those after them, until the matter reached us."

﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ by that prohibition, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾, in that they did what they were punished for, as indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾ ... the verse. And His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel forbade himself before the Torah was revealed. Say: Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful﴾, silenced them completely. It is narrated that when the Prophet (ﷺ) said this to them, they were confounded and did not dare to bring out the Torah. How could they, when it clearly explains that the prohibition of what was forbidden to them from the good things was because of their wrongdoing and their transgression, as a punishment and an aggravation, in the clearest explanation? And in this there is an alert to the distinction between them and others in the prohibition.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 119:

﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who did evil in ignorance﴾. That is: because of ignorance, or while being characterized by it, so that the ignorance encompasses ignorance of God, of His punishment, and of not reflecting on the consequences, due to the dominance of desire and evil, which encompasses fabricating lies against God, the Exalted, and other than Him.

﴿Then they repented after that﴾, that is: after what they did, and the explicit statement of it, together with the indication of "then" (thumma) on it, is for emphasis and intensification.

﴿And amended﴾, that is: they amended their deeds, or they entered into righteousness.

﴿Indeed your Lord, after it﴾, after the repentance, ﴿is Forgiving﴾ of that evil, ﴿Merciful﴾, who rewards obedience to Him, whether by abstention or by action. The repetition of His saying, the Exalted, "Indeed your Lord" (inna rabbaka), is for the emphasis of the promise and the showing of the complete care in fulfilling it. The mention of the attribute of lordship (rububiyya) together with its addition to his pronoun (ﷺ), while the effect is manifest in those who repent, is to allude to the fact that the outpouring of the effects of lordship, namely forgiveness and mercy upon them, is through his intercession (ﷺ), and through their being among his followers, as has been indicated previously.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 120:

﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation﴾, on his own, because he possessed human virtues that are scarcely found except scattered among a large community, as it has been said:

*"It is not strange for God to gather the whole world into one person."*

He was the leader of the people of monotheism (tawhid) and the model for the people of verification (tahqiq). He disputed with the people of polytheism (shirk) and silenced them with clear proofs that leave nothing behind and spare nothing, and he refuted their deviant doctrines with decisive arguments and crushing evidence. Or, because he (ﷺ) was a believer alone while all the people were disbelievers. It has also been said that *ummah* here is a form (*fu'lah*) with the meaning of a passive participle (*maf'ul*), like *ruhlah* (a chosen mount for travel) and *nukhbah* (a select group), from *amma-hu* when one intends him, or follows him, because people used to seek him out and take his way as a model, in accordance with God's words, ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader for the people﴾. The mention of him (ﷺ) directly after the refutation of the doctrines of the polytheists, their polytheism, their criticism of prophethood, and their prohibition of what God had made lawful, serves to indicate that the truth of the religion of Islam, and the falsity of polytheism and its branches, is a settled matter beyond any doubt.

﴿Devoted to God﴾, obedient to Him, standing by His command. ﴿Upright (ḥanīf)﴾, inclining away from every false religion toward the true religion, never departing from it in any way.

﴿And he was not among the polytheists﴾ in any matter of their religion, in its fundamentals or its branches. He stated this explicitly despite its being evident, not only as a rebuttal to the Quraysh disbelievers in their saying, "We are upon the creed of our father Abraham," but also against the Jews, who are polytheists by their saying, ﴿Ezra is the son of God﴾, in their fabrication and their claim that he (peace be upon him) was upon what they themselves were upon. This is like His words, glorified is He: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was an upright Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists﴾. By this, the matter of mentioning the prohibition and the Sabbath, both before and after it, is coherently arranged.

Shākiran li-an'umihi (thankful for His blessings) is a third attribute of the ummah. The form of the plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah) was chosen to signal that he, peace be upon him, would not neglect giving thanks for even a small blessing, so how much more for a great one! It is also to make clear that he, peace be upon him, was contrary to what they were upon in terms of disbelief in the blessings of God, Exalted is He, as explained by way of the parable.

﴿Ijtabāhu﴾ (He chose him) for prophethood, ﴿wa-hadāhu ilā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm﴾ (and guided him to a straight path), one that leads to Him, glory be to Him, and it is the religion of Islam. The result of this guidance is not merely his, peace be upon him, own being guided, but also the guidance of creation, with the help of the indication of the choosing.

**﴿And We gave him good in this world﴾**: a good state of remembrance and praise among all people, to the extent that there is no community of any religion but that they take him as their ally. It was also said: it is the close friendship (khullah) and prophethood. And it was said: it is the words of one of us who prays, "as You blessed Abraham." The shift (iltifat, a change in grammatical person) to the first person plural ("We") serves to show the complete care given to his station and the exaltation of his rank, upon him be blessings and peace.

**﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾**: among the people of the high ranks in Paradise, according to his prayer when he said: **﴿And join me with the righteous﴾** [26:83] **﴿And grant me a true tongue among the later generations﴾** [26:84] **﴿And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss﴾** [26:85].

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 123:

﴿Then We revealed to you﴾ along with the elevation of your rank and the loftiness of your station, ﴿that follow the religion (millah) of Ibrahim﴾. The millah (religion, community-law; a term meaning) is a name for what Allah the Exalted prescribed for His servants through the tongue of the prophets, peace be upon them, from amlaltu al-kitab (I dictated the book) when you dictate it. It is the very same as the din (religion), but considered with respect to obedience to it. Its verification is that the divine ordinance, whenever it is ascribed to the one who conveys it from Allah the Exalted, is called millah, and whenever it is ascribed to the one who establishes it and acts upon it, it is called din. Al-Raghib said: The difference between them is that millah is never attributed except to the Prophet (ﷺ), and is hardly ever found attributed to Allah, Glorified is He, nor to individuals of the community, and it is used only for the body of laws as a whole, not for its individual parts. The intended meaning of his millah, peace be upon him, is Islam, which was expressed just before as the straight path. ﴿Hanifan﴾ (p-150) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the genitive noun (mudaf ilayhi), because the mudaf, owing to its close connection with him, peace be upon him, took the place of a part of him; it is therefore counted among the type of: "I saw the face of Hind, standing." What is commanded is following in the fundamentals, not in the laws, which change with the changing ages. The sense of delay in rank conveyed by "thumma" is to indicate that this blessing is among the most excellent blessings bestowed upon him, peace be upon him. ﴿And he was not among the polytheists﴾ is a repetition of what came before, for added emphasis, and an affirmation of his, peace be upon him, freedom from what they hold of belief and practice. And the Exalted's saying:

**﴿Only the Sabbath was made [binding]﴾**, that is, its glorification was made obligatory, devoting oneself to worship on it, and abstaining from hunting in it. This serves to confirm that universal negation [of the Sabbath's place in the religion of Abraham], and to clarify it by refuting what might be thought to undermine its universality, as was already stated in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And to those who were Jews We prohibited...﴾ [Q. 6:146] ... and so on. The Jews used to claim that the Sabbath was one of the rites of Islam, and that Abraham (peace be upon him) observed it. In other words, the Sabbath is not one of the laws (shara'i') of Abraham or among the rites of his creed (millah) that you were commanded to follow, such that there would be some connection in general between him, peace and blessings be upon him, and some of the polytheists. Rather, it was legislated for the Children of Israel after a long period of time.

The use of the verb in the passive voice follows the customs of divine majesty (kibriya'), and signals that there is no need to state the agent explicitly, since attributing it to anyone else is impossible. It has also been read in the active voice [as *ja'ala*, "He made"]. The matter is expressed by "made" (ja'ala) with the preposition "upon" ('ala), and the people are referred to by the relative pronoun with reference to their disagreement. Thus it is said: **"Only the Sabbath was made upon those who differed concerning it"** [Q. 16:124, read in this sense], to indicate that it includes severity and a trial leading to punishment, and that it was made dependent on their disagreement about its status before it occurred, preferring it over what God the Exalted had commanded, and choosing the opposite. However, this is not in the sense that the causality extends to both sides of the disagreement, or that the harm covers both groups; rather, it is in terms of the condition of the origin of the disagreement from the side that opposed the truth. This is because Moses (peace be upon him) commanded the Jews to designate one day of the week for worship, and that this day should be Friday. They refused him and said: "We want the day on which God the Exalted finished creating the heavens and the earth," which is Saturday. Only a small remnant of them had accepted Friday; so God the Exalted permitted them [to observe] Saturday, and tested them by forbidding hunting on it. The ones who accepted Friday obeyed God's command and so did not hunt. But their descendants could not restrain themselves from hunting, so God, glorified is He, transformed them into apes, unlike those obedient ones.

﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them﴾, that is, between the two groups who differed concerning it.

﴿on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾, that is, He will settle the dispute and disagreement between them, and will recompense each group according to what it deserves of reward and punishment. This implies that what happened in this world, namely the transformation of one of the two groups and the deliverance of the other, is, in comparison with what will happen in the Hereafter, a thing of no account. This is what the inimitable nature of the revelation (i'jaz tanzili) calls for.

It has also been said that the meaning is: "Only the consequence of the Sabbath was made upon those who differed concerning it," namely the transformation [into apes], meaning that they permitted hunting in it at one time and forbade it at another. It was incumbent upon them to agree on its prohibition, as God, glorified is He, had commanded. The judgment between them was interpreted as recompense for the difference in their actions, by permitting at one time and forbidding at another.

The reason for mentioning this here is that it is intended as a warning to the polytheists of God the Exalted's wrath upon the disobedient and those who oppose His commands, like the parable of the town that was ungrateful for the blessings of God the Exalted. There is no doubt that the word "between them" ("bayna-hum") in "He will judge" indicates that by judgment is meant the separation of the disagreement between the two groups. And the placement of the account of the transformation between the mention of the Prophet's (ﷺ) command to follow the creed of Abraham (peace be upon him), and his command (ﷺ) to call to it, is of the kind of separating a tree from its bark. So reflect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 125:

﴿Call﴾, meaning: to all of the community to whom you have been sent, all of them. He omitted the object to make it general. Or, "perform the invitation" (al-da'wah), as in their saying "yu'ti wa-yamna'" (he gives and withholds), meaning he performs the act of giving and the act of withholding. Omitting the object here aims at bringing the act itself into existence, indicating that the general invitation needs no specification, and that what is intended is the command to bring it about in a particular manner.

﴿to the way of your Lord﴾: to Islam, which is expressed at one time as "the straight path" and at another as "the religion of Abraham," peace be upon him. In the mention of the title "Lord" (rububiyyah), which indicates ownership (malikiyyah), and in conveying the matter to its fitting perfection step by step, together with the attribution of the Lord to the pronoun of the Prophet (ﷺ) in a context of commanding him to invite the community in a wise manner, and of perfecting them with the rulings of the noble Sharia, there is an indication of showing kindness to him, peace and blessings be upon him, and an allusion to the reason for building the ruling upon this, which is not hidden.

﴿with wisdom﴾, meaning: with a firm and correct statement. It is the proof (dalil) that clarifies the truth and removes doubt.

﴿and good admonition﴾, meaning: persuasive exhortations and beneficial lessons, in a manner in which it is not hidden from them that you are advising them and intend what benefits them. The first is for inviting the elite of the community who seek the realities, and the second is for inviting their common people. It is also possible that what is meant by both is the glorious Qur'an, for it combines both qualities.

﴿and argue with them﴾, meaning: debate with their obstinate opponents.

﴿in the way that is best﴾: in the manner that is the best of the methods of debate and disputation, through gentleness and softness, choosing the easier course, and using widely accepted premises, to calm their agitation and extinguish their flame, as the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him, did.

﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way﴾, which He commanded you to invite creation to, and who has turned away from accepting the truth after witnessing what he witnessed of wisdoms, admonitions, and lessons.

﴿And He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾ to it by that. This is a reason for what was mentioned of the two matters. The meaning is: and God, exalted is He, is most knowing; follow in the invitation and debate the method mentioned, for He, exalted is He, is most knowing of the state of one who does not refrain from error according to his acquired disposition, and of the state of one whose affair will lead to guidance because of the innate good in him. So what He has prescribed for you in the invitation is what wisdom requires, for it is sufficient for guiding those who are guided and removing the excuse of those who go astray. Or, what is upon you is only what has been mentioned of invitation and debate in the best manner, while the attainment of guidance or error, and the recompense for each, belongs to God, glory be to Him, since He is most knowing of who remains in error and who is guided to Him, and He will recompense each of them according to what they deserve. The mention of "those who go astray" first is because the discourse is directed at them. The expression of error in the form of a verb, which indicates occurrence, is because it is a change of the natural disposition (fitrah) of God upon which He created people, and a turning away from the invitation, and that is an accidental matter. This is unlike guidance, which is an expression for steadfastness upon the natural disposition and continuing in accordance with the requirement of the invitation; for this reason it was expressed in the form of a noun, which indicates steadfastness. The repetition of "He is most knowing" is for emphasis, and to indicate the difference between the states of the two known groups and their outcomes of punishment and reward. After he commanded him, peace and blessings be upon him, in what pertains specifically to the matter of the invitation, with what he was commanded in the fitting manner, He followed it with an address that includes him and those who support him, in a matter that encompasses all, and so He said:

﴿And if you retaliate﴾: that is, if you wish to requite, in the manner of the physician's saying to one on a restricted diet: "If you eat, then eat only a little."

﴿then retaliate with the like of that with which you were afflicted﴾: that is, with the like of what was done to you. It is expressed as "punishment" by way of applying the name of the effect to its cause, as in the saying "as you sow, so shall you reap," or by way of *mushakala* (the rhetorical figure of matching one thing to another in wording). The intent is to require the observance of justice with those who oppose them, without transgression, once the dispute has reached fighting and the contention has led to combat. The call that is commanded can hardly be separated from this, and how could it be otherwise, since it entails turning faces away from the idolized directions of worship and bringing necks into a collar that is unfamiliar to them, a collar which pronounces upon them the corruption of what they do and what they leave undone, and the invalidity of a religion in which their forefathers persisted. Their stratagems have been exhausted, their excuses have failed them, the paths of argument and disputation have been blocked against them, and the doors of discussion and dialogue have been shut in their faces.

It has been said: when the Prophet (ﷺ) saw Hamza, may Allah be pleased with him, on the day of Uhud, mutilated, he said: "If Allah grants me victory over them, I will mutilate seventy of them in your place." Then this was revealed, and he expiated for his oath and refrained from what he had intended.

It was also recited as: (وَإنْ عَقَّبْتُمْ فَعَقِّبُوا), that is: "And if you follow up with victory, then follow up with the like of what was done to you, without exceeding it." Although the command indicates permissibility of matching in mutilation without transgression, its restriction by the phrase "and if you retaliate" is an allusive exhortation to pardon. It has been stated explicitly in the more emphatic form: ﴿And if you are patient﴾, that is: refraining from retaliation in kind, ﴿it is indeed better﴾, that is: your patience is better ﴿for you﴾ than victory through retaliation. The words ﴿for those who are patient﴾ are said as praise for them and commendation of them for patience, or as a description of them by a quality that is attained for them when they abandon retaliation. The pronoun may also be taken to refer to patience in general, as indicated by the verb, so that their patience enters into it, just as they themselves enter into the class of the patient by primary inclusion. Then the Prophet, upon him be peace and blessings, was commanded explicitly with what was recommended to others allusively, regarding patience, because he is the most worthy of people of resolute affairs, owing to the increase of his knowledge of the states of Allah, glory be to Him, and the abundance of his trust in Him. Thus it was said:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 127:**

﴿And be patient﴾, meaning: over what befalls you from them of various kinds of pain and harm, and what you witness of their complete aversion from the truth.

﴿And your patience is not except through Allah﴾. This is an exceptive construction lacking its complement (*istithna' mufarragh*, a construction in which the excepted element is not stated explicitly and the sense is supplied by context) taken from the most general category of things. Its meaning: your patience is not accompanied by or joined to anything among things except through Allah, that is, through remembrance of Him, complete absorption in watching over His affairs, and devoting oneself wholly to Him with the full concentration of one's resolve. In this there is consolation for him (ﷺ), and an easing of the hardships of patience for him, and an ennobling of him beyond which there is no greater. Or (it means): except through His manifest will, which rests upon profound wisdoms that lead to praiseworthy outcomes. So the consolation lies in the fact that it includes beautiful ends. It has been said: except through His enabling grace and His help, and in that case it concerns only His facilitating and easing (the matter).

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾, meaning: over the disbelievers, by reason of the despair of their believing in you and following you, like His words: ﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾. It has been said: over the believers and what was done to them. The first (interpretation) is more appropriate to the eloquence of the noble composition.

﴿And do not be in distress﴾. It is read with fath (*ضَيْقٍ*, with a fatha on the *ya'*), and it was also read with kasr (*ضِيقٍ*). Both are dialectal forms, like *al-qawl* and *al-qil*. The meaning: do not be in constriction of the breast and straitness. It is permissible that the first form be a lightened form of *dayyiq* (ضَيِّقٍ), like *hayn* from *hayyin* (هَيْنٍ مِن هَيِّنٍ), meaning: in a constricted matter. ﴿Over what they plot﴾, meaning: over their plotting against you in what is yet to come. The first (phrase) is a prohibition against grief over a sought thing from their side that has already escaped. The second is a prohibition against grief over a feared thing from their side that is yet to come. The prohibition against both, although the absence of both is among the necessary requirements of the patience that is commanded, especially in the first sense, serves to add emphasis and to show complete care for the matter of consolation. Otherwise, would anything of what is sought come to the mind of one who has turned toward Allah, glorified is He, with the very core of his soul, free of every preoccupation other than Him, so that he would be forbidden to grieve over its loss or over something forbidden? How much less (would he be forbidden) to fear its occurrence!?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 16, verse 128:

﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who are mindful of Him (taqwa)﴾. This is a reason (ta'lil) for what preceded of the command and prohibition. By "being with" (al-ma'iyya) is meant the constant support (al-wilaya al-da'ima) with which no trace of anxiety, sorrow, or constriction of the breast hovers around its possessor. What the entry of the word "ma'a" (with) suggests of the God-fearing being the followed party is only that they are the ones who directly practise taqwa. The same applies to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾ and all its counterparts. By "taqwa" is meant its third level (al-martaba al-thalitha), which encompasses what lies beneath it of the level of guarding against shirk and the level of avoiding everything that incurs sin, whether by doing or by omitting. I mean purifying oneself from everything that occupies one's inner self away from the Truth, and devoting oneself wholly to Him with the entirety of one's soul. This is the true taqwa, which inherits His, exalted is He, support (wilayatihi ta'ala), coupled with the glad tidings of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Surely the friends of Allah—no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾. The meaning is: Allah is the Protector (wali) of those who have wholly devoted themselves to Him, and purified themselves of everything that would occupy their inner selves away from Him, so that nothing of what is desired or feared comes to their minds, let alone grief over its loss or fear of its occurrence. This is what is meant by the patience commanded, as indicated, and by it the approximation is achieved and the reasoning is completed, as in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿So be patient; indeed the good end is for the God-fearing﴾, according to one of the two interpretations, as verified in its place. Otherwise, mere guarding against sins would not be the basis for anything of the resolute acts whose abandonment is permitted; how then for the patience referred to and its two companions? Rather, its basis is the aforementioned meaning. It is as if it were said: Indeed Allah is with those who are patient. The noble composition has preferred what it has, for the sake of emphasis in urging patience, by alerting to the fact that it is among the distinctive features of the most exalted of noble attributes and their attendants, just as His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And those who are doers of good (muhsinun)﴾ serves to indicate that it belongs to the category of ihsan, in which competitors compete, as detailed where it is said: ﴿And be patient, for Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good﴾. It has been pointed out that both patience and taqwa are of the kind of ihsan, in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever is mindful and patient—surely Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good﴾. The reality of ihsan is performing deeds in the proper manner, which is its descriptive goodness (husnuha al-wasfi), entailing its essential goodness (husnuha al-dhati). The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, explained it by saying: "That you worship Allah as though you see Him; and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you." The repetition of the relative pronoun serves to indicate that each of the two clauses suffices for His, glorified is He, support, without one being a completion of the other. The first is expressed as a verbal sentence (fi'liyya) to indicate occurrence (huduth), just as the second is expressed as a nominal sentence (ismiyya) to convey that its content is a firmly established disposition of theirs. The placing of taqwa before ihsan is because takhliya (emptying) precedes tahliya (adorning). By the two relatives (al-mawsulayn) is meant either the category of the God-fearing and the doers of good, into which he, peace and blessings be upon him, enters first and foremost; or it is he, peace and blessings be upon him, and those who follow him. He was referred to thus as praise for them and commendation of them with the two beautiful qualities. In this there is an allusion that his conduct, peace and blessings be upon him, entails the community's emulation of him. Like the saying of one who said to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, at the time of condolence:

Be patient, and we shall be patient through you, for the patience of the subjects is by the patience of the head.

From Hirm ibn Hayyan: it was said to him at the time of death: "Make a bequest." He said: "The bequest is only of wealth, but I bequeath to you the final verses of Surah al-Nahl." From the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever recites Surah al-Nahl, Allah the Exalted will not hold him accountable for what He bestowed upon him in the abode of this world; and if he dies on the day or night in which he recites it, he will have the reward of one who died and made a good bequest."

And all praise is due to Allah alone, and blessings and peace upon His Messenger and all his family.
